Bill is a member of the York Rite Bodies in Riverside and also a member
of the Long Beach Scottish Rite Bodies, where he has been honored with the
rank and decoration of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor. He is a
member of the Saint Gabriel Conclave, Red Cross of Constantine, and a
member of both AI Malaikah and EI Bekal Temples, A.A.O.N.M.S. He is the
Representative in California to the Grand Lodge of Delaware; and because
of his special feeling for our youth organizations, one of his most cherished
awards is the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay.
In addition to a devoted Masonic career, Bill has also served his church
and community. He is an ordained Elder of the Calvary Presbyterian Church
in Riverside, having served on the Board of Session; three times as chairman
of the Board of Trustees; Church School Superintendent; and chairman of
the Board of Christian Education. Riverside's Community Hospital is recognized as one of the foremost health care institutions in California, and Bill
served on its Board of Directors from 1961-1963.
During his travels throughout this great jurisdiction, his smiling face and
cheery greetings did much to renew the vigor in our fraternity. His efforts
on behalf of our youth orders will be remembered by our DeMolays, Job's
Daughters, and Rainbow Girls for years to come.
Bill Price's adult life has been characterized by service to others. The
Masons of this great jurisdiction have indeed been fortunate to have had such
a man as our 107th Grand Master. He brought to this office a broad administrative background in the field of business coupled with a rich 23-year
Masonic history. Combine these qualities with a genuine desire to serve others
and we have a Grand Master who has made a deep and lasting impression on
California Freemasonry.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Invocation
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Our Heavenly Father, we come to Thee in this hour with humble hearts, be
Thou our consolation and comfort. By Thy infinite power, make us feel Thy
presence here among us.

"Sometimes I walk in the shadow,
Sometimes in sunlight clear;
But whether in gloom or brightness,
The Lord is very near.
Sometimes I walk in the valley,
Sometimes on the mountain's crest;
But whether on low or highland,
The Lord is manifest.
Sometimes I walk in the desert,
Sometimes in waters cold;
But whether by sands or streamlets,
The Lord doth me enfold.
Sometimes I walk in green pastures,
Sometimes on barren land;
But whether in peace or danger,
The Lord holds fast my hand."
Death has summoned many of our brothers to their reward, a reward
well earned for having completed a beautiful and acceptable piece of work.
Their entering into this place of peace, security and rest marks their last
step on earth. From the cradle to the grave our every act, our love, our hate,
our envy, after each commitment is in the hands of death.
It has been the custom of our Fraternity from time immemorial to offer
to the memory of our departed brothers this last tribute of our affection. The
great creator has, in his infinite wisdom removed our brothers from the cares
and troubles of this earthly life, thus severing another link in the fraternal
chain by which we are bound together, and therefore, requiring that we who
survive be yet more strongly cemented by the ties of Brotherly Love and
Affection.
In our Christian way of thinking we have come to feel and to know that
the influences of life lived in this world continue even after the spirit leaves
the earthly body to enter life eternal. The richness and fullness of the lives of
our brothers who have entered God's Garden, their devotions, their aspirations and longings, their triumphs and defeats will not soon be forgotten.
Death terminates the labors of a man but it does not conclude the fruits
of those labors, they endure and not only are they reflected in the lives of
those we leave behind, but shall flourish and bloom in the realms of endless
bliss.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

The very basis of our thought and spiritual growth as Free M~ns of
whatever Degree, is the acknowledgment of God as creator and sustainer. of
all of life. Thus acknowledging his supremacy, we have as our strong faith
the belief in the immortality of the soul. In this comforting belief, we surrender in truthful faith, the souls of our departing brothers in the assuran~e
that a loving Father knows best, and that the temple of the human soul will
find its completion in the Heavenly Kingdom, from whose bourne no traveler
returns.
We mourn the loss of our departed and while we miss them in person,
their fine example of character and enthusiasm remain with us.

Devotional
This is a high moment and a sincere privilege. It is a great ho.nor to be in
this Grand Lodge Session, to be with Fraternal Brothers, to be with men you
love. Thank you for allowing me to share some thoughts in this brief moment,
in this devotional time that will be the beginning of this entire Grand Lodge
week.
Walk the world proudly whoever you are;
You're a soul out of space sent to walk this earth-star;
A Man of God with power and worth
Sent to bring a bit of heaven to earth.
Walk the world proudly; you're king of your life!
Empowered to conquer contention and strife,
Forces within you of measureless scope,
Eternal forces of faith, love and hope.
Walk tqe world proudly but walk with love, too.
For you have a purpose entrusted to you,
To lift those who stumble and those who would plod,
That they too may walk as a proud child of God.
(Helen Lowrie Marshall)

So we have a high and a noble and a worthy purpose. To come to San
Francisco with its sophistication, with its aristocratic atmosphere with the old
buildings and beautiful hills and streets with the classic cable cars up and
down these traditional areas ... it gives us a thrill I Those of us who are from
out of the city come back to San Francisco and enjoy it all. This past week
in one of the great department stores here there was this certain Greek who
went into a store and ran up to a very busy clerk and said, "Pleasa cana you
tell me quickly where is the restroom." The clerk was very busy and simply
pointed and said "escalator." And the response was, "Esca-later! I can't I got
to go now!" Well, it's a lot of fun to get together with upright men and fraternal Brother Masons. You know, there's a lot of traveling connected with the
Grand Lodge. Hither and yon across this state traveling by car, by bus, and
by plane. I'm not too sure of this story but I understand that one o~ the
Grand Lodge Officers was trying to make a plane at L. A. International

Airport, was late and was trying to make it and rushed to get to the gate, but
decided he wanted to read something on the plane. You know there's a bookshop at each one of these levels in the terminals and he ran in and bought
a beok very quickly. It was a high priced book, but it was a great title, "How

I'll share a story with you that's an interesting one about the Jewish
family that lived next to this Protestant family. The Jewish family had a
little son named Isaac who had a bad habit - sometime in the course of
the day or the week he would run into the other yard, through the flowers
romping with his dog into Mr. Johnson's flower garden. Mr. Johnson was out
watering his lawn and his garden and little Isaac ran through the flowers
playing with his dog and Mr. Johnson said, "Isaac, please don't run through
my flowers anymore I In fact the next time you do that I'm going to take this
hose and sprinkle you, baptize you, and make you a Christiani" Isaac looked
at him; he didn't really know what that meant, but he said "All right" and
continued to play, but he was so excited playing with his other friends and
with the dog that he didn't realize what he was doing and threw a stick. The
dog ran after it and Isaac ran right into the flower bed again. Mr. Johnson
turned with the hose, squirted him with the hose and said, "Isaac, there you
are! Baptized in the name of the Father, of the Son and the Holy Spirit."
And he laughed, but Isaac was soaking wet. Then the kid went back home,
in the house and walked into the kitchen and said, "Mama, Mama, a terrible
thing has just happened." She looked at him and said, "Isaac, you're dripping
wet, would you get out of the kitchen please; go to your room." He went
into the living room where bis dad was and he said, "Papa, Papa, a terrible
thing has happened; it's just terrible." Papa said, "Isaac, for God's sake, you
are dripping water all over the living room rug. Get out of here!" Then Isaac
ran upstairs to his sister's room. She's primping for her date, combing her hair
and sees Isaac come in. He said, "Rebecca, a terrible thing has just happened."
She said, "Isaac, you are soaking wet, get out of my bedroom and don't drip
on my new rug!" And the kid was rejected three times. He walked into the
bedroom, looked into the mirror, and said, "I've been a Christian for only five
minutes and I hate these Jews already.''
Sometimes we all get rejected. The preacher came to the Church and gave
his first sermon, and it was an arousing, exciting kind of a sermon and one
woman was really thrilled about it. In greeting him at the door when going
out she said, "Reverend, you've just filled my heart to overflowing; you have
filled my soul." And he said, "Well, thank you, Ma'am." Then he turned to
her little son next to him and said, "Did you like it, Sonny?" and he said,
"Yeah, I got a belly full, too." And this other gal who was so enthralled with
the sermon, she was so excited, it was the Minister's first Sunday there and
when she greeted him going out the door, she said, "Oh, Reverend, it was

For me that's Masonry! Having great dreams, thinking great thoughts,
drinking fr~m the fountains of the ages of philosophy, of religion, of theology,
of sociology, of civilization. Drinking from the spiritual fountains ?f ~e
ages - that's Masonry. A man is as great as those fountains from which his
spirit drinks. And we drink from vast, wide, refreshing, cool fountai.ns of
thought. From fountains of the spirit, of intellect, of the heart. Fountains of
love and honor •• • . fountains of patriotism and integrity. Fountains of
honesty, fountains of justice and mercy and righteousness. vye drink from the
purest fountains that civilization has ever known. A man is as great as the
truth he speaks as the worth he has attained. And I expect that's the
striving that ali of us try to do to make. In our Grand Lodge Family
we have traveled across this state with dedications, with installations, with
cornerstone layings, with receptions, with meetings and banquets and dinne~s
and luncheons and fellowship with fraternal brother Masons all over California. It's been a glorious experience in friendship. The bonds and the ties
that bind us together as upright men of the eternal God, who know that, who
believe that, and strive to live that way in peace, in harmony, in order, with
integrity. You know, friendships like that are something that go beyond
geography, go beyond time and history, for it's with that same kind of ~riend­
ship that we reach back with into history - three thousand. y~~us of hist?ry.
Symbolically we're reaching back to those Brothers bmldmg an ancient
Temple and it becomes the symbol of the "Temple in your soul." Isn't that
interesting and isn't it strange to think of an ancient temple built by an old
King named Solomon as being a symbolic building of charact~r, building. the
soul in the heart of man. I submit to you that our symbolic Lodge nght
here, upon this platform, is a Lodge that ought to be imprinted in its symbolic

way into your very life, with a central altar, with a holy of holies, with a
guiding light right there as your fountain from which you are drinking. And
somehow within your heart there is that part of you that sits in the East
that is the Master of your life. There is that part of you that is the Senior
Warden in your life in the West. There is that part of you that is the Junior
Warden, the playful fellow with whom we break for refreshments and things
like that. Within each of you is the Tiler and the Steward. Within each of you
is the Pursuivant. Within each of you is the Grand Organist. Within each of
you are the symbols of this Order circumscribing the bounds and the limits
within which you are a free man under God. A free man is one who is a
responsible man, one who is a citizen of a great nation and a citizen of this
world. A man who lives by the Level and the Square and by the Plumb and
who sees life guided by these symbolic instruments. The "little Lodge" that
is within your soul. Interesting to think about that.

"Thank God that we can growl
We are not bound to gaze at mud
And creep along the ground,
We can find the stars, tho our sins are low,
Thank God that we can growl

10

Another symbol is right here upon this platform. The symbol of man's
entire life. As the sun rises in the East, so a little boy is born, a little child
comes into the world. Life holds no guarantee of longevity, life is only a white
paper, a book with blank pages, an uncut stone from which we shape
the kind of life that we are to live. The sun rises in the East just as you are
handed a blank canvas and given the pigments and the brushes and the easels
to paint the story, the biography, the picture of your life- the way you want
to be.

As the sun rises in the East, so a man is born and grows through infancy,
through childhood, adolescence, through the teen-age years into young manhood, into the strong productive years and the sun is at its meridian. At its
height and at the heat of the day we are in our strongest and most productive
period of life. We marry, we have families, we see children come into being
for whom we are responsible up to a point, to make them responsible for
themselves, to allow them to become children of God. But the sun continues
in the course of a day until it comes across to the Western sky. The light
becomes mellower - more gentle, and finally, in the West the sun begins to
set. There is an afterglow - an afterglow of orange, lavender and scarlet, the
beautiful views of an afterglow of a sunset. Some day, somewhere, some place
at some time, the sun sets on the Western horizon and that man's life comes
to its close. His little day in God's tour of life is now complete, now fulfilled
in the sight of man. The afterglow of his life is the memory that lingers after
him. The memory of his personality, of his character, of those things that
mark him as a man of God. So Masonry celebrates life. From the East to the
South to the West, Masonry celebrates your life, your life as a man of the
Eternal.
In this day and to our age I share this with you.

To grow as a Man of God, to live as a Man of God and to love as a Man
of God - that's a part of our task-our calling. I want to share some thoughts
with you which, over the past year, I've shared with many men. Through
the good graces of our Grand Master, there have been opportunities to give
inspirational addresses at the openings of our Grand Lodge sessions - wherever they may have been. So I have enjoyed great experiences with friends
in towns and cities all across this state. One illustration that has been especially well received is that of the auctioneer and the old violin:
'Twas battered and scarred, and the auctioneer
Thought it scarcely worth his while
To waste much time on that old violin,
But he held it up with a smile.
"What am I bid, good folks" he cried,
"Who'll start the bidding for me?
A dollar, a dollar, now who'll make it two.

Going for three," but no,
From the room far back, a grey haired man
Came forward and picked up the bow;
And wiping the dust from that old violin,
And tightening the loose strings,
He played a melody pure and sweet
As a caroling angel sings.
The music ceased, and the auctioneer
With a voice now quiet and low,
Said, "Now what am I bid for this old violin?"

Going and gone I " said he.
And the people cheered but some of them cried
'
"We do not quite understand
What changed its worth?" Swift came the reply,
"The touch of the Master's hand."

I submit to you that in a time like this, men talk of war, we hear them
say that war will never cease. Men talk of war, but when they pray, they
pray for peace. Peace and Harmony is also what our Fraternity stands for.
Peace among Nations and among men. That is real friendship. We also stand
for a sense of humor. We laugh together, we smile together. We are all so
human in the sense of knowing that we have fallibilities, weaknesses, foibles,
and faults. But we acknowledge that very readily. As a preacher, I certainly
recognize that - although sometimes human weaknesses can be very
frustrating! For example, someone who falls asleep in a congregation or audience. You know, that can be quite vexing! One dear fellow went sound
asleep while the preacher was in the middle of his sermon - and that's
frustrating! He thought he would awaken him by using an old technique and
he simply shouted out to the congregation "If there's anyone here who wants
to go to hell, let him stand up I " And the sleeping brother only heard the last
two words. Immediately he jumped to his feet and looked around - and
every eye was on him. He collected himself together, threw his shoulders
back, looked right up at the preacher and said, "Reverend, I don't know what
we're voting on but it looks as tho' only you and I are for it!" Well, we'd be
in one terrible fix if we couldn't laugh at ourselves in the mirrors of life with
all of our idiosyncracies and fallibilities. A good sense of humor is really like a
shock-absorber for life - and we certainly have that among our great fellowship across this land.
Optimism is a part of our Fraternity - a part of Masonry. Though our
roots are deep and long lived, though we are steeped in tradition and the
ancient heritage, though we have our rituals that come out of the past through the Middle Ages, down through the Renaissance, the Industrial Revolution and into the 18th, 19th, and 20th centuries, we have our sights on the
Future I We believe in being bridge builders for those who will come after us
and looking toward the road that lies ahead:

And many a man with life out of tune
Battered and scarred with sin
Is auctioned cheap to the thoughtless crowd,
Much like that old violin.
A "mess of pottage,'' a glass of wine,
A game, and he travels on.
He's going once, he's going twice
He's going and almost gone. . . . '
But the Master comes, and the foolish crowd
Never can quite understand
The worth of a soul, and the change that's wrought
By the touch of the Master's hand.
(Myra B. Welch)
When the Almighty God reaches out across Eternity and gets a grip on
your life, then no one can quite understand the worth of a soul the richness
of a life, the magnitude of your scope, the horizons of your f~ture as you
walk as a person of God. Our world and our nation is saying "Bring me men
!o ma~ch my mountains, Bring me men to match my plains; Men with empires
m their purpose, Great dreams within their brains. Bring me men to match
thought's marshland and to cleanse old error's fen· Bring me men to match
' (Sam Foss)
my mountains, Bring me men I"
. Right now a war is raging in the Middle East.... a war that has repeated
itself over the ages and repeats itself again today in the modem states of
Israel, Egypt, and the Arab states. I expect a few of those Arab Nations wish
they had a on~yed General (Dayan), but, such a chaotic situation in the
lands of the Bible I That land which gave us most of our tradition most of
our perspectives and our philosophy, and gave us our Judeo-Christian
heritage on which this nation is built. The heritage of our great land is
founded upon its birth-certificate, the Declaration of Independence and the
Constitution. Those Masonic documents provide the foundation or' America
and the basic structure of what it is today. "Praise the Power that has made
and preserved us a Nation! Conquer we must when our cause it is just But
this is our motto, 'In God is our Trust!' And the Star-spangled bann'er in
triumph shall wave, O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave."

We should be glad for distant things,
For beauty 'round the bend;
For highways that lead on and on
With never any end.
Be glad for goals just out of reach,
The challenge of a star,
The glory of a distant light
That beckons from afar.
For hopes and dreams are built on
That enchanted distant mile,
And far off bright horizons
Make the road today worthwhile.
(Helen Lowrie Marshall)

Yes, the road we're walking today is building the foundation for the future.
The road of morality and integrity. The road of ethical behavior in our dealings with our fellow man. That's the road that we are laying and paving and
walking on. And it extends out to the bright horizons of the future.
A pilgrim going a lone highway
Came at evening cold and grey
To a chasm deep, and vast and wide;
The old man paused in the twilight dim,
The chasm held no fears for him;
But he paused when he reached the other side
And built a bridge to span the tide.
"Old man,'' said a fellow pilgrim near,
"Why waste your time in building here?
Your journey ends with the close of day.
You never again will pass this way.
You've crossed the chasm deep and wide,
Why build ye here at eventide?"
"My friend, in the path I've come," he said,
"There followeth after me today
A fair haired youth who must pass this way.
The chasm which held no fears for me
To the fair haired youth may a pitfall be.
He, too, must cross in the twilight dim.
My friend, I'm building this bridge for him."
(W. A. Dromgool)
And that's what Masonry is striving to do and attempting to do for
Manhood that follows us, for Womanhood that looks to us, and for the kind
of example this old world will need desperately in the years that lie ahead.
We're a fraternity that stands for friendship - with a sense of humor - with
an outlook that is optimistic.
We stand for character building in the heart and soul of man. We stand
with those who put their trust in the Eternal, Almighty, Dynamic, Creator,
Sustainer, and Redeemer God of this Universe. It is in that concept we speak
of the Master Architect, the Designer and Planner of this Universe and the
human Soul.
As a Master Mason, the citizen of a community, as a husband, a father, as
an uncle or a grandfather, as a citizen of a great nation, as a universal man
of God - a man of goodwill, I would like this to describe each one of you:
I love to see him walk. He never saunters,
For there is always purpose in his stride,
A buoyant joy in living there - a firmness,
A faith in life that gives him strength and pride.

He wears a cloak of confidence around him
As dashing as a cape on knight of old,
And yet his gentle smile belies his vigor For it's his faith in God that makes him bold.
I love to see him walk, for there is something
About his stride - his smile; his genial nod
That lends a certain aura to his passing And you know you've seen a man who walks with God.

With that, I salute our Grand Master. I salute my Brother Grand Lodge
officers. I salute each and every one of you as "Men who walk with God"
believing deeply in the brotherhood of man. GOD BLESS US EVERY ONE!
Necrology
To the bereaved relatives and friends of all of our departed brothers we
extend our sincere sympathy in this time of sorrow, and we pray that "He
who tempers the wind to the shorn Lamb" will give them His divine comfort
and consolation.
We shall ever cherish in our hearts the memory of our departed brothers.
We commend their spirits to Almighty God, trustingly leaving them in the
hands of that Beneficient Being who has done all things well: Who is
g~orious in His Holiness, wondrous in His Power, and boundless in His Goodness.
To me is allocated the privilege of naming those, whose demise came this
year, who have· rendered specific service to our Grand Lodge:
Lester E. Bond - Past Master of Normal Heights Lodge No. 632. Served
as Grand Chaplain for Grand Master Elmer W. Heald from October 1963 to
October 1964.
Adolph Kiersch - Past Master of Hills Ferry Lodge No. 236. Served as
a member of the Columbia Temple and was currently serving on the Board
of Library Commissioners.
Charles Warren - Past Master of Santa Rosa Lodge No. 57. Served as
an Inspector for Grand Lodge and was Senior Grand Deacon for the year
1960-1961.
Joseph W. Wright - Past Master of Russian River Lodge No. 181 and
served as Inspector from 1963-1972.
Donald C. Pitman - Past Master of Menlo Park Lodge No. 651 and was
a committeeman on Columbia Temple.

an Inspector for Grand Lodge 1965-1973.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My Brethren, it hardly seems that a year has passed already since you
humbled me with your expression of confidence by electing me to the highest
office which Freemasonry affords.
After the election and while awaiting installation I could not help but
reflect upon all of those great men who preceded me in this office and who
have served Masonry so valiantly and admirably.
So, as the mantle of leadership and responsibility descended upon me, I
commenced my duties with prayer - prayer of thanksgiving for your trust
and faith in me, prayer for wisdom and guidance in the conduct of the affairs
of Masonry in California, and prayer for sufficient stamina to perform the
arduous and challenging duties of this office.
Our Supreme Grand Master has been kind to me in granting general good
health and physical endurance. It remains for you, and time, to judge from
my stewardship report which follows and from observance of the execution of
my duties just how well my labors have been performed as your representative
in California Masonry.
In any event, I have been rewarded in a measure more than my due. I
have been overwhelmed at the display of friendship and fraternal regard expressed to me by the large number of Masons and their families whom I met
and with whom I've had even brief association in the past year. No one could
ever have received a more kind, gracious or generous reception from his
brethren and their families. For all of this I am humbly grateful. This wealth
of experience will never be forgotten.
STATE OF THE CRAFT

The general condition of Masonry in California is sound and harmonious,
except for relatively few incidents which would be expected in any organization comprising so many individuals. Decisions and recommendations covering
incidents that could not be resolved under current law will follow.
Only one seriously anxious time befell your Grand Master and the Grand
Lodge when early last February our Deputy Grand Master suffered a serious
heart attack. As you can see, the Right Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage is
completely recovered, and he re-assumed full responsibility and activity in his
office about the middle of June. All of us are pleased and thankful at his
recuperation.
Two problem areas still confront us and I believe are worthy of note.
They are: a continuing decline in membership and the average age of our
membership.
Earlier this year the Grand Secretary caused a survey to be made among
the constituent Lodges to determine the average age of our membership. 63 7
lodges (92%) responded and their reports included 207,000 members (also
92%).

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

25

To summarize this survey we find that:
20 % of our membership is past the age of 70
46 % of our membership is past the age of 60
74~% of our membership is past the age of 50
This is t!te fir~t such survey and, unfortunately, these results cannot be
compared with pnor years to determine a trend. Nevertheless, I am alarmed
at the fact that almost half of our membership is past age 60.
Even more alarming is the data accumulated at the other end of the age
spectrum for here we find that only 1.38% of our membership is below age 30.
It would seem to me that unless we can attract men, particularly younger
men, to our Fraternity that these statistics fortell a forbidding future. But,
how do we create such an interest?
I find that too often a veil of secrecy surrounds our Fraternity. Many
of our members won't discuss Masonry with anyone not recognized as a member. Even wives and children of many Masons remain in the dark as to what
Freemasonry is all about. Many of those who do discuss Masonry are so
super-cautious that their discussions are couched in language so general as to
also create a feeling of secrecy.
Th~re is SC? _little a~ut Masonry which is secret; I cannot comprehend
why this condition continues to prevail.
One needs only to read the printed Installation Service and Officers' Monitor to see the system of morality which we promulgate. We should frankly and
free~y tell eve~ interested perso!1 of the moral virtues of circumspection;
rectitude, equality, and truth as illustrated by the operative Mason's tools:
the Compass, Plumb, Level and Square; those tools which enable the operative
Mason to erect square and true buildings of great beauty and which illustrate
virtues which help us to erect beautiful and true moral and spiritual edifices
within ourselves.
There are no secrets in the recitation of Masonry's Cardinal Virtues of
Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence or Justice.
Nor. are our principal tenets of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth intended
to be hidden from so-called profane eyes and minds.
Several years ago P.G.M. Theodore Meriam prepared a booklet entitled
"If Freemasonry is Good, Let's Talk About It." Something must be done to
counteract the secrecy shroud surrounding our organization and I would
recommend that that booklet be reprinted in the California Freemason and
thus have general distribution.
. I also urge eve~ officer of every Lodge to encourage regular discussions in
his Lodge regardmg those portions of Masonry which should be openly
brought to the attention of our families and friends.
. P.G.M. Herbert A. Huebner established a DeMolay Liaison Board within
this ~rand Lodge to be of asmstance to this fine order for young men. Soon
after it was formed, the Board suggested to P.G.M. Huebner that he issue a
directive to the lodges to establish a similar liaison committee at the local
level, which he did enthusiastically.

26

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

P.G.M. McElwain and I issued similar directives, yet in this year we find
that only about 20% of the lodges responded to my directive.
In my visitations with our three Youth organizations (DeMolay, Rainbow
for Girls and Job's Daughters) I am pleased to report that a rapport exists
that has produced communication between the Grand Master and the members of these organizations.
These young men and women have found that they could speak frankly
with me, and I assure you, my brethren, that they have done so.
Although these young people deeply appreciate any assistance and support
given to their organizations they have been frank to say to me "Grand Master,
you Masons are hypocritical. Masons say they want to help us and yet
seldom, if ever, do they attend our meetings. We need adults for our advisory
boards, but willing volunteers are hard to find." While these young folks
admit to our generosity in buying tickets to breakfasts, car washes and the
like, still some are disappointed at the burdensome and excessive rentals they
must pay to lodges or Temple Associations.
There is to me a paradox that exists within our Fraternity: a generosity of
materiality (e.g., Homes Endowment contributions) as opposed to parsimony
in the giving of ourselves, our time and effort.
Whether they be the young men of DeMolay or the young ladies of
Rainbow and Job's Daughters I am convinced that a great measure of our
future depends on these young people and how they feel about the Masons
who compose our Fraternity.
The impressions they receive from us by our actions today develop their
concept of Masonry, what it is and whether or not a desire will be created in
them to become members or to encourage their loved ones to become members.
We'll never convince them of the worth of Freemasonry by words - the
young people of today depend on deeds to show them the way. If ever there
was one, this is a "show-me don't tell-me" generation.
How can we combat this apparent apathy among our members?
My Brethren, you are the Officers and Delegates of your Lodges and
Members of Grand Lodge. You are Masonry in California. You are the respected men who have been chosen to give leadership and direction to your
Lodges and to Masonry for several years to come.
From the lack of enthusiastic and general interest shown in various Grand
Lodge programs: such as youth programs, programs devoted to Public
Sehools, Patriotism and the Constitution, etc., I have come to the conclusion
that I must appeal to each of you for help.
Have you ever threaded a needle? You merely hold the needle in one hand
and gently push the thread through the eye with the other hand. But, if you
need a substantial length of thread through the eye of that needle so as to
have sufficient material to create a worthwhile garment or work of art, no
amount of continued pushing will effectively produce any quantity of thread
through the eye. How simple it is, though, to grasp the short protruding por-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

tion on the other side of the eye and you can pull any quantity of thread
through.
And so, my brethren, we, whom you have elected to lead our Fraternity,
can appoint committees and boards, we can push and shove programs, ideas
and information at you but until you grasp the thread of these programs from
your side of the needle and pull together, we'll never have sufficient material
to add to the beautiful tapestry of Masonry.
Therefore, my brethren, I urge you to reflect upon the thoughts I have
presented here. I ask that you return to your Lodges with the strongest resolution and determination to expend every effort to pull together with renewed
spirit and vigor so as to keep our beloved Fraternity progressive, active and
viable. Finally, make certain that your enthusiasm and determination are
communicated to everyone you meet, especially to the Officers who will succeed
you.
There are rays of hope for I know a number of Lodges which have received
applications from young men.
One such lodge, Triangle No. 548, celebrated its semi-centennial this
past year. I was present at that celebration and the Master presented to me
seven young men, all age 21, who had joined the Lodge that year. Another
young man who had entertained us that evening with his musical talent expressed to me that he could hardly wait to join that Lodge but it would be
almost a year until he became 21.
As I said, there are rays of hope, but all too few. I believe that we can
preserve our Fraternity and bring it to new prominence. However, the matter
rests in your hands - only you can bring added life to our beloved Fraternity.
Will you pull together - will you actively support my suggestions and respond to this appeal?
GRAND MASTER RELIEF

"To relieve the distressed is a duty incumbent upon all men but particularly
on Masons."
During the past number of months, the forces of nature have wreaked their
havoc and Masons in several sister jurisdictions have lost their homes, personal
property and even their lives. Money does not begin to compensate bereaved
families for loss of loved ones, nor does it entirely replace the loss of personal
treasures or compensate for the hardship and suffering.
Nevertheless, your Grand Master directed the Grand Secretary on November 9, 1972 to send a check to the Grand Lodge of South Dakota in the sum of
$1000.00 for the relief of those stricken in the flood in the Rapid City area of
South Dakota.
As a result of that tragic flood we learned that 97 Masons lost their homes,
17 Masons lost their lives, including a Brother and his wife, who were the
parents of four ( 4) young children. This was the second check in that same
amount which had been sent to this same Grand jurisdiction. On two occasions I have had the pleasure of meeting with the Grand Master of South

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

29

Dakota and on both occasions, in addition to letters from their Grand Secretary, the Masons of South Dakota have expressed their gratitude to this
Grand Lodge and its members for their generosity.
On October 9, 1972, I directed the Grand Secretary to send a check in the
sum of $100.00 to assist brethren in need who reside in the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of the Philippines. It had been estimated by the Grand Master of the Philippines that the total sum of $5,000
would enable their Grand Lodge to take care of the need created as a result of
a flood. The Grand Lodge of California was pleased to respond to this call
for assistance.
Then, on February 13, 1973, as a result of a disastrous and devastating
earthquake in Nicaraugua and after spending considerable time and effort in
an attempt to establish communication with the Grand Master and Grand
Secretary of Nicaraugua, I directed our Grand Secretary to present to that
Grand Lodge a check in the sum of $500.00.
It would be my earnest prayer that no more tragedies would occur to
necessitate our having to relieve the distressed. Yet, I am grateful for the
generosity of the Masons of California who have made it possible for your
Grand Master to make these contributions in their name.
MASONIC HOMES

How proud the Masons of California must be of their two Masonic Homes!
In these Homes needy brethren and their families are provided the love and
care that they would wish to do personally were they in a position to do so.
The Administrators of our Homes, Hugh B. Herring (Union City) and
James C. Blaine (Covina), their families and staffs are to be commended for

Special commendation and thanks are due to the Board of Trustees under
the superb leadership of its President, P.G.M. Myron E. Smith. The dedicated
and devoted brethien of this Board, as well as Boards past, epitomize Masonry in its finest sense. The Board of Trustees has a most interesting and
enlightening report soon to follow at this session. On behalf of all Masons in
California I take this opportunity to thank each of them for their selfless and
dedicated service.
At the time an endowment program for our Masonic Homes was conceived and initiated it was hoped that one day the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund would be of sufficient size that the income derived therefrom
would provide funds for the operating costs of the Homes, thus eliminating
the need for annual per capita taxation for this purpose.
While the fund has not yet reached such proportions, a giant step for
California Masonry was achieved this year. I am proud to say that contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund this year, and for the first
time in the history of this Grand Lodge, well exceeded the million dollar mark.
Such a gain could not have been possible had it not been for the untiring

efforts toward that goal on the part of every member of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, which was so ably guided and directed under the helmsmanship of its chairman, Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson. I have thanked
each member of this Board by private letter and I now do so publicly.
But, the goal would not have been attained had it not been for the efforts
in that direction within the constituent Lodges and the generosity of their
members. Thus, my brethren, it is you and each of those members of your
Lodges who made contributions who are deserving of the greatest measure of
thanks. I express my gratitude as well as the gratitude of our guests at our
homes to all who made this hoped-for goal a reality.
On August 18 the Grand Lodge of California laid the cornerstone and
dedicated the now nearly completed redevelopment of the new Home at
Covina. Twenty-four of the twenty-eight elected and appointed Grand Lodge
officers were present.
It was most interesting to listen to the Grand Secretary recount the
activities of the laying of the cornerstone at the first Covina facility in 1916 57 years ago. Accounts of that day in May 1916 revealed that there were more
than 1000 Masons assembled in white aprons and even in pre-World War I
Southern California there were approximately 600 automobiles parked at or
near the Home.
In removing the contents of the old cornerstone casket prior to laying the
new cornerstone, the Grand Treasurer was assisted by Worshipful Glen
Harnish, a Past Master of Covina Lodge who was present when the casket
was deposited beneath the original cornerstone in 1916.
The children at the Home assisted in the day's events by cheerfully acting
as hosts and hostesses. They presented your Grand Master with a silver trowel
which I proudly used in spreading the cement prior to laying the cornerstone.
They are wonderful young people and I am grateful to them for their thoughtful gift.
Slightly more than half the Lodges responded to my request for stones
indigenous to their local areas to be cast into the cornerstone of the Covina
Home. These stones were amalgamated into a beautiful cornerstone. It is
regrettable that all Lodges did not send stones so that they, too, could have
been "represented" in that cornerstone.
The day was very warm and humid which, no doubt, kept many Masons
and their families from attending this most important event. The hundreds
who were present were treated to fine music by the Al Malaikah Shiine Band
and to interesting ceremonies conducted by the Grand Lodge and to an excellent dedicatory address by Worshipful Ralph Head representing the Board
of Trustees of Masonic Homes.

GRAND MASTERS' ANNUAL CONFERENCE

During the week of George Washington's birthday, the Grand Masters of
the several Masonic Jurisdictions of North America annually meet in Washington, D.C. for a conference. Usually the Grand Master, Deputy Grand
Master and Grand Secretary from each jurisdiction attend this Conference.
Because our Deputy Grand Master had recently suffered a heart attack
and was temporarily disabled, I requested the Senior Grand Warden to
accompany me to the Conference in order to preserve continuity in that
program.
The Grand Lodge of California was represented at the Conference by
your Grand Master, the Senior Grand Warden, the Grand Secretary, together
with Past Grand Masters Eugene S. Hopp and Lester S. McElwain. Brother
Hopp is a fellow in the Philalathes Society which holds its meeting about the
time of the conference and Brother McElwain is a member of the National
Bicentennial Committee.
During its sessions, which run concurrently with the Conference of Grand
Masters, our Grand Secretary was elected President of the Grand Secretarys'
Conference. We can be proud that because of his ability and leadership
qualities Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems was elected to this distinguished
office and has brought this honor to California.
Due to the autonomy of each Grand Lodge in North America, no legislation can take place at the Conference. However, the Conference provides
an arena for informative and interesting exchanges of ideas among the leaders
of Masonry.
Past Grand Master Henry C. Clausen, Sovereign Grand Commander of
the Southern Jusisdiction of the Scottish Rite, hosted a luncheon at the
House of the Temple, the beautiful inspiring headquarters for the Scottish
Rite Southern Jurisdiction.
Other distinguished Californians who participated in some Conference
activities included Past Grand Master Earl Warren (former Chief Justice of
the Supreme Court of the United States and former Governor of California),
Robert B. Watts (former Grand Chaplain and former Grand Orator of the
Grand Lodge of California) and "Brother Thomas H. Kuchel (former United
States Senator from California).
STATEWIDE BLOOD BANK

At previous communications this Grand Lodge has determined that it
would be advantageous to the Masons of California to establish a Statewide
Blood Bank.
Efforts to initiate this program were instituted by the Grand Master
soon after entering office, but delays by the American Association of Blood
Banks have deferred its institution.
It is hoped that this association and the California Blood Bank System
will give approval at an early date.

SANTA .ANA LODGE No. 241

For some twelve years Boards of Control intermittently have been attempting to persuade Santa Ana Lodge No. 241 voluntarily to join the Orange
County Masonic Service Bureau.
This year the Board of Control had resolved all outstanding problems
with this one exception.
The circumstances indicated that three Masonic Lodges occupy the same
building in Santa Ana. Two of these Lodges belong to the Orange County
Masonic Service Bureau - one did not.
In order that there be equity in such a situation the rules of the Board
of Control direct that if two or more Lodges occupy one building each should
belong to the same Service Bureau or none should belong.
As attempts failed to persuade Santa Ana Lodge to join, suggestions to the
two other lodges to withdraw also failed.
An impasse thus existed. Santa Ana Lodge was outnumbered two Lodges
to one. Santa Ana Lodge also was in the minority by virtue of its total
membership relative to the aggregate membership of the two other Lodges.
I asked the Officers, Past Masters and other interested members of Santa
Ana Lodge to meet with me and the Chairman of the Board of Control. As a
result of that meeting the Master of Santa Ana Lodge agreed to re-submit
the question of joining the Service Bureau to the membership. The Lodge
again voted against joining.
Therefore, as prescribed in Section 603 of the California Masonic Code,
on August 3, 1973, I directed Santa Ana Lodge No. 241 to become a member
of the Orange County Masonic Service Bureau as of July 1, 1973 and to pay
such dues and assessments as are required of Lodges belonging to that Service
Bureau from that date forward.

GLENDORA MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION

When a DeMolay Chapter in Glendora surrendered its charter, the funds
remaining in its treasury were spent by the Glendora Masonic Temple Association to erect a fence around the Lodge's property. Such appropriation of
DeMolay funds by a Lodge or Temple Association not being legal, the then
Grand Master, Lester S. McElwain directed this temple association to repay
to the International Order of DeMolay the sum mis-appropriated.
Soon after taking office I was informed that the Temple Association had
not complied with Grand Master McElwain's directive and that $1300.00
remained unpaid.
I then directed the Temple Association to comply or advise me why they
had not complied.

Recently it was brought to my attention that a Lodge had sold its building
and did not retain rights to the cornerstone nor the casket buried beneath
the stone.
The demolition contractor claimed to have purchased all the rights to the
building. Eventually, however, the contractor did relinquish at least a portion
of the contents of the casket to the Lodge.
Lodges and Temple Associations are hereby cautioned to retain all rights
to the cornerstone and the casket of artifacts buried beneath the stone when
selling Lodge Buildings.

POWERS OF A MASTER

By virtue of the Masonic Code and the very nature of his office a Master

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of a constituent Lodge wields extraordinary power in the discharge of his
duties.
In the Installation Service a new Master is enjoined to be cautious and just
in the use of that power for the "gavel can become the instrument of great
good or of greater evil."
We have observed the result of one autocratic, even tyrannical, attitude
expressed by a Master whom I found it most judicious to remove from office.
A Master not only has the authority, but also, in some instances, the duty
to remove certain Lodge officers from their responsibilities and offices.
One Master removed a Secretary from office. The Masonic Code is mostly
silent as to the power of the Master to remove the elected Secretary or
Treasurer. In this instance the Secretary had indicated he would not serve
another term. Because of what appeared to me to be a personality clash
between the Master and Secretary, the Master chose to embarrass the Secretary and disrupt the harmony of his Lodge rather than to try to make the
best of their differences of opinion for the five months remaining in their
service to the Lodge.
Although I took no action in the situation just described, I would enjoin
Masters of Lodges never to use the autonomy of their stations in an autocratic manner. A position of leadership requires the most judicious use of the
power granted in such leadership. The preservation of Peace and Harmony in
his Lodge is the Master's first duty.

is referred to as "Master" yet we provide that any qualified Mason
may read the service.
In the ceremony for Dedication of Burial Plots he is referred to as
"Officiant."
Therefore, in my opinion, the use of the title "Master" in Fifty Year
Pin presentations should not be binding and hence limited to a bonafide
Master of a Lodge.
The ceremony of presentation refers to the acknowledgment by "The
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California" of a Brother having earned this award, and the
Grand Lodge directs the presentation to be made.
The instructions preceding the ceremony state "care ... be exercised
in selecting the officer who is to make the presentation and in the
planning of the program. Presentation by the Inspector is recommended." The italics are mine.
Because we now present about 1600 to 1800 such pins annually it
obviously is impossible for the Grand Master to conduct each such
ceremony.
Therefore, it is my opinion that the ceremony fundamentally is a
Grand Lodge ceremony. Since the Grand Master cannot make all such
presentations personally, it is the prerogative of his representative, the
Inspector, to be responsible for planning such programs and the presentation of the award. As the representative of the Grand Master, the
Inspector may designate any qualified member of Grand Lodge to
make such presentation. The Inspector, however, would remain responsible foJ the proper conduct of the ceremony."

Decision No. 1 - 50-Year Veterans' Buttons
The Grand Lecturer advised the Grand Master that there was some confusion and disagreement as to who was responsible for presentation of 50-year
veterans' buttons and for the arranging and planning for such ceremonies.
My response to the Grand Lecturer is quoted, in part, as follows:
"As I see it, we are not consistent in the use of a title for the Brother
officiating in several of our ceremonies. In one instance (funerals) he

37

I recommend that this decision be adopted as the policy of this Grand
Lodge. I suggest that where possible consideration be given to the wishes
of the recipient.
Prior to 1951, members of Lodges wishing to become charter members
of a newly instituted Lodge were required to submit demits with the application for affiliation with the new Lodge. A delay of one to several months
ensued in the institution ceremony of the new Lodge due to the schedule of
the Grand Master at that time, thus creating an interruption in the continuity of membership of the charter members affiliating with the new Lodge.
The law was amended in 1951 and since that time a letter from the
member's home Lodge stating that a demit would be issued as of the date of
institution of the new Lodge suffices and there is no interruption of continuous
membership.
In response to the Grand Secretary's question as to eligibility for veteran's
buttons of members involved in charter memberships of new Lodges which
occurred prior to the 1951 amendment, I directed that such members may be
considered to have continuous membership if a demit had been issued for the
sole purpose of becoming a charter member of a newly instituted Lodge.

Decision No. 2 - Concordant Bodies
The Grand Master's itinerary, published as an addendum hereto, shows
that on many occasions I have paid fraternal visitations to most, if not all, of
our concordant organizations.
On January 7, 1973, I held a meeting of all of the heads of the Shrine
Temples in California at Oakland. I found the 1973 Potentates and their
Divans to be most cooperative and desirous in all respects of conducting the
business of their various Shrine Temples in accordance with California Masonic law.
For all of the hospitalities shown to me and our Grand Lodge family

A Potentate of one of the Shrine Temples posed the following question:
"In our mutual effort to help and encourage our youth movements,
DeMolay, Rainbow Girls and Job's Daughters, we seek your permission to allow these organizations to sell books of tickets for the
Shrine Circus. In each book there are 10 tickets which sell for $2 .00
per ticket. For each book sold we would share the proceeds with the
youth groups at $6.00 per book."
·
The motive which sponsored this request certainly is commendable, yet
the possibility exists that in their zeal for selling circus tickets, the young
people in our youth organizations might well approach members of the
general public and such sales would be contrary to Masonic law. Therefore, I
declined to permit this Shrine Temple to pursue this program.
Decision No. 3 - Master's Right to Suspend Appointive Officer
On November 10, 1972, the Marshal of a Lodge appealed to the Grand
Master concerning his recent suspension from office.
This Brother presented a well-thought-out brief for the Grand Master's
consideration but much of his argument was directed toward the Master
having declared the office of Marshal "vacant" instead of having used the
word "suspend," as it appears in the California Masonic Code. This Brother
further questioned the Master's right to suspend an officer without his having
previously made a showing of cause that the officer had neglected the performance of his duties.
Inasmuch as a Master appoints several officers to serve in his Lodge at his
will and pleasure should they fail to perform the functions of their office to
his satisfaction, he would have the power and in some instances, the duty to
suspend such a Brother from further service as an officer of his Lodge.
Therefore, it was my decision that although the Master did not use the word
"suspend" but rather declared the office "vacant," that his intent was identical
to having used the actual word specified in the Masonic code and his action
was upheld by the Grand Master.
Decision No. 4 - Preservation of Non-Sectarianism
Last year a question was posed to Past Grand Master Lester S. McElwain

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

39

as to the propriety of singing the Christian Doxology at Lodge meetings,
dinners or other gatherings of Masons.
P.G.M. McElwain correctly ruled that Masonry recognizes no sect or
religion but is universal in its appeal to Masons of all faiths and therefore the
singing of a Christian Doxology is not to be permitted at Masonic gatherings.
That decision was not submitted to the Grand Lodge at its last Annual
Communication and hence did not become a matter of Masonic record.
The same question was submitted to me and I have made a similar ruling,
to wit:
"It is not proper to sing the Christian Doxology or to deliver any
invocation, benediction or prayer which would have a sectarian significance which might be offensive to some brethren or their families."
Decision No. 5 - Master's Dinner Fund
The question posed to me concerned the proper use of and accounting
for funds collected as a Master's Dinner Fund, and whether or not such funds
are Lodge funds.
The funds were collected from members of a Lodge on a voluntary basis
and from new candidates who, although advised that contributions were voluntary, might or might not have wished to exercise the option not to contribute.
Thereafter, all members of the Lodge and all visitors who attended the several
stated meeting - dinners were entitled to partake, whether or not they had
contributed to the fund, and without any ticket sales or collections at the
time of the meal.
Any funds left over at year-end were used by the Master to purchase some
equipment, furniture or accoutrement for presentation to the Lodge. The
presentation was selected solely at the will of the Master. There was little
accounting for the funds.

After consulting with the Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee, my
decision was as follows:
"First of all, this dinner fund, to be proper, must be established by
action of the Lodge as a Trust Fund. Secondly, I have concluded that
these funds are Lodge property and, therefore, are subject to regular
accounting. To sum it up, I have concluded that a "Master's Dinner
Fund," may be authorized by vote of a Lodge with language expressly
making it a trust fund, or with language stating that the funds collected
are to be used only for the purpose of paying for dinners, and further
provided that the language includes an annual or more frequent accounting of the trust fund. The establishment of such a fund is a
proper function of the Lodge and will comply with the requirements of
the California Masonic Code."
There has been a resolution submitted to this Grand Lodge which would
modify the above decision. I do not oppose that resolution and believe that it
may clarify a rather muddy situation.

Decision No. 6 - Solicitations
In November of 1972 I received a copy of a letter from the Chairman of a
Masonic Temple Association, directed to the Potentate of a Shrine Temple.
This letter requested the Shrine to supply a mailing list of its members to the
Temple Association in order that this Temple Association might contact as
many Masons as possible to request a minimum $1.00 donation to their building fund. This solicitation was prompted by virtue of the fact that the Lodge
building had recently been destroyed by fire.
Although I am sympathetic to and deplore the circumstances which created
this need of funds by the Lodge and its Temple Association, nevertheless,
Section 330 of the California Masonic Code prohibits Lodges from solicitations similar to that described above.
It was my decision that it would not be permissible for a Temple Association to perform an act of solicitation which would be illegal if performed
by a Lodge and therefore I directed this Temple Association to cease and
desist from its efforts.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The italics are mine. Since the Eastern Star proposed using

thereof) remains the prerogative of the Lodge.

RECOMMENDATION ( 1)
ELECTION OF GRAND LoDGE OFFICERS

In the event that the volume of business at the Annual Communication of
the Grand Lodge would permit, a considerable savings to the Grand Lodge
and the delegates thereto could be effected if the Grand Lodge were permitted to conclude its business and close in fewer than five (5) days.
I recommend, therefore, that Section 32 of the California Masonic Code
be amended by deleting therefrom on the fourth line thereof the words "Upon
the fifth day thereof" and substituting therefor the words "upon the fifth or
last day thereof, whichever comes first."
RECOMMENDATION ( 2)
INSTALLATION OF GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

Past Grand Master Huebner directed that the Ceremony of Dedication
of a Masonic ~emple be optionally "open" to the general public. The enthusiasm of Masonic wives, families and friends at such dedications has been
testimony to the wisdom of that decision.
A constituent Lodge has the option to have a public or private Installation
of its Officers (Sec. 474, CMC). Although the Code is silent on the subject,
Installation ceremonies usually are determined to be public or private at the
option of the incoming Master, altogether presumably the Lodge could direct
either a public or private ceremony.
An "open" installation of officers makes it possible for the incoming
Master's family and friends to share this wonderful experience with him as
well as to learn of his duties and obligations.
Since I find that there is nothing of an esoteric nature in the Installation
Service for Grand Lodge Officers (the service is printed), with the exception of
saluting the new Grand Master with Private Grand Honors, I recommend that
future installations of Grand Lodge Officers be either public or private at the
option of the incoming Grand Master.
The Installation should provide that the new Grand Master be accorded
Public Grand Honors at public installations and Private Grand Honors at
private installations.

GRAND TREASURER'S RESPONSIBILITY

My attention has been directed to the need for clarific~tion of the Grand
Treasurer's responsibility in processing the recommendations of the Grand
Lodge Investment Committee.
The Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Jurisprudence states as

"Section 227 provides that title to property of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple is in the Trustees, but says nothing about custody
or investment of that property.
Section 244 provides that the funds and securities of the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund be placed in the custody of the Grand
Treasurer to be held by him.
Section 245 as amended gives the Investment Committee the power to
invest and reinvest the funds of Grand Lodge and its entities, and also
gives the Committee the power to authorize the purchase and sale of
securities.
Section 245.1 authorizes title to the securities referred to in Section 245
to be held in the name of a nominee or a custodian nominee designated
as the depositary for such securities, but does not state who designates
the nominee or the custodian nominee.
So much for the Sections I have found relating to title of property
and the authority of the Investment Committee.
Section 146 Subsection 2nd relating to the Grand Treasurer provides
that it is the duty of the Grand Treasurer to take charge of all other
property of Grand Lodge (Subsection 1st.relates to fun~s~ except as
provided in Section 150 and 221. It specifies that secunties shall be
deposited in a bank or trust company or in safe deposit yaults selec:ted
as provided in Subsection I of Section 146 and Subsection I provides
that the Grand Treasurer selects the bank in which funds are to be
deposited, so it appears that the Grand Treasurer also selects the bank
or trust company where securities are deposited.
It further provides that securities, except bearer securities, shall be
withdrawn from the depositary only on the written order of the Grand
Treasurer. As to bearer securities, it requires two signatures.
Section 150 only refers to funds, and Section 221 does not seem to
apply.
From a review of these Sections it seems clear to me that the
Grand Treasurer is directly required by Section 146 - 2nd to take
charge of and keep control of the securities of Grand Lodge, select
the depositaries and authorize withdrawal of securities from ~e
depositaries. He alone can withdriiW cash for purchases and receive
cash from sales of securities.

RECOMMENDATION ( 5)
CLARIFICATION ON REMISSION OF DUES

The amendment of Section 577, CMC at the 1972 Annual Communication
permitting Lodges to remit dues of members to "December 31st of the then
calendar year" was the source of many questions directed to the Grand
Master.
Annotation (a) of Section 577 states "Remission of dues should be at the
(June) stated meeting."

46

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I think that it was the intent of the proponent(s) of the resolution which
resulted in that Amendment to Section 577 to provide the member whose
dues were remitted to December 31st a current or paid-up dues receipt froqi
his Lodge, thus avoiding possible embarrassment to such needy but worthy
Masons.
However, if the action to remit is taken at the June Stated meeting as
prescribed in Section 577 (a) the member whose dues are so remitted would
have a current dues receipt only from the June Stated meeting to December
31st of the then calendar year. From January 1st of the succeeding year until
the June stated meeting of that year he would not have a current or paid-up
dues receipt in his possession. His potential embarrassment would be avoided
only for little more than half of each year. Hence the confusion and questions
posed to your Grand Master.
I believe that the purpose desired by the proponent of the resolution on
this subject at the 1972 Annual Communication can be accomplished fully by
a further modification to the California Masonic Code.
Therefore, I recommend that Section 577 of the California Masonic Code
be amended by inserting the following immediately after the first paragraph of
said section:
"A member whose dues were remitted by a Lodge to December 31st of
the preceding calendar year as hereinabove provided should have his situation
reviewed by his Lodge at its January stated meeting. If, in the opinion of the
Lodge and by majority vote taken, the necessity for remission of his dues
still exists, the Lodge may remit said member's dues in advance to December
31st of the then calendar year. Having so remitted his dues a further review
need not be made by the Lodge at the ensuing June stated meeting."
To preclude confusion relative to payment of per capita sums levied by
Grand Lodge, I further recommend that Paragraph 5th (a) of Section 283 of
the California Masonic Code be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Master Masons who, at June 30 of any calendar year, have had
their dues remitted by Lodge action(s) for the preceding 12 months."
In my opinion, passage of these amendments will accomplish the intent
of action taken at our last Annual Communication and clearly delineate the
obligation of Lodges as regards Grand Lodge assessments of any per capita
sums.

GRAND LODGE OF HAWAil

Following their visit to the Lodges of the Hawaiian Islands, the Grand

Hawaiian Lodges regarding the formation of a Grand Lodge in Hawaii.

·
I agreed to permit a ballot, the third such ballot in the past four years. I
further agreed that the form of ballot and procedures would be essentially
the same as the format permitted by P.G.M. McElwain last year.
However, the proponents of the formation of a Grand Lodge in Hawaii
indicated a 90-day time limit to obtain the return of ballots was too restrictive. I have agreed to a 120-day time limit for that purpose.
The proponents also strongly expressed a desire to submit a "fact" sheet
with the ballot outlining the reasons why that Grand Lodge should be formed,
and so I agreed to the inclusion of their information sheet. The Grand Lodge
of California also will include such a sheet with the ballot.
I believe that although the Grand Master has a responsibility to those
Hawaiian Masons who wish to form a Grand Lodge, I also believe that he has
an equal responsibility to those who oppose the formation as well as to those
who don't care one way or the other. Perhaps the forthcoming ballot will more
truly reflect the opinion of the members of the Hawaiian Lodges if they have
the opportunity to read data presenting all the "pros" and "cons" before
balloting. These information sheets are attached hereto as a part of this
report.
I can understand why an area which has achieved Statehood would desire
eventually to form its own Grand Lodge. On the other hand I would urge the
utmost caution because, if formed, a Grand Lodge of Hawaii would be less
than half the size of the next smallest jurisdiction in the United States. Also,
approximately half the members of Hawaiian Lodges do not reside in Hawaii.
I am apprehensive that such a new Grand Lodge will face many problems,
including financial requirements, that its size alone will prove the greatest
hazard to success at this time.

ORGANIZATIONS OR SOCIETIES NOT CONFORMING

On January 29, 1973, I wrote to a Past Master of one of our Lodges a

and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons, U.S. Group.
Considerable research has been done regarding the Universal League
and I am satisfied that, based upon information that has come to me,
it could not qualify as an organization which could be recognized by
the Grand Lodge of California and is thus considered to be clandestine.
As you know, there are certain standards which govern regularity,
and fraternizing with clandestine groups is not conducive to maintaining recognition by Grand Jurisdictions throughout the world. My
opinion in this matter regarding the Universal League is shared by
many outstanding Masons and Masonic scholars. We know that it has
been abandoned by a number of Grand Jurisdictions.
In calling this to your personal attention it is hoped that you will
voluntarily cease and desist any further activity in that organization."

"Upon the recommendations of the Grand Lecturer, the Very Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons and Assistant Grand Lecturer for Division V,
the Worshipful George Perkins, I hereby suspend you from the exercise and duties of your office as Master of Belvedere-Sunrise Lodge
No. 522.
This suspension is effective immediately pending further investigation
into the circumstances of your alleged misconduct and will remain in
effect until rescinded by the Grand Master or until the next Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge.
You are advised that this suspension deprives you from the title of
Past Master unless restored by the Grand Master or the Grand Lodge."
Circumstances attending this alleged misconduct were as follows:
1. There was a distinct lack of harmony in Belvedere-Sunrise Lodge due
to the actions of the Master and a certain Past Master.
2. Contrary to the usual practice of the Lodge, a resolution was presented
at the August Stated Meeting to grant the sum of $600.00 each for the
Master, the Senior Warden, the Junior Warden of Belvedere-Sunrise Lodge,
and to the Secretary the sum of $200.00, for their attendance at the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge. In addition, the Lodge was presented
with a motion to grant the sum of $7 50.00 to purchase a life membership for
the retiring Master, the total sums voted at this meeting therefore, were
$2,750.00.

It is stipulated that it is not irregular for a Lodge to vote traveling expense money for certain of its officers or elected representatives to attend the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. However, tradition in this Lodge
indicates that such travel expense money was usually voted upon at the
September or October Stated Meetings. Since August falls during summer
vacation periods, attendance at the Lodge that particular evening was quite
small. The Master's dereliction of duty, however, is in regard to the sum of
$600.00 allocated to the Senior Warden, which office was vacant at the time,
but which sum was to be paid to a Past Master of the Lodge who was
occupying the station of Senior Warden on a meeting-to-meeting basis by
appointment of the Master. Since the Past Master appointed to that station
was not an elected representative of the Lodge, it was pointed out to the
Master that this was not a legal expenditure of the Lodge. The Master declared such discussion to be out of order and stated that until he had received
word from Grand Lodge, that Past Master would go to Grand Lodge and
would be paid the expense sum so voted for the Senior Warden. Since this

ACKNOWLE DGEMENTS

To single out certain individuals for commendation and thanks puts one in
the position of overlooking deserving contributors to Masonry. No such slight
is intended for virtually every member of the Craft, as well as the employees
of Grand Lodge and our Masonic Homes, have contributed significantly to the
cause of Freemasonry and I am grateful for their loyal support of the Grand
Master.
Preceding Grand Masters have stated that their corps of officers were outstanding in the execution of their duties. Without detracting from the perfonnance of previous corps of officers, I cannot imagine a corps who could
have served Grand Lodge in a more exemplary fashion than this year's team.
This year's elective and appointive officers have functioned as a "team" and
have labored valiantly in behalf of California Masonry. Not only have they
excelled in their support of and cooperation with the Grand Master, but a
special camaraderie has developed among us and our families. I am proud
of each of them and their combined efforts to make this an outstanding year,
and gratefully thank them.
Several of the Grand Lodge Officer Team are deserving of special commendation and I hereby pay tribute to:
Ray Ebbage, Deputy Grand Master, for the exemplary discharge of his
duties in spite of a temporary physical setback.
Burt Meyer, Senior Grand Warden, a long time friend who has been so
very helpful to me. He is an outstanding ritualist and adept at getting to the
heart of a problem.
John Roberts, Junior Grand Warden, who has brought extensive executive
ability tempered with a keen sense of justice to the Grand Lodge. John is a
man of great stature of character and a most welcome addition to the team.
Chet MacPhee, Grand Treasurer, who has been most helpful and considerate and lends extensive financial expertise to the benefit of our Fraternity .
Ed Siems, Grand Secretary, who has already been noted for his national
acclaim. I have the greatest of respect for him. No one works longer hours
and devotes more time to Masonry than does Ed Siems.
While commending the Grand Secretary, special thanks and commendations are due the Grand Lodge office staff. Verne Hendrix, Assistant Grand
Secretary; Gladys Wraith, Ed's secretary; Helen Castellotti, Receptionist;
and all members of the office staff have been cheerfully cooperative and have
labored tirelessly to perform every task or function I suggested. It should be

Doug Lemons, Grand Lecturer, whom I had the pleasure to recommend
for an appointment to the Inspectoral Corps several years ago. He has more

George Davis, Grand Chaplain, who has performed the duties of his

every one of them.

Fraterni ty who has labored in Masonry, I express my heartfelt thanks and
lifelong gratitude. All of you are the real workers and to you belongs the
credit.
I shall ever be thankful for having been given this opportunity to serve

and fulfilled my life beyond measure.

DECISION No. 7
YOUTH ORGANIZATIONS

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
In ParagrapM 61 7 and 8 of Decision 7 relating to youth organizations
the Grand Master stated that be had determined that to publish in Lodge
bulletins with any degree of regularity "news items" pertaining to concordant
bodies would be an attempt to evade the intent of California Masonic Code
Section 334, Annotation a.
The Annotation reads as follows:
"Lodges and concordant bodies may publish a bulletin without advertising, if the service is offered to all organizations on a proportionate amount per capita so that our Lodges will not in any manner
subsidize the publication by paying a greater amount than other
organizations, subject to the understanding that the Grand Master
may at any time order the books and records of any such publication
to be made available to him or his designated representative. The
decision is not to be construed to expand our present definition of
concordant bodies as bodies of the York and Scottish Rites only."
The heart of the annotation is that no Lodge should subsidize other
Masonic bodies by assuming their Bulletin costs by publishing what is a
joint bulletin solely at Lodge expense.

63

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The facts recited by the Grand Master in Decision 7 are as follows:
"A Lodge of this jurisdiction submitted a bulletin to me which they
publish and which contained calendar information and other data for
a number of concordant organizations, all the cost of which was borne
by the subject Lodge. Having been informed that when done without
charge to the concordant bodies this was improper, the Lodge then
asked whether the Lodge could regularly publish 'news items for the
concordant bodies.' "
The Jurisprudence Committee feels that the Grand Master's decision is
too broad.
If the news items were published on a regular basis with the intent or
result that the concordant body did not have to publish its own bulletin,
then the Grand Master's opinion would be correct. This intent or result
would be obvious if the membership roster of the concordant organization
were used as a mailing list.
On the other hand, where the printing of such news items is primarily
or solely to create greater Masonic intercourse and does not supplant a
bulletin of a concordant body there would be no subsidy by the Lodge
printing the news items. That the mailing was only to Lodge members would
be strong evidence of promotion of Masonic brotherhood and not of any
subsidization of a concordant body which presumably would have a membership roll and mailing roster not identical with that of the Lodge.
Thus, on the basis of the facts presented in the decision, the Grand
Master's decision is too broad.
We recommend the decision be disapproved.
The Committee on Youth Activities expressed its concurrence in the recommendation of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
By separate action Grand Lodge approved deletion of Paragraphs 6, 7
and 8, and approved in lieu the language expressed by the Committee on
Jurisprudence.
Adopted with deletion of Paragraphs 6, 7 and 8.

Annotation 409 (k) states that a Lodge cannot use its funds to pay the
rent for a chapter of the Eastern Star.
Section 409 was amended in 1957 to provide that Lodges or Temple
Associations could not use its funds to benefit any other organization using its
property. However, as stated by the Grand Master, the Section does allow
use of Lodge funds for the Masonic charities. And since the proposed use
was for such a purpose, the decision appears to be proper and should be
adopted.
We move the adoption of this report and urge a "Yes" vote.

RECOMMENDATION

No. 1

ELECTION OF GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committc;e on Policy and General Purposes concurs with the Grand
Master's recommendation and moves its approval.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Grand Master's Recommendation No. 1 that in the event the volume
of Grand Lodge business would permit closing in fewer than five days has
merit but does require an emergent legislative amendment to give effect
thereto.
Section 32 of the California Masonic Code provides that the election of
officers shall occur on the fifth day of Grand Lodge. Annotation 32b provides
such election shall be the first order of business on the fifth day.
We believe it necessary to alter the phraseology of the recommendation
to read:
"That Section 32 of the California Masonic Code be amended by deleting
therefrom, on the fourth line, the words, 'upon the 5th day thereof', and substituting therefor the words, 'upon completion of business thereof or upon
but not later than the fifth day at the discretion of the Grand Master', and
that Annotation 32b be deleted from the Code." This is an emergent matter
and we move it be received as such.

(By separate action Grand Lodge approved acting on this emergent
matter.)
We move the adoption of Recommendation No. 1 as amended and recommend a "Yes" vote.
Adopted 5/6 vote (as amended).
