RECOMMENDATION No. 5
CLARIFICATION ON REMISSION OF DUES

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends approval of
Recommendation No. 5, but with the observation that further clarification
may be required in order that there may be no misunderstanding both as to
the policy of the Grand Lodge and the procedures to be used in handling the
remission of dues.
I move approval of Recommendation No. 5 and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This recommends that a member whose dues were remitted to December
31st of a particular year should have his situation reviewed by his Lodge at
its January stated meeting of the next ensuing calendar year. It would give
the Lodge the discretion to remit the member's dues in advance for the then
calendar year and would obviate the necessity for further review by the
Lodge at its June stated meeting. The recommendation would require amendments to Sections 577 and 283-5th(a) of the California Masonic Code.
In order to accomplish the purpose intended the Committee on Jurisprudence proposes the following resolution:
BE IT RESOLVED that Section 577 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by inserting the following paragraph immediately after the first
paragraph of said Section:
"A member whose dues were remitted by a Lodge to December 31st of
the preceding calendar year as herein above provided should have his situation
reviwed by his Lodge at its February Stated Meeting. If, in the opinion of the
Lodge and by majority vote taken, the necessity for the remission of his dues
still exists, the Lodge may remit said member's dues in advance to December

66

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

31st of the then calendar year. Having so remitted his dues a further review
need not be made by the Lodge at the ensuing June Stated Meeting."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 283-5th(a) of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
Section 283-Sth(a). "Master Masons whose accrued dues for the preceding twelve months have been remitted by Lodge action at the June Stated
Meeting or whose dues for the calendar year have been remitted by Lodge
action at any Stated Meeting as permitted by Section 577 of this Code."
We move the adoption of this Recommendation.

No. 8 relating to annual administrative schools for Secretaries to he conducted
by the Grand Secretary was not adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

REcoMMENDA TION No. I3
SUNDAY CEREMONIES

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends approval of
Recommendation No. 13 but with the change of the word "including" to the
word "and" in the second line of the suggested addition to the California
Masonic Code. As written, the suggested Code addition might be subject to
the interpretation that Masonic buildings are public buildings, which they are
not. Further, the Committee wishes to confirm that every effort should be
made to schedule ceremonies at such times that will not conflict with normally
accepted periods of worship.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
We concur with Recommendation No. 13 for the reasons stated by the
Grand Master but must observe that the Annotation 326e of the Masonic
Code is a recommendation of a Past Grand Master heretofore adopted by
Grand Lodge which is not subject to amendment by a subsequent Grand
Lodge.
It will, therefore, be necessary that a new annotation numbered 326f be
approved and added to the Code, reading:
"f. Cornerstone laying and dedication ceremonies for public school buildings, and Masonic buildings, may be conducted on Sunday if in the discretion
of the Grand Master the same may be accomplished without infringing upon
the spirit of Masonry."
We move the adoption of Recommendation No. 13 and recommend a
"Yes" vote.
Adopted (as amended).

PROCLAMATION
DeMolay Week
March 11-18,

1~73

WHEREAS the Order of DeMolay will, in 1973, observe
the Fifty Fourth Anniversary of the founding of this outstanding Masonic youth organization; and
WHEREAS the teachings, principles and goals of the
Order of DeMolay are consistent with our Masonic philosophies
and build the character of young men to prepare them to be
better men and better citizens; and
WHEREAS the future of our great nation will be
placed in the hands of today's youth; and
WHEREAS the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California has
a continuing program to assist and support the Order of DeMolay
in such manner as is consistent with our Masonic law;
NOW, THEREFORE, I proclaim the week starting Sunday,
March 11, 1973, as DeMolay Week and urge each member of every
constituent Lodge in California and Hawaii to visit a DeMolay
Chapter and join in its activity during this week, or as near
to it as possible, and I further urge that the constituent
Lodges in this jurisdiction plan a program honoring the Order
of DeMolay.
FURTHER, I direct that this proclamation be read at
the Stated Meetings of each Lodge in February and March, or
that a copy be sent to each member of the Lodge, or that it be
printed in the Lodge bulletin.
'Dated:

January 24, 1973

77

PROCLAMA TION
PUl>lic Schools Month - April, 1973

It is a recognized fact that in ~is nation, endowed with great natur•l
resourc~s, there is no more precious asset than our youth. The future
well-being and security of this country will be entrusted to young
people now being educated. It is of the greatest importance that parent•
and other citizens support and strengthen the system of public education
which is molding our youth.
The Annual Observance of Public Schools Week was initiated by the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California and Hawaii in 1920.
Since that time the Masonic Lodges have annually sponsored the eve~t.
~his gives each citizen the opportunity to re-dedicate himself to the
importance of education and the support of our public schools.
I, therefore, proclaim the month of April, 1973, as Public Schools Month
and the theme for this annual observance will be "Preserve America's
Heritage For Tomorrow's citizens - Support Public Schools". The importance of our educational system in awaking our citizens to the principles
and values of our American heritage cannot be stresse~ too strongly.
I further direct that:
All constituent Lodges in California and Hawaii actively participate
in an appropriate Public Schools program.
The suggestions offered by the Public Schools Co111Dittee be
followed whepever possible.
No Lodge meetings be held during the local observation of Public
Schools Month with the exception of Stated Meetings.
Publicity be given Public Schools Month in the Trestleboard of
constituent Lodges where practicable.
This Proclamation be read at the March and April Stated Meeting&
of all Lodges.
Dated: February 6, 1973

PROCLAMATION

CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
PROCLAMATION

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT .MONTH

As Masons of California and Hawaii we should be well aware
of the importance of our permanent Endowment Fund, the income from
which is a source of operating funds for our two Masonic Homes.
Income from the fund is not large enough to cover the
operating expenses of the Homes and must be supplemented, in part,
by the per capita tax.
However, we may not be genuinely aware"of the greater needs
today for operating funds for these two Homes.
There are over 400 guests, members of our Masonic family,
at the Home for the elderly at Decoto, which is the largest population in the history of the Home. At Covina there also is substantial need, for the care and security for children.
A review of the operation expenses of our Homes indicates
the need for the help of every Brother, regardless of the size of
his contribution, so as to increase the permanent Endowment Fund
to a paint where it will more adequately provide income for
operation of the Romes.
This is our opportunity to express our love and consideration
for the elderly at Decoto and for the children at Covina in a way
that we can assure their care and security.
Accordingly I proclaim the month of May, 1973 to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
I direct that this proclamation be read at the March and
April Stated Meetings of each Lodge,and I suggest that wherever
practicable copies of this proclamation be sent to each member of
the Lodge.

Dated:

On September 17, 1787, the continental congress adopted the
constitution which established a form of government to serve the
Thirteen States. It is considered one of the greatest documents
devised by man and was completed in just ninety-one days. After
186 years this document, with relatively minor modifications,
still serves as the framework of our government and the protector
of freedom for Fifty States and 205,000,000 Americans.
From the firm foundation of our constitution has evolved a
heritage of freedom unparalleled in history. constructed by
dedicated men who valued, above all, its precepts of freedom this.
document has been preserved by citizens who recognize the importance
of these freedoms.
Freedom, as granted by our constitution, is not a birthright.
The mere fact that we were born in the United States does not mean
that we can languish in the patriotic accomplishments of past
generations. constant vigilance is. required to protect the freedoms
granted by the constitution from erosion.
Masons are enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of civil
duties and never to lose sight of the allegiance due our country.
such conduct on the part of every Mason, both within and without
the Lodge, will help to uphold the spirit of patriotism of which
Americans have always been so proud.
I, therefore, declare that the month of September 1973 will be
constitution Observance Month and direct every Lodge in this
Jurisdiction to promote, support and participate in a meaningful
patriotic program during the month. Lodges may join with one or
more other Lodges in such an observance. In every such event
programs should be well-planned and you should strive to encou+age·
public attendance and participation.
I further direct that this Proclamation be read
and September Stated Meetings and, wherever possible
in Lodge Bulletins for September 1973.
Dated:

February 15, 1973

July i6, 1973
Grand Master

To the Masters of all Constituent Lodges
SUBJECT: Suspensions for Non-Payment of Dues
The continuing high rate of suspensions for non-payment of dues alarms
and concerns me. Every brother who is in arrears in his dues should be given
every opportunity and encouragement to become current.
For the brother who is unable to pay his dues, we are granted lawful
means to show him our fraternal regard by properly remitting them.
I direct, therefore, that no member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction be
suspended for non-payment of dues unless he has been visited personally by
the Master of the Lodge or the committee appointed by the Master for that
purpose and then only when it has been determined to the satisfaction of the
Master that the subject brother has no wish to pay his dues, provided, also
that the Master is satisfied that said brother has the financial ability to pay.
If it be determined that it would work a hardship upon a brother to pay his
dues, then I direct that his dues be remitted as prescribed in the California
Masonic Code.
If the brother whose dues are in arrears resides at some distance from
his Lodge, thereby making it impractical for a personal visit, I direct that
all other means of communication be exhausted prior to taking action to
suspend, including courtesy visitations conducted by any Lodge adjacent to
his place of residence.
Cordially and fraternally,
W. H. PRICE
Attest:
Grand Master
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

the City of Sonora. To reserve a date for the use of the Temple, communicate
with the Grand Secretary's office. There is a $25.00 charge for the use of the
facilities but it is worth it!
A number of Lodges have planned trips to Columbia, a visit to Decoto, a
lunch in San Francisco and sometimes a guided tour through the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. Please make advance arrangements, however,
through the Grand Secretary's office for a tour through the Memorial Temple.
Special meetings can be held in the Old Masonic Hall in El Pueblo de
Los Angeles State Historical Monument at Los Angeles. A charge of $25.00
for the use of th.e Hall prevails here also.
For Youth Groups the charge is $5.00 per meeting during the week.
Saturdays are reserved for constituent Lodges at Columbia and the Old
Masonic Hall. If a Saturday is open, Youth Groups may use the Temples but
the charge is $2 S.00. These nominal charges help to maintain a custodian
who opens the facility and sees that all is in readiness on your arrival.
All of the above are fine possibilities. I hope that many of our Lodges
will take advantage of the opportunities for good Masonic fellowship by
planning to use these Temples. Please see Section 324, C.M.C. Supplement,
for further details.

To The Lodges of The Jurisdiction:
In order to remain viable as well as financially sound our youth groups
are experiencing an increasing burden. They need the assistance of every
Mason in the jurisdiction.
How can we assist them? There are a number of ways.
For example:
Masons are needed to serve on the various advisory boards or councils.
Masons must attend youth group meetings as well as make certain
that adult leadership is available when assistance is requested.
Let these groups run their own programs as long as they are within
established guidelines as determined in their rules and regulations and
the California Masonic Law.
I find that some Lodges or Temple Associations are charging the youth
organizations rentals equivalent to those charged adult orders. In a
number of instances, these rentals are excessive or at least create a
real burden on the youth organizations who have very limited sources
of income.
Your Lodge or Temple Association can be helpful by reappraising the
rental charged youth groups for meetings. Our regulations are permissive in this respect and I personally request that such appraisals be
made by the Trustees or Officers governing Temple rentals. Become
acquainted with your youth group budgets and their reserves, and
you will then know whether or not the rental you charge is burdensome
to them.
Lodges may grant financial assistance. (See Section 412 in the Supplement to the California Masonic Code.)
Masters should include the degree work of the youth groups in their
schedule of meetings for the year. Make every effort to see that you
have a "full house." The young people will realize that Masons, by
action as well as by words, are behind them.
On December 29, 1972, I was privileged to install the Officers of Frank S.
Land Lodge No. 819. Every Officer installed was a Senior DeMolay. We
are advised that this was a "first" in the nation and perhaps the world. There
is a message here for all Masons and especially Lodge Officers.
I am requesting the Lodges to review their planned programs for the year.
Our young people are looking to us for leadership, guidance, direction and
assistance. I am confident that if we Masons do our part they will do theirs.
March 22, 1973
Attest:
Cordially and fraternally,
EDWARD H. SIEMS
w. H. PRICE
Grand Secretary
Grand Master

OF CALIFORNIA
MAY 14, 1973

To The Masters of Constituent Lodges:
In my visitations throughout the State it has been brought to my attention
by some of the Lodges that they were experiencing difficulties in meeting the
costs of their operations.
This factor has been most acute for Lodges in the last two years because
costs everywhere have been increased while the income for the Lodges has not
always kept pace.
Our law provides that all of a Lodge's funds must be available for charitable purposes if required. However in many cases the demand for charitable
funds has not been as great as in years past due to improved economy and
Federal and State assistance of varying kinds, as well as the fact that continuing relief cases are usually handled through the Masonic Homes of
California outside relief cases. In spite of such limited charitable expenditures, many Lodges are still operating under financial strain. A number of our
Lodges have had the fortunate experience of having had a solid investment
program and their annual dues when combined with income from their investments are adequate to meet the increased operational costs of their Lodges.
Others are not so fortunate.
It is not the intent of this letter to suggest that your annual dues be increased, I am, however, convinced that many Lodges have been subject to
inevitable operating costs increases without fully realizing the necessity of
offsetting such increases by increasing their income. The average annual
members' dues throughout the Jurisdiction as of June, 1972, were approximately $20.00. In 1962 the average dues approximated $15.75. A summary of the changes during the last 10 years will be found on Page 88 of the
1972 Annual Proceedings.
We suggest that you appoint a small committee of knowledgeable brethren
of your Lodge to analyze your current income from dues and/or other sources
and compare it with actual expenses of your Lodge. Thus your current
operations as well as the future of your Lodge will not be handicapped in the
purposes for which it was intended, if your income structure is strengthened.
Possibly your present dues are adequate. It is also possible that they may
need adjusting to meet the tremendous increase in costs which have occurred
since your present dues amount was established. We are sure that the welfare
of your Lodge will be enhanced by such a review.

Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

Cordially and fraternally,
W. H. PRICE
Grand Master

TO: District and County Superintendents
FROM: WILSON RILES
SUBJECT: Public Schools Week 1973
Since 1920, California has observed Public Schools Week each year,
usually in April.
This worthy tradition began that year when California Masonic leader
Charles Albert Adams asked every Masonic Lodge to hold an open meeting
during the week to discuss public schools.
As a result, public schools annually hold open house and invite community members t~ visit, .to see demonstrations of student learnings, to
become better acquamted with the schools and their personnel, and to discuss
public education, its problems and possible solutions.
For 1973, however, the Grand Lodge of the Free and Accepted Masons of
California has instituted a change in its Public Schools Week tradition a
change with which I concur and support. Instead of the designation of a
specific week statewide, the month of April is proclaimed as PUBLIC
SCHOOL MONTH.
It is suggested that each school district determine mutually with its local
lodge or lodges which full week during April 197 3 it chooses to observe as
Public School Week.
The flexibility of selecting one week as Public Schools Week during April
makes it possible to avoid some of the problems generated by the designation
of a single week for statewide observance.
Education is today's contract for tomorrow. The public schools belong
not only to teachers or trustees or administrators, but to the people. The
public should be involved first hand in the public schools, not just during a
week in April but all during the year. Public Schools Week in a formal
recognition of the interdependent bond between the public schools and the
public they serve so well .
The theme for Public Schools Month this year is "Preserve America's
Heritage for Tomorrow's Citizens - Support Public Schools."
I commend the Masons for their public school support and invite all
California superintendents to join in the observance of the 1973 PUBLIC
SCHOOLS MONTH.

History
Lodge le Progres chartered April 8, 1843. Grand Lodge of California
formed April 19, 1850, preceding entry of California into the Union by several months. Statehood in Hawaii is fourteen years old. Ten Hawaii Lodges
chartered by California. Membership 3300.
Masonic Related Bodies
Four Valleys of Scottish Rite, Supreme Council 33°, Four Bodies of York
Rite, Conclave Red Cross of Constantine, Aloha Temple, AAONMS, Shriner's
Hospital, Court #1 R.0.J., Cabire, Ten Chapters Eastern Star, Orders of:
Nile, Beauceant, Amaranth and White Shrine. Orders of: DeMolay, Rainbow
Girls and Job's Daughters. Three Square and Compass Clubs, Two Hi-12
Clubs and Two Chapters National Sojourners.
Fiscal
Inaugural Fund $10,000 already subscribed. Initial free office space available. Bequests $25,000 and Masonic Library $200,000 have been made. Blue
Lodges have varying assets up to $250,000. Masonic related bodies have substantial assets.
Facilities
Three Masonic Temples, Scottish Rite Cathedral, Shriner's Hospital, and
Aloha Temple Beach Home.
Budget
Budget matters have been studied with Certified Public Accountants in
committee which indicate we can operate as a Grand Lodge within the
amounts now expended. We have been conservative in budget; e.g. in the free
office rent item we include the amount of estimated cost and treat it as a
reserve.
Relief
Studies of U.S. Grand Lodges by insurance executives strongly suggest no
Masonic Home; rather a Capital Fund with an initial goal of $100,000 to be
subscribed. Income to be used to supplement Blue Lodge relief when necessary.
Ritual and Code Leadership
Adopt Ritual and Code of the Grand Lodge of California.
Grand Lodge Line Officers and District Inspectors appointed by G.L.C.,
Imperial Potentate AAONMS, ten deputies in 100 years to the Supreme
Council 33 °, special representatives and deputies York Rite, Grand Almoner
Red Cross of Constantine, Grand Master International DeMolay, one Supreme Queen of Nile, two Grand Masters of Grand Lodge of Japan, as well as
many leaders in Hawaii business, professions, churches and government at all

levels including Legislature, courts and military services. Masonic leadership
abounds.
Comments
Masons of Hawaii will have pride and confidence in their autonomy. A
Grand Lodge of Hawaii would place Masonry in Hawaii on a welcome and
equal footing with all jurisdictions recognizing it.

Information Prepared By Grand Lodge of California Re Formation of

August 6, 1973
History
This would be the third ballot on this subject in four years. Hawaiian
member~p has rejected formation of a Grand Lodge on the last two ballots.
10 Ha~auan ~dges now have 3156 members of which only 1638 (or 53%)
are residents ID the Islands.
The 1972 ballot indicated that many more non-resident members favored
formation than resident members. More than half of all members did not cast
any vote.
.
Masonic Related Bodies
SuPP?,rt. of concordant Masonic groups is desirable but the Grand Lodge
of Hawau, if formed, must not become subservient to these bodies for their
income or continued support. A Grand Lodge must be the supreme Masonic
authority in its jurisdiction.
Fiscal
Free office space for Grand Lodge is a generous offer so long as it requires
no reciprocity or favoritism.
. . G~~d ~ge of ffii:waii would be less than half the size of the next largest
JUnsdiction ID the Uruted States. A Grand Lodge normally acquires funds
through taxation of members. Average dues of Hawaiian members is now
$17.10 annually. Dues might necessarily have to be increased to support the
proposed Grand Lodge. A substantial increase in dues could lead to nonresid~nt members transferring their membership resulting in a progressively
heavier burden for the members remaining in the new Grand Lodge.
Budget
The proposed budget is $30,000 per year of which 25% is for salary of a
secretary. Costs for required inter-island travel of Grand Lodge Officers visitations required to other Grand jurisdictions, expenses of visitors from 'other
Grand jurisdictions, committee and other expenses could well exceed budget.
Many other expenses would be incurred, including cornerstone ceremonies
and annual communications of the new Grand Lodge. The Capital Fund for
relief has not yet been raised.

Relief
Hawaiian Lodges now have five guests in the California Masonic Home
whose support costs more than $25,000 annually. Future relief cases would
be supported by members of the new Grand Lodge. Convalescent care could
cost approximately $10,000 annually or one-third the proposed budget for
each relief case. It is fundamental to Masonry that we care for our own without reliance on government agencies to do that job. Income from the proposed
Capital Fund would not cover the cost of one relief case. If Relief is to be
borne by an individual Lodge, the cost could overburden some Lodges.

VETERANS BUTTONS

Analyses of the membership records of Brethren eligible to receive Fifty
Year Veteran Buttons and Certificates continue to require the effort of members of the staff in the membership division. This year, as for several years
past, a great number have been presented. For the period between Septemrn:r
1, 1972 and September 1, 1973 the total number of awards was 1,SSl. This
brings our total presentations to 20,219 since the program was instituted.
TAXATION MATTERS

Concerted effort has been made to furnish Lodges with information from
this office relative to the requirements of the Tax Reform Act of 1969. Several
"tax packages" with summaries of the law and examples of required filings
have been submitted to the constituent Lodges. As nearly as we can determine, all of our Lodges are presently complying with tax filing requirements
of both the Federal and State Governments.
Because the officers of Temple Associations change and a variety of
ownership interests exist, it is often difficult to reach responsible officers of

97

the Temple Associations. They are subject to certain requirements of filing
appropriate tax reports and many of them have done so. We continue to urge
Secretaries of Lodges, who often serve as Secretaries of Temple Associations,
and the Masters of the constituent Lodges to make certain that the Temple
Associations are observing the tax reporting requirements of the State and
Federal Laws.
As a result of certain changes in reporting of payroll taxes, which have
occurred in the last two years, and because the Lodges were uncertain as to
whether or not their payrolls might be subject to taxation, a payroll tax
reporting service was instituted through this office. Completed State and
Federal quarterly tax reports and summaries are currently being furnished
to participating Lodges. Approximately 6S% of Lodges which might be subject to payroll tax are now participating in the program through the Grand
Lodge office.
ACCOUNTING RECORDS

Studies continue as to modern methods of effectively recording accounting and membership information.
Our own personnel, in conjunction with the Special Advisory Committee
on Fiscal Affairs, secured advice relative to the most economical and practical accounting machine techniques. Effective in the second six months of
the fiscal year 1973-74, a new accounting machine (a "mini-computer") will
be installed in our office. We anticipate the possibility of producing on our
own machine various reports now provided by outside data processing services for this office, the Grand Treasurer and the :Masonic Homes Trustees.
CoNFEI<ENCE OF GRAND SECRETARms IN NORTH AMERICA

After twelve years of membership in and service to the Conference of
Grand Secretaries in North America, your Grand Secretary has been honored
by election to the presidency of this group.
The Conference is comprised of Grand Secretaries from each of the Grand
Jurisdictions throughout North America. They meet annually during the
month of February and review matters pertinent to making the work of the
Grand Secretaries more effective in their respective jurisdictions.
The Conference in 1974 will be similar to those in the past, but I look
forward with personal anticipation to being the presiding officer. Norman
Vincent Peale, who is the Grand Prelate of the Grand Encampment of
Knights Templar, will be the principal speaker at the Annual Banquet held
by the Conference. I sincerely appreciate this recognition of the Grand Lodge
of California through me.
GRAND LODGE COMMITTEEMEN

One of the largest groups of "unsung heroes," among the many active
Masons in our Jurisdiction, are the members of the Grand Lodge Committees.
Their activities may be on Boards, Standing Committees, Special Commit-

98

PROCEED INGS OF THE

tees or special assignment groups. In many cases it is our privilege to work
directly with them or to supply information at their request. We continue
to feel great satisfaction in observing the results of the hours of committed
and gratuitous service to our organization. For the Fraternit y to compensate
these devoted Brethren for their practical knowledge and experience would
be impossible. We should be grateful for their service.
LODGE SECRETAR IES

Our respect for Lodge Officers, and particula rly Lodge Secretaries, continues to be strengthened each day. Their conscientious maintenance of Lodge
records and promptness of communication with this office make the workload
easier, both for the constituent Lodges and for this office. Lodge Officers
would do well to become aware of the many details which are so efficiently
handled by their Secretaries and which are so importan t to the smooth operation of their Lodges. We are grateful for the opportun ity of working with
these fine Brethren.
Before closing this report I would be remiss if I did not express the
appreciation of the entire staff for the unstinting and unselfish support given
by the loyal and dedicated Elective Line Officers. The leadership of Grand
Master William H. Price has brought distinction to the office. His relationship with our office staff has been warm and effective. It has been a privilege
to serve the Fraternit y through this team effort.
No man can build or stand alone. Being assured of the loyalty and support of the Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, Committeemen, Inspectors and members of Grand Lodge gives us courage and incentive to
face the future with confidence and the desire to serve the Fraternit y to the
best of our ability.
Respectfully submitted,

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:

With six of its seven members present Sunday morning, October 7, 1973,
your Committee on By-Laws began its review of the matters referred to it.
Your Committee checked and rechecked one hundred five changes made by
constituent Lodges. All of the reviewed amendments and resolutions were
found to be in order.

102

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Exhibit :S of the Grand Secretary's preliminary report, to which members
of the Grand Lodge may refer, sets forth ninety-one changes. The fourteen
changes approved by the Grand Master after said preliminary report was sent
to the printers were found to be in order. Your Committee moves that they
be included in the Grand Secretary's final report. They are

affected, the date of any Annual Communication may be changed for any
year, so the contingency should be provided for.
In ~eviewing the resolutions. having to do with the change of meeting place
by various Lodges, your Comnuttee found that in several cases a Lodge moved
to a new location without following the formal procedures set forth in the California Masonic Code, and when the Lodge notified Grand Lodge it was meeting
at the new location, such notice was the first knowledge that Grand Lodge
would have of a move having taken place. Thereafter, the Lodge would have to
take the necessary procedural steps that it should have completed prior to any
move. The procedure for changing the meeting place of a Lodge is set forth
in California Masonic Code Section 372. We would like to impress upon all
the officers in attendance here that they should check the Masonic Code and
By-Laws of their respective Lodges before making any changes in meeting
places, so that the required formalities will be completed before the move
'
rather than afterward.
This Committee wishes to commend the officers of the Lodges who so carefully followed our Masonic Code.
W~ .wish 1'? th~. the Grand Secretary and his staff for their efficiency
and diligence m gmdmg those who needed assistance in properly adopting
the changes.
Most Worshipful, we move that Grand Lodge approve the amendments
and resolutions listed in Exhibit B of the Grand Secretary's Report distributed
at this Communication with the additions hereinabove specified, and the report of the Committee on By-Laws be adopted.

Charity C<nnmittee: (C.M.C. Section 360, Article X). Chico Lodge
No. 111.
Provision for Legal Holidays: (C.M.C. Section 343, Article Ill). Alta
Loma No. 643.
As in the past, your Committee suggests that the Lodges review Article X
of their By-Laws which sets forth the maximum authority of the Charity
Committee of the Lodge during the interval between Stated Meetings.
Your Committee would like to point out that the charity provision is a
very important part of your by-laws and a ten dollar amount between Stated
Meetings may not be any charity at all.
Even though all of the amendments reviewed were approved, your Committee found that the matter of designating holidays in the by-laws remains
troublesome. Article III of the Uniform Code of By-Laws, which permits exceptions to the regular date of the Stated Meetings of a Lodge, limits the exception to legal holidays and during the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge.
With regard to legal holidays, these should be specifically named so that
there will be no misunderstanding as to whether a particular day is or is not
a holiday. Further, the particular legal holiday should be identified by NAME
and NOT by date; that is, New Year's Day is preferable to January 1 and
Independence Day is preferable to July 4, because such description leaves
no doubt that the exception applies when these days are celebrated on Monday in a year when January 1 or July 4 falls on a Sunday.
Particular attention should be paid to this point of designation of holidays, and especially for Monday night Lodges. By action of Congress, several
holidays will be celebrated on Monday even though they fall on another day
of the week. All Monday night Lodges should contact the Grand Secretary's
office before changing the holidays.
Also, a Lodge should provide for an alternate date in case its Stated Meeting falls during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. While only those
Lodges whose Stated Meeting is during the second week of the month are

Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES H. GRACE, Chairman

reviewed each record and finds that the proper procedure was followed in each
case and that the results are supported by the respective records and that
there were no miscarriages of justice. We, therefore, offer the following
resolution:
RESOLVED: that in each of the above numbered Trial Records the
judgement and the result thereof be ratified, approved and confirmed.
A petition for restoration in Trial Record 789 has carefully been considered, we believe the applicant is worthy to be restored to the rights and
privileges of Masonry, and we, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: that the petition for restoration in Trial Record 789 be
granted.
Your Committee feels it is appropriate at this time to remind all officers
and particularly Secretaries of subordinate Lodges that it is necessary to have
a trial master appointed for every Masonic trial. The powers and duties of a
Master of a Lodge do not include the authority to preside over a trial or
make investigation and findings where no trial is had. That authority comes
only from appointment by the Grand Master. We further suggest that the
members of the ~rievance Committee, as well as that inexhaustible source of
information, the office of the Grand Secretary, are available throughout the
year to assist in meeting the technicalities of Masonic trials. Please call on
any of them should you feel you need assistance or desire information.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1421
An application for restoration has been received from a former member of
San Mateo Lodge No. 226. The member was originally charged in the courts
with the commission of felonies, to wit: the commission of abortion and
conspiracy to commit abortion. His conviction in March of. 1954 after a plea
of guilty, later resulted in his expulsion from our Fraternity after a trial by
commission in his Lodge on November 4, 1954, which was affirmed by this
Grand Lodge on October 27, 1955.
He has now submitted an application for restoration, supported by many
letters of recommendation and evidence of rehabilitation. This application
was submitted to our Grand Lodge on August 15, 1973, after notification to
San Mateo Lodge No. 226 on July 24, 1973.

106

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Section 767 of the California Masonic Code sets forth:
"Whenever any expelled Mason desires to petition the Grand Lodge for
restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry, he shall, in writing, notify
the Lodge which expelled him, if it still be in existence, of his intention so to
do, at least 60 days before the Annual Communication at which his petition
is to be presented, accompanying said notice with a copy of such intended
petition and before said petition shall be considered by the Grand Lodge,
proof of the giving of said notice to the Lodge shall be furnished."
As set forth in this Section, the purpose of this requirement is to permit
the members of the Lodge to be thus informed and to, thereafter, vote by
written ballot to approve or disapprove the petition, which approval or disapproval must then be reported to the Grand Lodge.
The record discloses that no copy of the petition was presented to the
Lodge and as a consequence no ballot by the Lodge was taken. In fact, the
petition itself was not presented to the Grand Lodge until August 15, 1973,
less than 60 days before our Annual Communication.
It is regretable that proper procedure was not followed, but under the
circumstances your Committee has no alternative but to recommend denial
of the petition, and to request the Grand Secr~ta7 to ~otify the appli.cant
of the reasons therefor in order that the application nught be resubnutted
at our next Annual Communication, if the applicant so desires, so that proper
consideration might be had on its merits.
For the reasons heretofore stated we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED that the application for restoration to San Mateo Lodge
No. 226 in Trial Record No. 1421 be denied.
Adopted.
TRIAL REcoRD No. 2017
The accused, a member of Oceanside Lodge No. 381, was charged with
lewd and lascivious conduct with a nine year old girl, a misdemeanor. He
plead guilty and the court placed him on probation subject to certain conditions, including a requirement that he obtain psychiatric care and that he
not allow children to be alone with him in certain areas of his place of

In 1972, charges were filed to which the accused plead guilty, though he
maintained he intended no improper conduct. The trial master found the
accused guilty, received letters of character reference and fixed the penalty
at suspension.
In the opinion of your Grievance Committee, the record amply supports
the verdict of guilty of Unmasonic conduct.
However the serious nature of the offense, that of improper and illegal
sexual cond~ct with a nine year old girl, is so violative of the principle of
Masonry as to warrant expulsion rather than mere suspension.

Adopted.
TRIAL REcoRD No. 2018
The accused, a member of Oroville Lodge No. 103, was charged with Unmasonic conduct, specifically that "on or about the 10th day of January,
1967, he was convicted of perjury in the Superior Court of Butte County."
The charge was dated September 1, 1972. The charge did not specify that the
accused did in fact commit perjury. The accused entered a plea of guilty, but
alleged mitigating circumstances. The Master investigated the matter and
suspended the accused.
By his plea, the accused did admit his conviction, but did not admit having
committed perjury. In his explanation to the Master of the Lodge of the
"mitigating circumstances," the accused denied having done anything wilful
or deliberate to constitute perjury, thus denying one of the elements of the
offense.
Conviction of a crime in a State or Federal Court, even conviction of a
felony, is not at this time a Masonic offense. By admitting his conviction for
perjury, the accused did not admit any Masonic offense. A finding that the
accused was guilty of having been convicted of perjury is not a finding that
the accused committed perjury and is, therefore, not a finding that the accused
committed a Masonic offense.
Since no Masonic offense was shown to have been committed, your committee offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption.
RESOLVED, that action of the Master be reversed and set aside and
that trial record No. 2018 be returned to the Lodge for the filing of such
amended charge as appears appropriate and for any resulting proceedings.
Adopted.
TRIAL REcoRD No. 2019
The accused, a member of Indian Wells Valley Lodge No. 691 was charged
with Unmasonic conduct in two specifications.
The first specification alleges that the accused, for a period of time
visited the accuser's home while he (the accuser) was at work and while
attending Lodge meetings.
The second specification alleges that the accused transported the accuser's
wife and her children to San Francisco and that she later wanted a divorce
and the accused wanted to marry her.
The accused plead not guilty and a trial was held. The accused was found
guilty and the penalty of suspension was imposed by the trial commission.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

PROCEE DINGS OF THE

108

The issue which concerns the Grievance Committee is whether the specifications as written set forth specifically conduct which is Unmasonic.
Committing a crime is Unmasonic conduct. Committing an immoral act
is Unmasonic conduct. Neither of these are alleged in these specifications.
Visiting another Mason's home while he is away is not Unmasonic conduct.
That is all that he is charged with in that specification.
In the second specification we find the accused took the accuser's wife and
children to San Francisco arid she later wanted a divorce and the accused
wanted to marry her.
The evidence revealed that the accused did take the accuser's wife and
children to San Francisco to visit her relatives.
Further evidence presented in this case would support charges far more
serious than those originally filed, consequently the following:
RESOLUTION is submitted and we recommend its adoption.
RESOLVED that the finding of the Trial Commission be set aside and
that the trial record be returned to the Lodge for retrial and that the Lodge
be directed to amend the specification to conform to the evidence.
Adopted.

The accused answered the charges and admitted he falsified his application. His excuse was that he said something about it and was told that since it

reasons for any previous rejection. Your committee has traditionally held that
any falsification of an application is most reprehensible and deserves expulsion. We therefore offer the following resolution:

TRIAL REcoRD No. 2022
The accused, a member of Capital City Lodge No. 499, was charged with
unmasonic conduct in that he was alleged to have taken property valued in
excess of two hundred dollars.
The accused pled nolo contendere to the charges of grand theft in the

The accused did not request a Masonic trial and admitted his guilt to the
Masonic charges. The Trial Master properly found the accused guilty and
fixed the penalty at suspension.
It has always been the policy of the Committee that, after a member has
committed an act serious enough to be classified as a felony, he should be
expelled.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption.
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master in Record No. 2022
be approved, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that the member
be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

At the Ritual Committee meeting of December, 1972, the Grand Lecturer
instructed each of the Assistant Grand Lecturers to arrange scheduling of
Inspectors Conferences in their respective Divisions in such manner that the
Ritual work could be concluded by noon on Saturday, thereby leaving the
entire afternoon free for discussion of a proposed leadership program to be
developed by the Ritual Committee for the use of the Lodges of California,
this, together with a Lodge system of Candidate education.
The response of the Inspectors to these two proposed programs was almost
overwhelming, and the Ritual Committee is now proceeding with all possible
dispatch in the preparation of a complete program of leadership and Candidate
education for the use of the Lodges.

INSPECTORAL CORPS

The past twelve months has brought further changes in the Inspectoral
Corps, and several of our old and respected friends have retired after many
years of devoted service to Masonry.
Such men as, John Cunning and Frank Valentine in Division One: Lewis
Tarr, Clyde Sinclair, Ray Burdg, and Preston Mecum in Division Two: Paul
Turner, Hazelton French and John Burzan in Division Three: Leo Brenneman
in Division Four: Ray Peterson, Jim Wellet, Clete Smith and Irving Zuckerman in Division Five: and Bob Higgins, Gene Gilbertson, Leonard Babcock,
Milo Ensminger and Roy Knapp in Division Six. Two of our fine Inspectors
from Division Three resigned at the close of Grand Lodge last year to accept
assignments in the Grand Lodge Line for this year. Dan Rowlands was appointed to serve as our Grand Bible Bearer, and John F. Roberts was elected
Junior Grand Warden. Both have brought even further honor to the Inspectoral Corps through exemplary service in these new assignments.
Death claimed one of our Inspectors this year. We were both shocked and
saddened at the sudden passing of Earl Lowe, Inspector of District 610 in
Pomona. Earl was truly a giant among men; a true Mason in every respect
who believed in, and exemplified the basic tenets of our Ancient Craft. To all
of these good men and devoted workers in Masonry who gave so much and
asked so little in return, we extend our sincere thanks and appreciation.
Vacancies were created by each of these departures, and we feel that the
Corps has been greatly strengthened by the appointment of several eager
young Inspectors who are establishing new standards of excellence in performance by utilizing new concepts in leadership . . .
They are: - Kenneth Himmler and Delbert Wade in Division One:
Charles Pitt, William Rose, Ray Young and Lowell Daniels in Division Two:
George Carter, Louis Rusconi, Bernard Cohn, George Brown and Roland
Renshaw in Division Three: John Bench in Division Four: Robert Woodburn,
Samuel Harris, Richard Read and Robert Lawson in Division Five, and
Lavergne Gallagher, Joe Negus, Wally Lewis, Walter Marshall, Ron Broaddus, Melvin Schuster, and the newest Inspector in California, Zeke Nakamatsu

LODGE ACTIVITIES

The highlight of Lodge activity for 1973 is the long hoped for and finally
achieved million dollar total of individual donations to our Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund. What a magnificent achievement, and how very proud we
can all be as members of a Fraternity that literally "puts its money where its
mouth is."
The Inspectors' reports also indicate satisfactory performance for all
Lodges in the required program area, with all Lodges having either sponsored
or participated in, programs of Public Schools Week observance and Constitu~
tion Observance. A small percentage of the Lodges have also sponsored some
Gra~d Lodge Activity such as, Cornerstone Ceremonies for Masonic Temples,
Pubhc Schools and other Public Buildings, as well as Dedication Ceremonies
for Temples, City Hall Buildings and Libraries. It is pleasing to note that in
the main, all Lodges are holding sufficient Ritual practice sessions to assure
continuing high levels of proficiency among their Officers, and all but a few of
the Lodges are members of, and participate in, District Officers Associations
which are formed and maintained by the Inspectors.
That portion of the Inspectors' reports concerning Lodge growth, availability of leadership and community involvement reflects problems of some
magnitude, and it is here that our attention should be focused. Lodge membership is on the decline - Lodge attendance is extremely poor - Lodges are
experiencing great difficulty in obtaining new Officer material - Losses by
death, suspension llnd <limit are up; petitions for the degrees are down. 52 of the 183 Inspectors report that 208 of our Lodges are NOT filling the
needs of their Community, and 62 Inspectors feel that in 248 of the Lodges
Masonry is NOT advancing. Startling? ... Yes, and I think it is high tim;
we faced a few facts:
Masonry in California is NOT growing, it is losing ground! Young men
are no longer seeking admission to our Lodges because they do not relate to
our ideals. By the same token, it must be noted that millions of our young
people find it impossible to adjust to our society. Reasons for this perplexing
phenomenon are not clear, however, I suspect that an answer must be found
somewhere in the region that we are just not communicating with them.
When men seem to lose interest in the finer things of life - when our
Churches and all associations of noble purpose are suffering losses in membership and seek in vain for devoted members, can we in Freemasonry expect to
escape a like portion? In spite of all this, there are remedies to apply, and it is
imperative that we immediately set about implementing such remedies.
Our Ritual says that we are a "Progressive Science," and yet, we refuse
to really make that come true. The education of our Craft in the principals,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

meaning and History of Freemasonry bas been sadly neglected. In many of
our Lodges, Masonic education begins and ends with the conferral of the
Third Degree.
There is no question that the Ritual of Freemasonry, when properly
conferred is the best devised by man for Fraternal purposes. The Ritual is the
means b.j which men become members of the Fraternity, but the conferring
of degrees, no matter how well done, was never intended to be.the whole ~dea.
Important as the conferring of degrees may be, a total emphasis on the Ritual
tends to obscure other important parts of Masonry. We must start to give to
our members an understanding, and the meaning of the degrees through which
they have gone. We must give them the historical background and explain
what it has stood for in the past and what it must stand for now. This, we
cannot do unless we ourselves have the knowledge and ability to impart it to
others hence the importance which the Ritual Committee bas placed upon
the p;eparation of a program of leadership and candidate education. We
believe the only way to stop the downward trend of Masonry is through good
strong, intelligent, well informed and understanding leadership at all levels
of Masonry! The Good Lord willing and the creeks don't rise, a program to
assist in the development of this type of leadership will be forthcoming from
the hands of the Ritual Committee in the early part of 1974.
In the meantime, considering the great difficulty many Lodges experience
in obtaining new Officer material, I must again strongly recommend that all
Lodges do away with the traditional 7 to 9 year line, and i~ediately institute
the practice of commencing the progressive line at the Junior Deacon's
station. I am convinced that this shortened period would induce many excellently qualified Brothers to accept appointments as Lodge Officers and continue through the chairs to the Station of Worshipful Master.

HAWAllAN MASONRY

I was privileged again this year to visit the Lodges of Hawaii. In early
March, in the company of Assistant Grand Lecturer lnysses G. Patropulos, I
flew to the fiftieth State, and while observing at first hand the condition of
Masonry in the Islands, we conducted schools of instruction for the Officers
and Brethren in the Lodges of Kilauea, Maui and Kauai, then moving into
Honolulu we conducted all day schools on Saturday and Sunday for the
Officers, Coaches and Brethren of all ten Hawaiian Lodges. Each of these
schools was very well attended, and never before have I witnessed such eagerness to properly exemplify the Ritual. The three island Inspectors, John
Pringle, Alex Bell and Bill McKee continue to do a splendid job in the
Lodges of Hawaii even though they are handicapped by the great distances
which separate the Lodges in the outer islands, and the fact that unlike the
California Inspectors, they are exposed to schools of instruction on the mainland only twice each year. In consideration of the Hawaiian Lodges having
requested it, it is our intention to have the Assistant Grand Lecturer conduct

CORNERSTONE CEREMONIES

On twenty-five occasions this year the Grand Master assembled the Grand

Officers at various locations within the Grand Jurisdiction for the purpose
of laying the Cornerstone of a material building. The majority of these Ceremonies were performed at buildings already completed, and where wall
plaques, or nameplates were placed rather than an actual Cornerstone. Following the Annual Communication of 1972, the Ritual Committee was appointed
as a Special Committee to study our Grand Lodge Cornerstone Ceremony and
make the necessary changes to adapt it for use at Ceremonies where plaques
or nameplates were placed. Jn our study it became almost immediately apparent that any change would destroy the Antiquity of this beautiful Ceremony. The Committee agreed that the Ceremony could be just as well adapted
by presentation of a short preamble explaining the use of the Cornerstone
Ceremony for placing a plaque.
The Ritual Committee, utilizing works of Past Grand Master Eugene S.
Hopp, Past Grand Master Herb Huebner and Grand Master William H. Price,
has prepared such a preamble, a copy of which we append to this report for
the approval of this Grand Lodge, and having to the best of our ability discharged the duties of our assignment, we respectfully request that this Special
Committee be now discharged.
At each of tpe aforementioned Cornerstone Ceremonies, and at many
other Ceremonies and receptions this year, the Grand Master bas delivered
addresses of great interest to the Craft. Unfortunately, a relative few were
privileged to hear these very informative speeches, and the benefit of these
remarks has been lost to us because no permanent record was made. The
Very Reverend George L. Davis, Grand Chaplain, recognizing the great value
of retaining such material, bas suggested that recordings could be made on
each such occasion, and the tapes sent to the Grand Lodge for storage. I am in
complete agreement with this suggestion, and in order that speeches of future
Grand Masters may be retained for the benefit of the Craft, it is my recommendation that this Grand Lodge adopt the policy that henceforth, all major
addresses of the Grand Master be recorded on cassette tapes of good quality,
such tapes to be placed on file in the Grand Secretary's office for future use of
the Lodges, to be distributed by the Grand Secretary with the approval of the
Grand Master.
INSPECTORS' TERM OF OFFICE

The Grand Master, in his message to the Grand Lodge last year, questioned the reasonability of the term of office of Inspectors commencing on
January 1st and ending on December 31st each year. It was his opinion that

128

129

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Inspectors' terms of office should run concurrently with the term of office of
the Grand Master. All committees concurred, and the recommendation was
adopted. This change has not proven as beneficial as was anticipated, and in
some areas it has actually proved a detriment, particularly in the qualification
of Lodge Officers. The mid-October appointment of a new Inspector requires
that he become familiar with, and qualify all Lodge Officers who require
certificates, in less than 45 days. Other problems are created by the Inspector's term concluding on the last day of the Annual Communication: This
requires the retiring Inspector to attend Grand Lodge, and denies the new
Inspector the benefit of attending the Annual Grand Lecturer's School and the
Annual Communication. Masonry is not served by this practice. Difficulty is
experienced by new Inspectors in filling out the Inspectors' report forms at the
conclusion of each Lodge's fiscal year which falls on June 30th due to the
fact that he has been in office only one half year. All of these disadvantages
would be resolved if the Inspector's term of office started and stopped in midyear instead of October. In an effort to better serve the needs of Masonry in
general, I recommend that the Inspectors' term of office be changed to end
on June 30th and commence on the 1st day of July each year.
It would be impossible to thank all those who have so graciously assisted
the Grand Lecturer in carrying out the duties of this office, but I must extend
our deepest gratitude to all of the 183 District Inspectors who have more
than adequately demonstrated their complete loyalty and devotion this year.
To the six wonderful Masons who serve as Assistant Grand Lecturers,
without whose total cooperation all efforts would have been in vain, I say,
Thank you, from the bottom of my heart! Thanks are also due the Grand
Secretary and his wonderful office staff, all the Appointive Grand Lodge
Officers, the members of the Elective Grand Lodge Line, and particularly the
Grand Master, who has taught me so very much, and whose friendship and
support have meant so very much to me this year, for they have been the true
inspiration of my Masonic career.
And now, in conclusion I must remind us all that much hard work is required of us all, particularly all who are leaders in Masonry. We know from
past experience that Freemasonry has survived in worse times than these.
What we now must do is stop feeling sorry for ourselves and start acting like
Masons - and remember, when Lodges make Masons in fact, as well as by
Ritual, our losses will cease to be a problem and Masonry shall once again
grow in California!

Through the years this Cornerstone Ceremony has remained unchanged,
and its beautiful symbolism is as meaningful today as in ages past. To some,
the words you are about to hear in this Ceremony may be meaningless; but if
each of you will listen carefully and think about these words as they are
spoken, you will find them fraught with significance, expressing a beautiful
conct.pt and philosophy.

APPENDIX A
PREAMBLE TO CORNERSTONE CEREMONY
The Ceremony which you are about to witness is one which has been
employed for many centuries in the laying of Cornerstones. Operative Masons
are credited with the Ceremonial laying of Cornerstones from time immemorial. They had, and our present day Speculative, or Philosophical Masons
have a ceremony which originated before any record was kept.
As far back as Biblical times, the words, cornerstone and foundationstone had become so commonplace that they were used in the Old Testament
in both a figurative and literal sense. We read in Isaiah 28: 16 "Therefore
thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation, a stone, a
tried stone, a precious Cornerstone, a sure foundation," and in the book of
Job the Lord posed the rhetorical question to Job, concerning the earth;
"Wbo laid the Cornerstone thereof; when the morning stars sang together, and
all the Sons of God shouted for Joy?"
The cornerstone of an edifice in ancient times was laid in the northeast
corner of what was to be the building, and the stone to be laid had to be the
most perfect that the builders' art could produce. Each surface of the stone
was at a 90 degree angle relative to each adjacent surface, thus it was considered to be square, or true.
From it and upon it radiated the structure which formed the walls, and
. stone.
' roof of the' edifice. It was truly and literally, foundation
eventually the
With modern building construction, cornerstones are now symbolic rather
than functional. They are frequently laid when the building is complete, and
oft times are simply wall plaques or nameplates, placed in a wall, or in the
floor of an approach.
Some people are naturally curious as to why Masonic Lodges are chosen
to perform Cornerstone Ceremonies. We feel it both proper and fitting for
Masons to participate in such Ceremonies, because Traditionally and historically Masons are builders: From those Operative Masons of the Middle
ages wh~ constructed stately cathedrals and other magnificent edifices, some
of whlch still stand today; to the modern Speculative, or symbolically attuned
Masons who are builders of character in Men. Today's Ceremony is identical
to that which was used by George Washington in 1792, when acting as Grand
Master of Masons in Maryland, he laid the Cornerstone of our Nation's
Capitol in Washington. It is also the same as that used by the Grand Lodge
of California in 1861 to lay the Cornerstone of our State Capitol building in
Sacramento.

DEVELOPMENT AT DECOTO

At the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge in 1972 the Trustees reported the Geological and Seismic Site Evaluation under the able direction of
Dr. Lloyd S. Cluff, a partner of Woodward-Lundgren & Associates of Oakland
and one of the world's leading authorities in the study and evaluation of
earthquake faults. It was concluded that the beautiful site of the Decoto
Home was not bisected by the Hayward Earthquake Fault, as had once been
thought, due to an inaccurate U. S. Geodetic Survey, and the actual location
of the fault was finally and accurately determined.
This encouraging intelligence compelled a study and report from a design
standpoint with respect to the structural stability of the present buildings
as well as the requirements of future buildings for reasonable safety in relation to earthquak~ hazards. The study was undertaken by the architectural
firm of Hertzka & Knowles, A.I.A., in conjunction with Pregnoff-MatheuBeebe, Structural Engineers. The results of their investigation were coordinated with the findings of the geologists and on February 1, 1973, a comprehensive final report was issued, stating in part as follows:
"The results of our study indicate that the presently developed area
of the site is essentially underlain by stable materials and the building
areas should perform satisfactorily even under the largest postulated
earthquake loading conditions. The natural materials at the site have
high bearing capacities and excellent resistance to deformation during
seismic events."
Certain additional test borings were requested and resulted in equally
satisfactory findings. Some preliminary cost studies were undertaken to determine the feasibility of the rehabilitation of the existing buildings to conform to the new and very strict building codes applicable to facilities such as
our Home. It was determined that although it is economically prudent to
rehabilitate the existing nursing home and Adams Hall, it will be necessary
to replace the Administration building, the north and south wings, and the
dining and kitchen facility in various phases.

During the past year, meetings have been held on a twice a month basis
by the Decoto Redevelopment Committee in conjunction with the architects
and structural and mechanical engineers, geologists, and food experts as required. Long term projections of our care needs have been made and the
financial requirements carefully evaluated.
At a meeting of the full Board in Los Angeles on March 11, 1973, a resolution authorizing the architects to prepare a Master plan was unanimously

Masonic Homes with the adoption of a Master Plan. This Plan will be

and the details explained in open session.

scheduled for rehabilitation), plans were undertaken to provide interim
kitchen and dining accommodations on the ground floor of the Administration
building. This initial step has now been completed and is not only functional
and attractive but also allows the continuance of our own food preparation
as opposed to a program of catering meals.

Trustees are pleased to report that this need has been partially filled by
George Jeffery with extensive experience in Y.M.C.A. activity, who will serve
as an administrative assistant.

DECOTO OPERATIONS
The resident population at the Decoto Home has remained well over 400
since the last Trustees' report to Grand Lodge. As the Lodges were notified by
the Grand Master, the maximum capacity has been reached for the care of
non-ambulatory residents resulting in approved applications being assigned
to a waiting list and investigating outside relief as an alternative. This points
most effectively to the important need our Home fulfills, but at the same time
reminds us of the urgency of providing facilities for a greater number of our
elderly brethren, their wives, and widows.
Worshipful Hugh B. Herring, Administrator of the Decoto Home, has
not only continued his service to the residents in the outstanding manner for
which he is noted, but has been of invaluable assistance to the Board in
making studies and supplying data essential to decisions necessary to the
redevelopment program. Among his well-received innovations was the creation
of "satellite" dining rooms in Adams Hall and in the north wing so that all
other residents may be comfortably accommodated in the new main dining
area. Brother Herring has also arranged to have much of the remodeling
work undertaken by the present staff of the Home, devising the means of
moving all kitchen, dining equipment, and furniture to the new location at a
considerable savings in cost and at a minimum inconvenience to the residents.
Our Administrator has been laboring under the handicap of being without
assistance in the heavy responsibility of not only day by day operations but
in the planning for the rehabilitation and redevelopment program. The

135

OUTSIDE REUEF
From time to time the Board of Trustees extends outside relief in the form
of a monthly monetary allowance in those instances where admission to the
Home is not advisable or practical. Such financial assistance does not exceed
the per capita cost at the Home and is usually considerably less. While
residents at the Home assign such assets as they may have to the Home upon
admission, there has been no assignment required from applicants for outside
relief.
With the advice of legal counsel, the Board has adopted a form of agreement to be executed by recipients of outside relief by which they agree to
repay during life as they are able, in whole or in part, any relief funds advanced to them, and in the event of death, then repayment shall be from their
estates.
In equity and fairness, and in consideration of the assignments required
of residents, the Board recommends the foregoing reimbursement procedure as
a policy, and requests that it be referred to the proper committee for study
and recommendations to Grand Lodge for approval.

COVIN A OPERATIONS AND REDEVELOPMENT
The dream of 196 7 which envisioned a new Home for Children which
would provide for family style living in residential type of homes became a
reality with the Cornerstone and Dedication ceremonies at the Covina Home
on August 18, 1973. Ten new cottage units have been completed along with a
magnificent Community Center, all surrounded and entwined with sweeping
lawns, shrubbery, and flowering trees.
The cost of the entire building program, estimated at $2,700,000 has
been completely financed by reserve funds, accumulated over the years
through the generosity of the Fraternity and its friends. With no fear of
contradiction, the Covina Home for Children now stands as the finest facility
of its kind in the country and one in which the Masons of California and
Hawaii can take the greatest pride.
Brother James C. Blaine, whose account as Administrator of the Covina
Home accompanies this report, now has under his supervision, in addition to
ten family homes, a modern infirmary, recreation, library, and study hall
facilities, a beauty parlor, a most modern kitchen, dining room, parlor
laundry, and administrative offices. The ever-flowing DeMolay Fountai~
reminds the children of the love and concern others have for their future.
The new Home, however modem and beautiful, is not the end goal. The
principal objective of the Home is to prepare the children, whose care is the

privilege of the Masonic Fraternity, for a full and enriched life in the !~rs
following their departure from Covina. The Trustees are most appreciative
and grateful for the dedication and devotion of Administrator James C.
Blaine in his guidance and help toward achieving this aspiration.

Gifts and bequests specifying use at the Covina Home totaled $283,167

HISTORY AND DEDICATION CEREMONY

DONALD B. MCCAW,

BURTON MEYER, JR.

MASONIC HOME FOR CHILDREN
By RALPH HEAD, Trustee
AUGUST 18, 1973
From the beginning of recorded history and before, men have been builders. As men of the New Stone Age moved from their caves, they began to erect
shelters from the elements which, eons later, the Old English would describe
by the word "home."
Over the centuries men have continued to build factories, hospitals, libraries, schools, and office buildings which seem to scrape the sky.
In California, first Indians, then Spaniards, immigrants from Mexico, and
the early Americans who came across the plains and by way of Cape Hope
all contributed to the building of the Golden State.
After the organization of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
in 1850, Masonic temples began to rise along the shores of the Pacific Ocean,
in the mountains, in the valleys, and on the deserts. Freemasonry's first, most
imposing structure was the Grand Lodge Temple erected in San Francisco in
June, 1860, but that in which the fraternity took its greatest pride was the
Masonic Home at Decoto, dedicated in October 1898, and first occupied by
widows and orphans in 1899. By 1909 the children had moved to a new home
in San Gabriel, and when river flood waters invaded the property a trade was
effected which resulted in a new home on the very property on which we now
stand and whose cornerstone was laid on May 20, 1916.
And so it was for fifty-three years a surrogate home for children until in
1969 construction began on a new home whose design provided for family
style living and whose aura of protection, safety, comfort, and stability surrounds us today.
It has been a custom dating back to antiquity to dedicate or consecrate a
building to a divinity, just as the Temple of Solomon was erected to God and
dedicated to His Holy Name. Later, those things which were sacred were consecrated to the worship of God, while the profane were dedicated to a patron
saint, or to certain principles or ideals.
A Masonic lodge is consecrated to the Glory of God, dedicated to the
memory of St. John the Evangelist and of St. John the Baptist, while Masonic
temples are dedicated to Freemasonry, Virtue, and Universal Benevolence.
Today we have given pause in our daily lives to lay the cornerstone for a
new, yet continuing home for children, whose care and keep for a relatively
short segment of their lifetime is the great privilege of the Fraternity of Free
and Accepted Masons of California and Hawaii.
We now wish to rededicate this home built for the continuing protection

Ass't. Vice-President
L. HAROLD ANDERSON

Most Worshipful, it is recorded that on the twentieth .of May, 1916, the
Grand Lodge of California was opened in the hall of Covma Lodge No. 334
at Covina for the purpose of laying this cornerstone. The ceremony was
presided over by the Right Worshipful Francis V. Keesling, Deputy Grand
Master.
It is interesting to note that the cornerstone was laid on May 20th of th~t
year, but the ceremony of dedication of the new b~ildings did not occur un~il
September 8, 1917. It would seem to be an indication of progress that, while
seventeen months separated the two ceremonies 57 years ago, today we are
.
conducting the corresponding ceremonies on the same da~.
The record shows that the laying of the cornerstone m 1916 was billed as
"the most important public event of the year." In quoting from the 1916
Proceedings, "It was an ideal day and the little city of Covin~ was decked out
in flags, bunting and flowers, while thousands of people lmed the avenu~
along the line of march to the Home. Of automobiles alone there were SIX
hundred parked near the place of the ceremonies."
The parade was formed at the hall of Covina Lodge No. 334 and consisted of more than twenty marching units including bands, drill teams,
commandries the tilers of all the Lodges of Los Angeles County with drawn
swords, stew~rds of all the Lodges, deacons of all the Lodges, secretaries a?d
treasurers of all the Lodges, followed by hundreds of Master Masons in white
aprons.
.
On the day of the dedication, which was September 8, 1917, cunously
enough, Francis V. Keesling was then Grand Master and presi~ed over the

Home participated in the ceremony.

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

of the children entrusted to our care, recognizing the important responsibility
which is ours. In order to fulfill this duty, we now dedicate this Home to
Love, to Learning, and to Loyalty.
To Love, because it is the most noble of all human emotions, just as the
Apostle Paul wrote ". . . abideth Faith, Hope, Love, these three, but the
greatest of these is Love." May this Home continue to abound in that allencompassing Love which binds us together into families, into circles of
friends and brothers, and which gives us strength and joy throughout our
lives.
To Loyalty, because it is the epitome of those great and honorable lineaments to which, it is our hope and prayer, the children who bless this Home
will aspire. Loyalty is faithfulness to family and friends. Loyalty is devotion
to God. Loyalty is allegiance to Country. May Loyalty be the scholarship
which the family members of this Home will carry out from these walls and
maintain for the rest of their lives.
And finally, we dedicate this Home to Learning, because from Learning
evolves knowledge and only from knowledge do men gain access to the truth.
Learning is the means by which we come to know the seven arts and sciences,
but more important, how to live abundantly and harmoniously with each
other. This Home, dedicated to Learning, is the teacher of the lessons of life
for tomorrow's leaders who pass along this way.
Within these walls may Love and Peace prevail, may there always be
Loyalty which is allegiance to family, God, and Country, and may Learning
lead to knowledge and knowledge to the truth.

397 Lodges in California and Hawaii; 29 states and 6 foreign countries;
Switzerland, India, England, Germany, China and Scotland.
Our residents have been very active this year. Shopping trips are daily
now. The Arts and Crafts Department is being used to its capacity and our
"Masonic Mall' is always crowded. Our Brethren from the United (Airlines)
Square Club hosted a trip to the San Francisco Airport and arranged a tour
through the United Airline shops and served refreshments aboard one of their
large planes. Our thanks to the United Square Club also for the console color
television set they donated to our Nursing Unit.
Did you know that:
Since our Masonic Home was opened to residents on October 12, 1898,
we have admitted 4,098 residents up to the end of the fiscal year
June 30, .1973?
That the operating budget for the Home at Union City for the fiscal
year 1972-73 was $2,388,284.88?
That the Masonic Home at Union City employs 215 people?
That no monies or aid of any type is accepted from Federal, State or
local agencies? The Home is supported by the Brethren of the Masonic Fraternity only.
That visitors are welcomed and urged to visit your Masonic Home any
day of the week?
Our Fraternal thanks to the many Brethren, Lodges, Chapters and other
organizations who donated many useful articles, from clothing to jams and
jellies, television sets to material for our Arts and Crafts. Your donations are
appreciated and are put to good use. Our thanks also to the many groups who
put on very entertaining programs for our enjoyment.
My thanks to the Board of Trustees, the San Francisco Grand Lodge
Office and our own loyal employees who have made this a successful year.
Respectfully submitted,
HUGH B. HERRING, Administrator

illnesses. We have continued our yearly physical examinations and have been

Our children have been involved in many and varied recreational and
cultural activities: Concerts, weekend and residential camping at Big Bear
and at the beach have been enjoyed by all. Special trips to cultural and fine
arts exhibits have been arranged. Opportunities to develop special skills in
music, dancing, scuba diving, oil painting have proven to be extremely meaningful in the lives of the children.
We are proud of the children under our care. As is the case with all
families, our children also have responsibilities that go with the many
privileges that they receive. Each child has daily and weekly responsible
chores to complete. These include table waiting, dishwashing, sweeping, lawn
mowing, weeding, car washing, sidewalk cleaning, scrubbing, window washing
and other responsibilities that go with "home living."
Each child maintains a small "checking" account, from which he is paid
his allowance, and each child is encouraged to establish a savings account so
that he may have a small "nest egg" when he graduates.
It is gratifying and heartwarming to observe the continuous benefits
presented to our children through the dedicated efforts of the Masonic
affiliated groups. As a result of these donations, our boys and girls have received special sports equipment, interesting and valuable stamps for their
collections, tickets to outstanding events, (i.e. plays, movies, sports events,
circuses), ponies and riding equipment, picnics with clowns, puppet shows,
and other specialized entertainment. All of these contributions have helped
provide special and memorable events in the lives of our youngsters.
We extend tQ our many brethren and friends an invitation to visit Covina
when time permits. We are grateful to the Board of Trustees and the Masons
of California and Hawaii for their continued interest and support.

It is with pleasure that the annual report for the Masonic Home for
Children for the year 1972 -1973 is hereby submitted.
June 1973 saw four seniors graduate - Sylvia Cabana, sponsored by
Fontana Lodge No. 658; Debra Richardson sponsored by Fresno Lodge
No. 247; Robin Gockley sponsored by St. Elmo Lodge No. 697; and Allan
Petzold, a sojourner from Warwick Lodge No. 544 from Warwick, New York.

of June 30, 1973 remained at 57 - 18 girls - 39 boys.
