Our Covina Redevelopment Program will soon be at an end, with the
completion of our final two resident cottages. Upon completion, we will be
equipped and licensed to accommodate a maximum of 80 children. The floor
plans of our cottages allow for brothers and sisters to remain together. The
cottage plan for Masonic Home living has surp~ed all expectations.
This past year has seen our first year in our new Administration Complex.
We are making full use of a small infirmary, a more "formal" parlor, a
beautiful new dining room and kitchen complex, and a multi-purpose library
room. Music and quiet recreation are held in a leisure time room. These
facilities with the Administration Offices surround a multi-purpose patio,
which bas, as its focal point, the DeMolay sponsored Fountain of the Future.
The Administration Complex has proven to be very functional.
Our children are an integral part of the larger community. Many of our
boys and girls are active in Scouting, Camp Fire Girls, Little League, Pop
Warner Football, DeMolay, and other community activities. In turn, we
share our facilities with the Citrus League, DeMolay, local Job's Daughters
Choirs, P.T.A. Council Board, and other committee groups. Our children,
staff, and administration are actively engaged in many and varied activities.
Currently, we have 16 Masonic Home alumni furthering their education
with funds made possible by the Fraternity. Following this report is the current list of those deserving young men and women.
This past year has seen our Home family enjoying relatively good health.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

LODGES WITH LARGEST AVERAGE GIFTS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 4lst Annual
Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1972.
INCOME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND
During the past year our Permanent Endowment Fund earned
$1,355,619.31, which amount has been transferred to the operating accounts
of our two Masonic Homes. This amount would be equivalent to an additional contribution of $6.05 from each member. We can be thankful for
these earnings from our Permanent Endowment Fund.
BEQUESTS, GIFTS AND MEMORIALS
Bequests in the amount of $305,591.06 were received into the Endowment Fund. In addition, $920,902.07 were received by the Homes in bequests
from estates where the Endowment Fund was not specifically designated in
the will.
Gifts from individuals and organizations amounted to $8326.56, and
Memorials added $31,001.24 to our funds. Thus, bequests, gifts from organizations and individuals, and memorials amounted to a total of $1,265,820.93,
or $202,881.34 more than a year ago.
You can readily understand that bequests are a source of substantial
funds so necessary to the operation of our two Homes.
INDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTIONS
THROUGH LODGES
We are most pleased to report a new all-time high as individual contributions through Lodges totaled $1,010,382.92. This amount is $51,225.02 more
than was contributed in 1972. The average amount per contributing member
is $9.08 as compared to $8.60 last year - making the percentage 49.72% as
compared with 49.06% a year ago. This is indeed a fine accomplishment, yet
it still represents the efforts of less than 50% of our membership.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

You are well aware of the need to rehabilitate and to replace obsolete
facilities at Decoto. There are funds apart from the Endowment Fund which
will be used to initiate the program of rehabilitation of Decoto, which are
now invested, with their earnings going to the operational budget of the two
Homes. When these funds are spent for capital improvements, they will no
longer earn income. Thus, other sources of revenue must be found to make
up the difference as well as to cover rising costs for operation.
Increasing our Endowment Fund is one way to supply these additional
operating funds. Therefore, in light of increasing needs, your Board proposes
two recommendations:
First, the establishment of a program to seek our and encourage special,
large gifts.

CONCLUSION

Throughout the year, many Brethren put forth efforts beyond the general call of duty, and we wish it were possible to recognize and thank each
one. Special mention must go to our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful
William H. Price, who has carried our message to the hearts of all who heard
his stimulating addresses throughout the jurisdiction. His sincere love for
Masonry, and particularly for our elderly at Decoto and our children at
Covina, was apparent to everyone. We have gained by his leadership and
dedication to Masonry.
We thank the Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, and Grand
Lodge committeemen who have wholeheartedly supported our Masonic
Homes. To the Grand Lecturer, Assistant Grand Lecturers, Masters and
Wardens, and Endowment Committeemen, our thanks for helping us to
implement our program and to reach out to the members of the Lodges.
Our Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems, and Assistant Grand Secretary
Verne W. Hendrix, along with their staff, gave us complete support. We
sincerely thank them for their assistance, which was invaluable to the success of our program.
We are most grateful to the 111,2 50 Brethren who contributed
$1,010,382 .92 for our permanent Endowment Fund.
Your Chairman commends each member of the Board for his total effort
and his dedication to the task of communicating to the Brethren the need
for an endowment fund adequate to support our two fine Homes. Your Chairman has found this assignment a most rewarding one. Our success has been
the result of a team effort. Contributions through individual members of the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As the result of the realignment of the Santa Monica Bay Bureau, the
following new compacts were executed:
West Adams No. S6S
Alexander Graham Bell No. S95
James 1\fadison No. S72
James A. Foshay No. 64 1
Valley Forge No. 587

REPORTS
All Bureaus submitted the required Report of Elections, Budget and the
Annual Statement of Income and Expenses, Balance Sheet and Annual Statistical Report. Recaps of some are herewith set forth:

178

\VITHDRAWALS APPROVED
American River Lodge No. 795 requested to withdraw from membership
in the Sacramento Masonic Service Bureau. The request was approved by
our Grand l\faster.
TRANSFERS APPROVED
Mother Colony Lodge No. 750 moved to the Orange County Masonic
Service Bureau area an<l was therefore required to transfer their membership from the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau.
NEW MEMBERSHIP APPROVED
The request from Orange Grove Lodge No. 293 to join the Orange County
Masonic Service Bureau was approved by the Grand Master.
NEW FORMS
The new uniform method of recording the number of miles driven by the
Secretary of the Bureaus in establishing expenses and recordation of information relative to funerals for our Sojourning Brethren was put into operation as of January 1, 1973. Uniform methods of recording such information
is a necessity not only for the purpose of audit by your Board , but it also
provides a permanent record of funerals conducted, by whom, and also other
pertinent information.
EXPANSION
Two of the Bureaus have discussed the possibility of expanding the areas
that they now serve. We will continue to work with them for the best interest
of serving the fraternity.
NEW EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES
New Executive Secretaries have taken over the duties of men who have
retired in five of the Bureaus this year. We welcome Howard Van Arsdale as
the new man in San Jose, Russell G. Crowe in Stockton, Harry W. Flanders
in The Santa Monica Bay Bureau, Paul ~L Porter in the East Bay Bureau
and T. Paul MacQuiddy who takes the place of Delmer W. May who served
the Santa Barbara Bureau for over twenty-five years as its Secretary.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
herewith submits its Nineteenth Annual Report.
At the close of the 1972 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its
Annual Meeting. The Board of Trustees then proceeded to nominate and
elect the following officers to serve for the ensuing year until new ones are
elected.
DeWald M. Baum ..............•..........•....... . President
Ira W. Coburn, P.G.M ........................... Vice-President
Chester R. MacPhee, P.G.M .......................... Treasurer
Edward H. Siems, P.G.M ............................ . Secretary
Raymond A. Ebbage .................... . Deputy Grand Master
The term of the appointive Trustees of the Board of Trustees are, as
follows:
James Craven ( 770)
( 1974)
(1974)
Samuel I. Jacobs (216)
(1973)
Wayne R. Lee (296)
Otto Rohwer (3)
(1973)
Subsequently James Craven and Samuel I. Jacobs, because of personal
reasons, resigned as Trustees and Varnum Paul and Wallace Honeywell were
appointed Trustees by the Gran<l Master in their place, for the unexpired
terms of their service.
This year our Masonic Memorial T emple celebrated its fifteenth birthday.
Because many members of the fraternity were not Master Masons at the time
of its dedication, we believe that it is appropriate to mention that this
magnificent building is our first Grand Lodge Temple, conceived and built
by the craft as its permanent headquarters. Its conception and birth took
eleven years filled with vision, frustration and finally achievement. It can
truly be said that when our brethren built a building of their own, they did
it in magnificent style. Kot for nothing are we as Masons called builders. We
practice what we preach.
Our California Masonic Memorial Temple, located at the top of prestigious Nob Hill, has each year added to its fame as an outstanding complex
for the cultural, civic and educational activities of this great metropolitan
city. We here present to all our visitors and gues ts visible evidence of our
pride as Masons and our contribution to the beautification of San Francisco
and the advancement of civilization in general. May the Great Architect of
the Universe grant that this building will always shine as a beacon light of
our fraternity's determination to always support and advance a free public
school system for the education of generations yet to be.

INCOME

During the past year the income from the building and garage
reached
an all time high. The fiscal year of July 1, 1972, to June 30, 1973,
shows a
22 7o increase in building income over that of the last fiscal period.
Throug h judicious supervision the operati ng expenses, salaries, supplie
s,
repairs, maintenance, including real and personal taxes, increased
only 3.3 % .
The garage showed an increase of 37 .8 over the previous fiscal year.
This
income will always continu e to fluctuate because it is largely based
on the
occupancy created from the use of the Auditorium and Exhibition
space and
the parking tax levied by the City of San Francisco. Thus more
use of our
facilities means more income from this source.

PINE S TREET PROPERTIES

During the past year these properties were again inspected by the code
enforcement program of the City and County of San Francisco and we have
complied with all their requirements. The present cash flow still justifies the
maintenance of the old buildings as an important source of revenue.
The Grand Lodge Insurance Committee has reviewed all insurance coverage of the Temple and the Pine Street properties and has approved them as
proper and appropriate.
During the past year construction was started on the luxury 17 story
apartment house immediately west of the Temple. It has 270 apartments in
an L-shaped design surrounding a courtyard. Through the efforts of counsel of
the Board of Trustees, an agreement was negotiated that will protect the
Temple for any future needed expansion in height.
To properly protect the boundaries of our property before construction of
the apartment house was started, it was necessary that a survey be made to
ascertai n the exact measurements of the land. This was required because of
the inaccurate measurements of the block since different corners were originally used as a base for the survey due to the loss of original records in the
great fire. This survey will prevent any future litigation when construction
on the Pine Street properties is desired. We now know accurately the extent
of our holdings.
Your Trustees are committed to a policy of fiscal responsibility because
they believe that no further expenditures should be made for any contemplated capital improvements to be erected on the properties fronting on Pine
Street until the present indebtedness of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple incurred in acquiring them has been paid in full. We believe that this

REPOR T OF CALIFO RNIA FREEMASON
PUBLIC ATION BOARD
To the Most Worsltipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. 111. of California:
The publicatio n and distributi on of the Californi a Freemaso n is administered by a board comprised of the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary ,
such advisors as may be desirable, and an Editor-in -Chief, who is appointed
by the Grand l\faster.
The magazine has completed its 20th year of publicatio n. The 80 issues
during these years constitute a readable history of Grand Lodge and Masonry
in this state during these years. 'While a quarterly publicatio n cannot serve
adequate ly as a news magazine, each issue has been diversified to supply its
readers with Masonic informati on and inspiratio n. Some space is allotted to
Grand Lodge so that Masons may know about statewide activities. Long,
scholarly articles, excellent in themselves, are avoided because they lack appeal for the majority of our quarter of a million readers.
As we have reported in previous reports, the cost of producing the magazine has steadily increased. By exercising every economy which does not
reduce the quality of the magazine and by stimulatin g paid subscript ions
from sojournin g Masons and from interested persons in other states and
countries , we find it impossible to continue with the present per capita.
During the last seven years the per capita for the magazine has been 35
cents. We recommend that it be raised to 40 cents for next year.
The financial report for the past fiscal year will he found in the report
of the Finance ('ommitte e.
Respectfu lly submitted ,
NEwco.!\IB CONDEE, Editor-in-Chief

. recomme ndation for an increase in per capita to 40 cents has been referred

The per capita for publicatio n of this magazine bas remained at 35 cents
for several years with deficits encounter ed in some years. The operation for
the year ended June 30, 1973 resulted in a near break-eve n point.
We are happy to note that the Grand Master has recommended that a
special committe e be appointed to determine the advisabil ity as well as .feasibility of a monthly Californi a Freemason. We trust that the Committee
will make every effort to hold costs to a minimum regardles s of a ny possible
changes in this publicatio n.
In our opinion, any change in the per capita assessment would be .premature. Conceiva bly this Grand Lodge may be asked for a substanti ally
higher per capita when the Committe e has finished its task.
The Committe e on Finance recommends a "No" vote.
A majority voted against the proposed increase in per capita tax.

REPOR T OF TAXAT ION COMM ITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your Committe e on Taxation came into existence in the 1930's to deal
with problems generated by the Social Security laws. In 1971, Grand Lodge
approved a recomme ndation that the "taxation committe e's functions ~e
expanded to include all types of taxation." Our present Grand Master, m
appointin g this Committe e, suggested it would be beneficial if the Co~mittee
"could counsel and advise the Grand Master, the Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges on all general tax matters."
Your Committe e on Taxation recognizes that its purpose is not to attempt
direction of all tax activities . The Grand l\Iaster and Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge, the trustees of the various entities of the Grand Lodge, the
Worshipf ul Masters and Secretarie s of Constitue nt Lodges, and elected
or appointed officers and trustees of various other Masonic groups have, by
necessity, the basic rrsponsibili ty for dealing with appropria te tax matters.
Your Commi ttee on Taxation can function only as an advisory committee.
Your Committe e has been available to provide tax advice. During the course
of the current year your committe e gave its best advice when it was solicited.
It also, on occasion , gave unsolicited advice where it seemed appropria te. In
this report for the year it again gives its unsolicited advice.
The tax problems of all segments of Grand Lodge have multiplied within
the past few years. The federal governme nt and the State of Californi a have
evidenced new interPs t in th e status of all tax exempt oq•;anizations. Tbis has
resulted in increased reporting requireme nts and potentials of audit review by
government agencies. Increased coverage by federal social security laws and
new covtrage by Californi a unemploy ment and disabili ty insurance laws also
has resulted in greater reporting requirements. Brethren in responsible positions have personal liabilities to comply with the laws and to protect the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

assets of their organizations from punitive taxation or from penalties for
noncompliance with the laws.
Your Committee is impressed with the variety of difficult tax problems
relating to the Grand Lodge and its Entities· Masonic Homes of California
California Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, to~
gether with the pension fund for certain of the employees. The tax laws regarding these ta.'< exempt organizations are complex and difficult of interpretation. Very substantial assets are involved and the returns are subject to
ever more critical scrutiny. The advice of your Committee is that the Grand
Master, Grand Secretary, and the trustees should continue to consult legal
and accounting professionals. Every effort should be made to assure the legal
tax status of the organizations and the accuracy of the reporting.
The Constituent Lodges are now required to file tax exempt organization
reports with the Internal Revenue Service and the California Franchise Tax
Board and generally to file returns for federal and state payroll ta.xes. These
reports constitute a real problem for many Lodge Secretaries. The Grand
Secretary's office has made substantial efforts to assist the Lodges. There is,
however, sometimes evidence of noncompliance, presumably through ignorance. The advice of your Committee on Taxation is that each Worshipful
Master and Secretary make positive that their Lodge complies with the
laws of our state and country.
Your Committee has worked with the Board of Control during the past
year in order to assure proper tax exemption is obtained and required tax
returns are filed by the Masonic Service Bureaus. Your Committee believes
the Board of Control should be complimented on its efforts toward tax compliance.
Adequate information does not appear to be available to judge the extent
of tax compliance by Temple Associations. The advice of your Committee is
that any Lodge or brother involved in a Temple Association make positive
tax requirements are being observed.
There are other Masonic organizations such as Masters and Wardens
Associations and Secretaries Associations which may require tax exemption
status and reporting and payroll ta.'{ reporting. The advice of this Committee
is that elected officers determine the tax responsibilities of their organizations.
In addition to the ta."{ exempt organization and payroll requirements,
there may be other taxes involved and, in particular, the advice of this Committee is to review property tax responsibility and possible sales tax involvement especially in regards to the sale of meals.
Your Committee agrees again that ta.-<es have become a great burden on
the fraternity. It reminds the brethren that these ta.'tes are the law of the land
and as good citizens we must comply with the law. The government has
granted us tax exemption and given us a responsibility to be worthy of that
advantage. If, for any reason, these responsibilities are not met the penalties
may be severe. It is most important that each of you in any Masonic connection be certain that there is full compliance with the tax laws.

REPORT OF DEMOLAY LIAISON BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:

The DeMolay Liaison Board was established on February 22, 1971, by
our then Grand Master, l\fost Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner. In the nearly
three years that this Board has been in existence much progress has been
made, but there is still much to accomplish.
Operating on the executve level with the Executive Officers of the Northern and Southern California and Hawaii Jnrisdictions, order of DeMolay,
your Board has been contacted when problems have arisen. Our thanks to
the entire Board and the Executive Officers of DeMolay for their dedication
and untiring efforts.
From reports and surveys made by Melvin A. Pixley, Executive Officer,
Southern California Jurisdiction, Order of DeMolay, your Board continues
to be deeply concerned by the lack of cooperation from some of the Lodges
and Temple Associations regarding the high rentals charged to some of the
local DeMolay Chapters. Some rentals are in excess of $100.00 per month.
A few lodges have reduced their rental charges when requested to do so.
Your Board is fully aware of the many financial problems that confront
our constituent Lodges. Taxes continue to spiral upward along with other
expenses. However, if the Masons of California are going to support the
Order of DeMolay, we must find a way to be of more assistance than we
have been in the past.
On January 5, 1973, our Grand Master, Most Worshipful William H.
Price, issued a directive to the Worshipful Master of each constituent Lodge
in California and Hawaii, to appoint a DeMolay Liaison Committee within
each Lodge and to make quarterly reports of their activities to the Board. Of
the 691 Lodges in this Jurisdiction, only about 20% of the Lodges have appointed such a committee and only about 20 7o of those have submitted
quarterly reports.
My Brethren, it is obvious that apathy exists in many of the Lodges and
with the general membership. The conclusion is; the Master Masons of California and Hawaii are going to support the Order of DeMolay, or they are
not. It is not possible to accomplish our goals with the present attitude of
some of our members.
Today, more than ever before, the DeMolay needs Master Masons who
can and will provide strong leadership. Strong leadership with dedication and
purpose. It is vital that this leadership be provided NOW. The continued
existence of our DeMolay depends upon it.

The infractions or violations have been handled through discussion and

examples of items referred to the Commercialism Committee are as follows:
Several of the clandestine bodies were in violation of using the Square
and Compass in advertising. Those in violation were instructed that the
Square and Compass is the property of the Grand Lo<lge of California and that
permission to use same must come from the Grand Master of this body.
A travel agency arranged an Hawaiian Trip and sent flyers to approximately
400 Masonic Lodges throughout the State, requesting the Masters of the
various Lodges to publicize the tour in their Trestle Boards. It was the
co ncern of the Committee that a Grand Lodge Roster was being used to promote this business venture, a clear violation of the California Masonic Code.
Several members of the Committee had a meeting with the owner of the
travel agency. and he agreed to withdraw the offer an<l return all funds.
An investigation was started on February 4, 1972, on the use of the
Square and Compass on the si<le of several cars used in a construction security
patrol business. This was a difficult situation, sinC'e the owner of the business

to cease and desist, and after several letters from one of our available attorneys, the owner did finally agree to our request and the case was closed
on May 14, 1973, thus ending a 16 months effort on behalf of the Committee.

with complaints which are referred to the Committee. A member of the

is forwarded to the Grand Secretary. Continual education of the Brethren
will help to reduce the number of complaints. Tf in doubt as to the legality
of an affair a letter to the Committee asking recommendations will further
reduce violations anri infractions.
Your Committee appreciates the helpful cooperation of the Grand Master,

have worked with each of them.

members of this Lodge cut the grass, sprayed the weeds, repaired the walkways and generally maintained the grounds. They also resolved to do this
every year. This is real Masonry at work.
Jamestown: It was necessary this year to do considerable work at this
cemetery to repair the ravages of time and also to repair some of the vandalism. This was in addition to the usual cutting of weeds and spraying. Hugh
Kellogg did a good job in supervising the work done and Jamestown is now in
pretty good condition.
Columbia: This cemetery is located in Columbia State Park and therefore
it attracts more visitors than the other cemeteries owned by Grand Lodge.
The usual sprayng and weeding was done and the general appearance is good.
Considerable work will have to be done next year to keep it that way. Again
we are faced with increasing vandalism, mainly tipping over headstones
which of course results in additional needless expense.
Fiddletown: Under the able supervision of Buck Nelson, all necessary
srraying of weeds was done by the Amador County Department of Agriculture. This cemetery is in good condition and thanks to the Lodi Explorer Scout
Post under the leadership of Brother Dan Meek, the grounds are cleaned
annually.
Peter Lassen Gravesite: Very little was done here outside of cutting weeds

and generally keeping the site in a presentable manner. Basil Gillette is attempting with the aid of the Master of Susanville Lodge to ascertain just who

Fallbrook: This cemetery is not owned by Grand Lodge but is wholely
owned by Fallbrook Lodge No. 317. In last year's annual report, this committee dwelt in some length on the problems of The Fallbrook Cemetery
Association. Last year 's report mentioned that a breach of contract suit had
been filed against the Lodge and the cemetery association. They in turn filed a
counter suit for recovery of expenses paid by the cemetery associatfon. Both
of these suits are still pending in the courts. At a meeting at Fallbrook on
September 5th, with the approval of the Grand Master, I requested them to
attempt, through their attorney, to arrive at a fair and equitable settlement out
of court. This is now in the process.
Every effort will be made to arrive at an amicable solution, however, it
may take Solomon himself to resolve some of the conflicts in personalities
involved. As Chairman of this committee I firmly believe that Brotherly
love will prevail and that peace and harmony will continue in Fallbrook
Lodge.
We believe that the actions taken this past year will prevent a recurrence
of their problems. All of the stock of the cemetery corporation previously
issued in the name of one trustee and held in his safety box has been reissued
in the name of Fallbrook Lodge and is now in the safety box of the Lodge.
Fallbrook Lodge, at the insistence of this committee and with the full
backing of our Grand Master, at a specially called meeting elected three
trustees to administer the voting rights. These trustees, each to serve three
years, replaced the single trustee. At the start, however, one trustee would
serve one year, one would serve two years and the third would serve three
years. One new trustee would be elected each year at the annual election of
officers. The Fallbrook Lodge voted at this special meeting to elect the Master
and the Wardens to be the trustees, the Master to serve one year, the Senior
Warden to serve two years and the Junior Warden to serve three years.
Presumably this pattern will be continued.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the last communication there were no Lodges carried over under dispensation and there have been no Lodges instituted in the meantime, so, for
the second time in over thirty years, your Committee on Charters has no
Lodges U.D. upon which to report.
Early in the year, in the hope that we could revive interest, we sent out
a questionnaire to the Inspectors that had been involved with clubs, that had
been in existence after 1960, for the purpose of forming new Lodges. The
Inspectors were most cooperative and in some cases went to considerable
trouble to seek out information on these clubs. A more detailed report of our
findings is being made to the Grand Secretary, but in brief, the results were
mostly negative. We did not find a single club still actively working to form a
new Lodge. In some cases other new Lodges had been formed which made this
new Lodge unnecessary, and in other cases the leaders of the clubs had moved,
died or lost interest.
Your Committee on Charters fully realizes that the decreases in the influx
of new people into California has greatly decreased the need for new Lodges,
but we cannot accept the premise that there is no need whatever! Changing
population patterns are still creating new vigorous communities with no
l\fasonic representation at all.

GRAND ORATION
THE TIME IS NOW
HARLAN P. HUEBNER, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters
'
Distinguished Guests, and my Brethren:

The year is 1717, and the time is now. The year is 1733, and the time is
now. The year is 1848, and the time is now. The time is 1973 - yes my
brethren - the time IS now.
These periods represent a beginning and a challenge for Speculative Masonry. From the past our Fraternity has become as a phoenix rising from the
chaos and adversity created by the social, economic and intellectual problems
of the moment. It grew and winged its way to every civilized part of the
world, our nation and our state. Freemasonry could not be stilled, it was a
force for the betterment of man under the Fatherhood of God. Through its
teac~ings, its tenets and precepts men have found a brotherhood. Temperance,
Fortitude, Prudence and Justice are not just empty words but a way of life
and a belief.
What would have happened if dedicated Masons had not worked and
strived to perpetuate Freemasonry? Our forebearers had the same problems
as we have today. They could have become selfish and lazy and forgotten
:Masonry. If that had happened I would not be here today, probably none of
us would be here in a Grand Lodge Communication. Probably there would
not be a Grand Lodge. But my brethren, there is a Grand Lodge and we are
here. Masonry is alive - however, it is in danger. As with all things good,
we must fight for it.
Return with me to 1717. The tenor of life in England had sunk to a low
level of morals; the people had few, if any, rights. England had just emerged
from a war and her economy was just beginning to prosper, she was embarking
on a period of world-wide maritime and commercial supremacy. However,
contrast this with some of the other social problems of the day. Towns were
dirty and unsafe, inhabited by mobs.
Further, the religious life of England at this time engendered a constant
figh t between those who desired the supremacy of Catholicism and the Pope
and others who desired a Church of England as the only religion for that
country. There was religious unrest.
Politically, England was ruled by a Germanic King, and the Stuarts
sought the crown, thus adding more strife to the times and the hardships of
the people.
Ycs, in 1717 it was time to find a philosophy and teachings to give
st~ength and support to the people. Out of those trying times there emerged
this force and an influence. Albert Mackey in his words "The History of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

201

Freemasonry" has stated it this way: " ***the gentlemen of education and
refinement who constituted the theoretic element or the Honorary membership
of the four lodges then existing in the city of London, resolved to change the
character of these lodges, and to withdraw then entirely from any connection
with Operative or Practical Masonry."
Thus in 1717 four operative lodges met to form the Grand Lodge of
England. From St. Paul's churchyard came the brethren of the Goose and
Gridiron Ale-house, from Parker's Lane near Drury Lane came the brethren
of the Crown Ale-house, from Charles Street, Covent Garden came the
brethren of the Apple Tree Tavern and from Channel Row, Westminster
came the brethren of the Rummer and Grapes Tavern. They met at the
Goose and Gridiron Ale-house, elected a Grand Master and Speculative
Masonry emerged to become a force and a way of life.
While Operative Masonry faded, Speculative Freemasonry was erected
on its ruins, and lives as a perpetual memorial in its symbols and its technical
language of the source whence it sprang.
Yes, the times were tumultuous but the Masonic Lodges became places
where worldly distinctions were forgotten and all men were equal. Politics and
religion were forgotten , harmony prevailed and all earthly problems were
transcended. Masonry became a force w;th no equal.
The original Speculative Masons fought for survival - they did not give
up and withdraw under the pressure of the times.
Within a matter of a few years Masonry as we know it spread to the
thirteen American colonies and elsewhere. In 1731 the American colonies were
by no means somnolent. They had not only internal colonial problems of
religious intolerance, but economic boycotts and other interferences. We became more and more a puppet to be used at the whim of the King of England.
Additionally a new land demanded of these pioneers their full endurance to
establish themselves.
However, as we see, men of vision and assurance were able to lay down
their hoes, set down their pens, replace their daily aprons with the lambskin
apron and divorce themselves from all daily threats and problems to bring to
this shore the light of Brotherly Love. Yes, in 1731, St. John's Lodge in
Boston, l\fassachusetts was formed under authority of the Grand Lodge of
England. In 1733 the appointment of Right Worshipful Henry Price as Provisional Grand Master of New England was an accomplished fact and
Masonry came of age in America.
T he members of this and other lodges in our colonies, the pioneers of our
country recognized the force for good which Freemasonry provides and gave
of themselves to further that force. This could have been the beginning and
the end in America. The War of Independence was on the horizon, political
infighting was developing and self-preservation was the order of the day. However, faced with all of these adversities Masons emerged to not only lead the
country but to disseminate the Masonic spirit.
Nor did our leaders in the I 700's forget their Masonic heritage and les-

202

203

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sons. Recall with me a few passages from our Declaration of Independence,
"Prudence, indeed , will dictate that governments long established should not
be changed for light and transient causes." Also, further on in that document
we fmd the words, "Nor have we been wanting in attentions to our British
brethren." These leaders were great men who epitomize our ritual wherein it
teaches that, we are "an institution having for its foundation the practice
of the social and moral virtues; and to so high an eminence has its credit
been advanced, that in every age and country, men pre-eminent for their
moral and intellectual attainments have encouraged and promoted its interests."
Our forefathers did not become complacent and allow Masonry to die. To
them the time was now to move and rededicate themselves to their country,
their families, themselves and to Masonry. They recognized the force for good
found within the Masonic Lodge.
Moving forward in time to another critical period in our history we next
arrive at 1848, the place an area known as California. "GOLD" was the
magic word. Men from every corner of the globe converged on a relatively
few miles of earth to seek their fortune. Most of you are familiar with accounts of the times. The chaos, lawlessness and rough and ready times that
pervaded the mining camps seems to us unreal and ficticious.
But amidst all of this chaotic existence Freemasonry appeared. First with
the chartering of Western Star Lodge No. 98 in May 1848 by the Grand
Lodge of Missouri, and finally with the institution of our own Grand Lodge
in 1850.
My brethren, what prompted men confronted with the rigors of gold
mining camps, rampant with disease, no law, save the Miners Law, to come
together under one roof with guns left outside, personal feuds dismissed and
work together as Masons?
These California pioneers probably had less reason to take time out to
start :Masonic Lodges or attend lodge than any other time in history, yet they
did. What drove them to give that extra effort to create a lasting institution
in our State? I believe it was that men at every age in time who possess the
teachings of our Craft wish to perpetuate the principles by passing them on to
others and also to reaffirm their own learning.
Doesn't this speak one of the highest praises for our institution - they
did not forget Masonry, they gave of themselves to practice its teachings and
help bring calm out of chaos.
What about today? Are the problems so different than in the previously
alluded to milestones of Masonic history?
'Ve read every day about lawlessness in our cities and, yes, even in our
schools. Special guards have to be hired to monitor the school halls, our police
forces are yearly increased to combat crime. As it was in the past some of our
cities are plainly unsafe and dirty and mobs run rampant, lawlessness is not
an unknown word.
Politics of today can really claim no great distinction over the past. We

are confronted on every side with apparent deception and, yes, corruption .
But again it is the fault of the apathetic American citizen which fosters such
cancer. We must involve ourselves in an effort to combat such political
practices. Our youth are certainly becoming more active politically, why
aren't we as individuals practicing the lesson of good citizenship. Early in our
Masonic teachings each one of us was "enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of your civil duties, by never proposing or countenancing any act
which may have a tendency to subvert the peace and good order of society;
by paying due obedience to the laws under whose protection you live, and
never losing sight of the allegiance due to your country."
Nor did our Speculative Masonic founders have a monopoly on religious
problems, intolerance and bigotry. One has only to read the papers to see as
late as just a month ago intolerance still prevails in America. Witness the
Florida Methodist Church that wished to baptize a black man and the Ku
Klux Klan appeared in robes to protest, harass and threaten all who were
present.
Yes, witness the youth of 19 73 who say, " God is Dead." , :\l. itness others
who brag of their atheistic beliefs.
Fortunately these examples are in the minority - but, they do exist and
cannot be ignored.
No my brethren, our times are not really different than they were in the
past. True we have progressed in science, education and personal comforts
over our earlier brethren, but the problems still remain the same.
\Ve in 1973 :Masonry have a challenge and more important we have a
legacy from our brethren of the past. Anywhere along the road of M asonic
time our brethren could have given up. They could have said, "I'm just too
busy to worry about my Lodge." They could have used reverse logic an d said,
"I've learned my lessons, I live by Masonic Principles, that's enough." But
they did not. They worked together in harmony through all types of external
adversity for a common goal to spread the teachings of our Fraternity, yes,
they sacrificed themselves to Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. They by their
everyday lives showed others that Masonry has a philosophy for all, they
were active and participated. They grew in number, from the handful of 1717
to over 223,000 members of our own Grand Lodge plus all the other Grand
Lodges around the world.
This statistic may give some comfort, but it should not. Masonry needs
help. We in Grand Lodge, nor any of our brethren whithersoever dispersed
can afford to relax and consider our work is done. Each year our membership
decreases and each year our attendance at Lodges decreases. On all sides we
hear "I'm too busy to attend the meetings," or " It's too long a drive from
my home to Lodge." My brethren, I ask the rhetorical question, what would
have happened if George Washington would have said, " It's too long a horseback ride from Mount Vernon to Alexandria," or other early leaders had such
a ready excuse?

205

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

\.Ve must show ou r young men of today that we are not leaving everything
up to them to solve, we must work with them and show them by examples
Masonry in Action.
We must conduct ourselves by the precepts we learned. We must remember
the Masons of the past, and that their daily struggles were no different from
our own. We must, each one of us, take an active part in our Masonic work.
We cannot leave it to others. Masonry is a force for the betterment of man
under the Fatherhood of God. Our principles go back before recorded time,
we cannot let them die or even wane. We in Masonry must become involved in
life at all levels, in order to foster understanding, compassion and a better
world.
Take a moment and mentally review the First Degree Charge. This, my
brethren, says it all. We are charged as Masons with duties to God, our
neighbor and ourselves, as citizens and as individuals. If we but practice those
charges given to us at the conclusion of our first exposure to the teachings of
Freemasonry we can grow and perpetuate our Fraternity. We can become a
greater force to preserve our freedoms, strengthen our religions and most important find a peace within ourselves.
YES, THE TIME IS NOW.

I am pleased to report at this time, however, that the property has been
sold, title thereto having passed on February 9, 1973, and the proceeds of
the sale, consisting of cash and notes secured by trust deeds on the property
are in our portfolio. The total purchase price was $550,000.
Parenthetically, I should mention that this is not the same sale which was
reported to the 19 72 Grand Lodge Communication. At that time, an escrow
had been opened, and we had every reason to believe that the sale would be
completed, but it was aborted by the buyer through no fault of ours.
In addition to the invested proceeds from the earlier sale of the U.C.
Berkeley Clubhouse, and the proceeds from the sale of the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse, we also have assets totaling some $215,000 which were turned over to
us by the Order of the Amaranth during the 1971 - 72 fiscal year. This was
reported last year in detail, but I would like to express, again, our deep
appreciation to our brethren and friends who are members of the Order of
the Amaranth for this most generous gift, and to assure them that the income
therefrom has been, and is being, used to good advantage for the benefit of
females under 21 years of age, which is a condition of the trust agreement
under which the transfer was made.

The Grand Oration was received with a standing ovation. The Grand
Master directed the Grand Secretary to have printed copies of the oration to
be made available to the members of Grand Lodge.

The Foundation's Board of Trustees consists of 15 members, all of whom
must be members of Grand Lodge. They are selected from different geographical locations in California, and one is from H awaii.
The officers are: a President, a Vice-President, a Treasurer and Assistant
Treasurer, and a Secretary and Assistant Secretary. The names of the current
members appear at the end of this report. It will be noted that the Grand
Treasurer M .W. Chester R. MacPhee is our Treasurer, and the Secretary is
M.W. Edward H. Siems, Grand Secretary. These offices are occupied by
these distinguished brethren in accordance with the recommendations of the
In-Depth Study Committee, but neither is a member of the Board as such.
All of our Board members have performed sincere and dedicated services.
We have four principal committees as follows: Scholarships; New Projects; Public Relations and Legal. More will be said about them later.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

As an introduction to this report, it seems appropriate to relate some
further facts about the California Masonic Foundation, since we have found
many brethren who are completely unaware of the nature of the organization,
what it does, how it operates, etc.
Briefly, then, the Foundation is a separate corporation, organized in 1969
by and with the approval of Grand Lodge, for the purpose of taking over the
proceeds of the Masonic Clubhouse at U.C. Berkeley, which had then been
sold, and devoting them and other funds and property received later, to
charitable purposes.
Shortly after the corporation was formed title to the Masonic Clubhouse
at U.C.L.A. was also transferred to us, since it was no longer being used by
the students there to an extent which justified the cost of maintaining it,
and the duty of selling this property devolved upon our Board of Trustees.
Unfortunately, this required a great deal of time and effort during the
first three years of our existence, and this, plus the cost of maintenance
limited our capacity to perform the charitable functions which we would
have desired to do, and for which we were organized.

STRUCTURE OF THE CORPORATION

FINANCIAL

As above stated, our financial position has improved tremendously during
the past year. Total assets on hand are in excess of $1,000,000. We anticipate
"spendable" income during the 1973-74 fiscal year of something in the
neighborhood of $70,000. Since the expense of the upkeep and maintenance
of the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse has been eliminated, our expenses are comparatively minimal. Our accounting is taken care of through the office of the
Grand Secretary, plus a regular audit by the same C.P.A. firm which audits
Grand Lodge, and other associated entities.
Accounting records are on file in the Grand Secretary's office, and are open
for inspection.

206

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
PAST ACTIVITIES

Thus far, our charitable activities have consisted primarily of scholarship
awards, and they have averaged about $400 per student per year. Formerly,
these were limited to undergraduates, but recently we have authorized
awards to worthy graduate students in certain cases. Our scholarship committee, composed of Brother Ed Rowins, Chairman, Brother Pete B. Florio,
Secretary, Brother Robert Holt, and Brother John Gordon, has done a tremendous job in reviewing all applications frequently, and determining who is
eligible for an award.
Applications are made by the student on a printed form and submitted to
Brother Florio; who keeps all records, and takes care of all correspondence.
His task is monumental, and he performs it with great efficiency and dedication.
Applications are usually initiated through the Master or some other officer
of the local Lodges, and when an award is made, the student is invited to
attend a dinner or some other Lodge event and an award ceremony is held
with the Lodge Officers participating.
During the past fiscal year we have awarded some 90 of these scholarships,
of which 59 came out of the general funds for a total of $24,350, and 31 to
females under 21 years of age out of the Order of the Amaranth funds, for a
total of $11 ,900. In addition, the total amount of $1,000 was awarded to two
DeMolays out of a special fund known as the Altenberg Trust. This makes a
grand total of $37,500 for scholarships above.
Awards other than scholarships were: $2 500 to assist the Southern California Jurisdiction of De:Molay in their leadership seminar program, and a
like amount to the Northern California Jurisdiction of D e:Molay for the same
purpose. There were also loans to DeMolay boys from the Altenberg Fund.
We have found without exception that the students who have been
granted awards are of very high caliber (not necessarily with the highest
grades), but with great potential as leaders. All of them have been most
appreciative as is illustrated by some of the letters we have received, and it is
the firm belief of our Board that our program to date has aided many people,
and has served to foster and improve the image of Masonry wherever knowledge of it has been disseminated.
FUTURE PLANS

Despite the success of our scholarship program, we do not by any means
intend to confine our activities to that alone. During this new fiscal year, we
project the use of at least half of our income to other projects. Many suggestions have been submitted, including participation in an anti-drug abuse
program, the encouragement and development of various leadership programs,
such as we have already done with DeMolay, assistance and sponsorship of a
center for nutritional studies, speaking and essay contests on citizenship,
programs relating to the 200th Anniversary of the Nation in 1976, and cooperation with the Public Schools Committee and the Constitution Observance
Committee in developing significant programs.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most ·worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The members of this Committee wish to express their appreciation to the
Grand Lodge and our Grand Master, William H. Price for the p rivilege of
serving. The cooperation of the Grand Lodge and the Grand Master has
made this year a pleasure.
A meeting of the Committee was held at Grand Lodge on Saturday,
February 10th, 1973. At this time we integrated all of the information sent
in by the various Lodges into the History Committee's files in the Grand
Lodge Library. We are still a long way from completing t he info rmation
needed to bring these files up to date. This coming year we hope to send out
a new questionnaire to help us in our task.
We again bring to your mind the slide lecture, "Some Came by Land and
Some Came by Sea'', depicting some of the historic Lodge buildings in California. This very interesting view into our colorful past can be had for Lodge
programs by contacting the Chairman of this Committee. I am sure all who
see it will enjoy it.
Through our studies one interesting aspect came to our attention: t he
Daylight Lodges operating in our State.
There are, in the State of California, three Lodges of Free and Accepted
Masons, which meet in the daytime rather than in the evening. These Lodges
are all located in Southern California. Ironically, the index of "One Hundred
Years of Freemasonry in California" refers the reader to page 11 80, which
gives the history of Jewel Lodge No. 374 of San Francisco. This Lodge was
conceived by a number of brethren who, because some must work while others
play, could not attend Lodges which met in the evenings, but were desirous
of organizing a Lodge that they could attend. Among the twelve who held a
preliminary meeting with that end in view, six were theater musicians, five
were newspapermen and one was a businessman. By their efforts, Jewel Lodge
No. 374 received its dispensation from Grand Master Motley H. Flint,
November 21, 1905 and was constituted by Grand Master Edward H . Hart,
October 19, 1906. However, this Lodge voted to become an evening Lodge in
June of 1941 and now, as was heretofore mentioned, there are but three
daylight Lodges; all located in Southern California.
Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415, F. & A. M. meets at the Hollywood Masonic
Temple on Wednesday mornings and is comprised largely of musicians , actors,
stage hands, projectionists and other craftsmen, who earn their livelihood in
the evenings or at night and arc thus deprived of the opportunity of attending
evening Lodges. In December of 1909, fourteen Master Masons, who could
not attend regular Lodges, met for the purpose of taking whatever steps were
necessary to form a daylight Lodge. There were present six musicians, a
stage hand, an attorney, a restaurant owner, a detective, an accountant and a
member of the Tax Collector's office and, in an advisory capacity only, the

211

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master Dana R. Weller and Worshipful
E. B. Spencer, Past :Master of Southern California Lodge No. 278.
After several more meetings a dispensation was granted April 25th, 1910
by the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Frank Pierce. Silver Trowel Lodge
No. 415, F. & A. M. was granted a charter on October 25th, 1910 and has
become one of the best known lodges in Southern California. It is interesting
to note that its nan1e was chosen because, at the time of its organization, a
large silver trowel had been sent around the United States, Canada and
1\1exico, bearing a message of brotherly love and affection to all Masons. It
had started its journey in 1905 and had covered over 20,000 miles through
the United States, Canada and Mexico and was in Los Angeles, California at
the time Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415 was being formed. The foregoing
abridged history of Silver Trowel was furnished by Brother Jerome B. Rosen,
Past Master.
Queen Beach No. 540, F. & A. M. - In the early months of 1922
several Masonic Brethren got together informally to discuss the possibility of forming a daylight lodge in Long Beach. These meetings usually
took place at band headquarters of the Long Beach Municipal Band, since
many of the band members, along with musicians of local orchestras and
theatres, were also members of the Cra ft. Many of the Masons of Long Beach,
who, because of their work were unable to attend evening Lodges would put in
two or three hours of travel time and 40 to 50 miles each meeting, to attend
Silver Trowel Lodge in Los Angeles, Silver Trowel being, at the time the
nearest "daylight Lodge."
After several informal meetings, a number of l\Iaster Masons assembled
at the Masonic Temple at 234 Pine Avenue, Long Beach, for the purpose of
establishing a daylight Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons in the Long
Beach area. The name Queen Beach was chosen because Long Beach was
then known as the Queen of the Beaches. A dispensation was requested of the
Most Worshipful Samuel E. Burke, Grand Master of Masons in California.
The dispensation was granted by Grand Lodge on October 9, 1922 and
Brother Clark H. Shaw, Inspector of the 74th Masonic District, installed the
officers of Queen Beach No. 540, F . & A. M. on November 2nd, 1922. Queen
Beach No. 540 was chartered October 11, 1923 and constituted October 25,
1923.
More and more men who worked odd and unusual hours were applying
for degrees and affiliation and enjoyable meetings with their brethren.
On March 8, 192 7 Queen Beach held its first midnight meeting. It convened one minute after midnight and conferred the 3rd degree upon Brother
Rezin A. Henry.
The second midnight meeting was held July 3 1, 1928 and the Metro
Goldwyn Mayer Masonic Degree team was invited to exemplify the third
degree. Thereafter midnight meetings were held at two and three year intervals. On December 20, 1932, the now Senior Past Master (James Solomon

Terry) was raised at a midnight meeting after which the more than 150
brethren present retired to the banquet room and enjoyed a ham and egg
breakfast.
Special music for these midnight degrees was composed by a member of
Queen Beach, though the records fail to show the composer's name or when
the music was first used.
lle!ng a daylight ~ge, Queen Beach has attracted, not only musicians,
but railroad men, policemen, firemen, movie projectionists and others whose
working hours made it impossible for them to attend evening Lodges.
The first Master of Queen Beach was a musician and since then we have
had sixteen more musician Masters. The present Master Senior Warden
Junior Warden and Senior Deacon are all professional musi~ians. Four of th~
Past Masters were police officers; three railroad men and one a mortician.
On November 14, 1972 Queen Beach Lodge celebrated its 50 th anniversary. The affair was held in the dining room of its present location at 3610
Lo.cust, Long Beach. Our Guest of Honor was 1\fost Worshipful William H.
Pnce, Grand Master of Masons of California and Hawaii. Worshipful Master
Willian1 H. Stovall presided.
Incidentally, "One Hundred Years of Free 1\1asonry in California " makes
no mention of the fact that Queen Beach No. 540, F. & A. M. is a "daylight
Lodge." The foregoing history was graciously supplied by the Senior Past
Master, Worshipful James Solomon Terry.
The following short history of Opportunity Lodge No. 740 is quoted
verbatim, as furnished by Joseph W. Condo, W.1\1. 1973:
"Opportunity Ko. 740 - A Daylight Lodge - About one-third of the
workmen and technicians employed in aircraft and other industries comprised
a group referred to as "swing shift" and "graveyard shift." :rvlany thousands
by choice or necessity, were working during nighttime hours. A survey of
three leading aircraft manufacturers in the immediate vicinity of Hawthorne,
Inglewood and El Segundo, disclosed that approximately 1,500 Masons were
employed during these hours. It was deemed reasona ble to assume that
throughout the southwest Los Angeles area there must be many thousands
more, who would welcome a daylight Lodge.
A chance meeting of two brothers in a cafe, each with insufficient lists of
brothers interested in forming a daylight Lodge, culminated in the fi rst
meeting of these interested brothers - on February 5, 1954 - in the Hawthorne Masonic Temple. Hawthorne Lodge No. 64 7 offered the group free
usage of the Temple and their paraphernalia, until Grand Lodge convened in
October.
At this first meeting Brother Harold A. Zillman was elected Chairman.
Opportunity Lodge was suggested and agreed upon for the name of the new
Lodge. It was agreed to meet the first and third Tuesdays of each month for
business pu rposes, from 11 :00 A.~I. to 1 :00 P.M. A collection of $1.00 each

was collected from the brothers present to help defray mailing and incidental
expenses. $38.00 was collected. It was agreed, that members not being able to
be vouched for must attend a regular meeting, preferably as a group, to be
certified. From this humble beginning Opportunity Lodge No. 740 was conceived.
Opportunity Lodge U.D. was instituted on July 20, 1954 by the Most
Worshipful Frank Harwell, Jr. Grand Master of l\Iasons in Cali fo rnia. Constitution of Opportunity Lodge No. 740 F. & A. M. by Most Worshipful
Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., Grand Master of Masons in California occurred on
November 15, 1955.
The two brothers at the chance meetin g were Harold A. Zillman, Worshipful Master in 1960 and Jack M. Weidner, Worshipful Master in 1957.
Worshipful John A. Owen, P.M., Inspector of the 550th Masonic District,
spent countless hours in coaching, training and counseling. To these three
brothers Opportunity Lodge No. 740 owes its existence."
In regard to resolution 23 at this year's Communication, we report the
following:
We realize the importance of preserving our history and the physical
aspects of ou r beginnings. But the expenditure of Grand Lodge funds to
expedite this could be a drain difficult to accept. We realize that at the
present time there is policy with respect to the acquisition, restoration and
preservation of historical sites. We believe that this must be left in an open
position. The Temple at Columbia State Park is the Archives for the records
of Grand Lodge. The Old Masonic Hall at Los Angeles was restored by the
State of California at their expense and leased back to Grand Lodge at $1.00
per year. For the Brethren of any area to try and preserve their Masonic
beginnings is a commendable act. Your Committee believes this should be the
first line of approach in this matter. We therefore recommend a "No" vote
on resolution No. 23.
In order that your Committee on Masonic History may continue its work
for the corning year we submit the following budget :

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

On behalf of the members of our committee we wish to thank the Grand
Secretary for the assistance he has given us in the past.
Our committee held one meeting this year at the Old Hall in which we
discussed ways and means of increasing the use of our Temple. Also brought
up for discussion was a request to be made to Grand Lodge for the lowering
of Temple fees to Junior organizations who use our Temple. This request, I

.

opposed. AB 1742, which is a "tax credit" bill for students attending private
schools, was passed by both Houses, signed by Governor Reagan, but a
preliminary injunction has been granted on the bill on Constitutional grounds.
This bill was scheduled to go into effect on January 1, 1974. The chances now
look very slim.
On a legislative basis it must be pointed out that on June 25, 1973, the
United States Supreme Court declared tax credits, tuition subsidies and
voucher payments (directly or by subterfuge) to pupils in private or religious schools, their parents or the school itself, to be unconstitutional.
Despite this mandate by the United States Supreme Court, the California
State Senate passed S.B. 600 which does exactly what is prohibited by the
highest court in the land. Senate Bill 600 was submitted to the House with
the amendment that any non-public school endorsed by the program must be
totally under the control of the public school officials, as the California Cons titution requires. This version passed the House and was sent back to the
Senate for action and presumably eliminates the Constitutional issue.
Many other topics involving public education are currently under study by
the Committee such as 1) certification of teachers, 2) why our students are
using text books written 10 years ago and longer and 3) a new one that will
be discussed tomorrow is why a sociology book currently being used in our
Junior College System relates the First Degree of Masonry in its entirety,
including the pass word. As we widen our scope of activities as a Committee,
more and more of these disturbing items are brought to our attention. Your
suggestions and help as Brother Masons are always welcome. Our Deputy

Grand Master has chosen the slogan for Public Schools Months in 19 74 to be
"Public Education - The Foundation of Democracy. " Your Committee feels
that is a most appropriate theme and pledges to give our utmost effort to make
the forthcoming Observation a huge success.
A budget of $8,400.00 bas been requested by the Committee for its operation in 19 73- 74 and complete details of this budget have been forwarded to
the Finance Committee.
Three years ago from this same podium I made a challenge to Grand Lodge
and since it is even more true today I would like the privilege of repeating it.
"I need not remind you of the great and important challenge that confronts
us in our endeavors to support the public school system and the separation of
Church and State, upon which this Nation was formed. Your help is needed
now as it never was before. Masonry has never failed to respond when needed
and, my Brethren, the need is here."
That was the challenge. Thirty Masons on a Public Schools Committee
can't do it but 220,000 Masons, their families and friends sure can! What I
am sincerely asking for is your help. Can we count on you?

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the past month we have experienced the 186th Anniversary of
the adoption of"... the most wonderful work ever struck off at a given time
by the brain and purpose of man." So said the great English statesman,
William E. Gladstone. Our Constitution is 186 years old and still it is considered to be one of the greatest plans ever devised for a government
". . . of the people, by the people and for the people."
Our Constitution is not a patent we can use without regard for responsibility, it is not a license to permit freedom without controls, it is a way of life
for the American people to live in peaceful harmony so long as each does
his own part in preserving these rights for future generations. Our Grand
Master called it like it is in his Proclamation - " Freedom, as granted by our
Constitution, is not a birthright. The mere fact that we were born in the
United States does not mean that we can languish in the patriotic accomplishments of past generations. Constant vigilance is required to protect the freedoms granted by the Constitution from erosion."
This quotation from the Proclamation of Constitution Observance Month
also tells the story of the long and sometimes tedious efforts that have been
made by the 23 members of your Committee on Constitution Observance.
They have dedicated many hours and undergone countless frustrations in
their desire to do their part. The Chairman cannot say enough about the
untiring efforts, the willin1mess to help and the genuine integrity of each and
every one of these 23 l\Iasons. These men endeavored to contact and aid the
Constitution Observance Chairman of each Lodge in over 182 Districts
throughout the length and breadth of California and Hawaii. In addition to
many local meetings, they attended three Grand Lodge Committee meetings
during the year and wrote countless letters to the Lodges and District representatives. The expression of the gratitude and appreciation of the Chairman
seems so inadequate and certainly far less than deserved.
Programs that took months of planning and long hours of preparation
by dedicated officers of Lodges and assisted by thousands of equally dedicated
Masons, were held during September. Accounts of the many successes woul<l
take far too long, so just a brief note of the type of programs held may help
those preparing now for 1974. l\Iany Lodges held their own individual programs which included potluck dinners, Barbecues, musical entertainment,
skits, stage plays, and picnics, with speakers and other forms of portrayal of
the Constitution . Groups of Lodges joined together for similar programs.
Groups of Districts held joint programs with a wi<le variety of entertainment
and speakers, including patriotic demonstrations at sporting events. The
most successful programs appeared to be those which included joint efforts of
several Lodges or Districts with the Knights of Columbus, Youth Groups,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Because Masons played so very important a part and were greatly instrumental in the drafting of the Constitution of the United States, as well as on
July 4, 1776 in the signing of our Declaration of Independence from England,
the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North America at its February
22, 1971 meeting held in Washington, D.C., elected the following seven Grand
Lodge representatives to serve as a Committee for the purpose of assisting
in the promotion of 1976 Bicentennial celebrations of that important event in
the various Grand Lodge Jurisdictions of the United States:
THOMAS B. McINTOSH of Louisiana, Chairman,
HIRAM P. BALL of Pennsylvania,
CHARLES F. GosNELL of New York,
HERBERT H. }AYNES of Massachusetts,
LESTER S. McELWAIN of California,
WARREN A. McMINIMEE of Oregon,
ROBERT L. PUGH of North Carolina, and
DWIGHT L. SMITH of Indiana, with
G. EGERTON BROWN of Canada named as an Observer and
WILLIAM B. STANSBURY, JR. of Maryland assigned as
Secretary to the Committee.
All of these individuals are Past Grand Ylasters of their respective Grand
Lodge Jurisdictions.
In the Fall of last year the then Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California wrote to the ·Master of every Masonic Lodge in California and Hawaii
and requested that plans be instituted by each Lodge, or in conjunction with
other Lodges or concordant Bodies in the area, for a Bicentennial celebration
in 19 7 6 of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. This letter was
sent with quadruplicate copies to each Master, with the suggestion that the
copies thereof be distributed to the two Wardens and the two Deacons of his
Lodge; for it was considered that the then Junior Deacon of the Lodge might
likely be the Master of the Lodge in 1976. It it believed that each Lodge now
has formed a local 1976 Bicentennial Committee and has preliminary plans
under consideration for an appropriate celebration in 1976.
The Chairman of the Bicentennial Committee of the Conference of Grand
Masters of North America has written to the Grand Master of every Masonic
Grand Lodge in the United States and urged them to appoint a similar type
of Bicentennial Committee in each Grand Lodge Jurisdiction, and also has
suggested that each of the above named individuals be appointed by the
Grand Master of his jurisdiction to chair the Bicentennial Committee in that
jurisdiction.
In accordance with the latter suggestion, the Most Worshipful WILLIAM
H. PRICE, Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii, in the Fall of

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Correspondence Committee respectfully submits this Review, covering Masonic Jurisdictions, of the United States, other than California, and
with whom California maintains Masonic recognition.
The various jurisdictions' common problem is that of a decline in applications for the degrees, particularly from young men, and which is accompanied
by the difficulty of securing qualified line officers. i\fany articles have been
written on these problems, and while the problems have not been solved yet,
there are indications that the various Grand Lodges, as well as Senior Officers
of the constituent Lodges are making some progress in meeting and solving
them.
It is obvious from a review of the proceedings of the Grand Lodges that
the various other problems which were previously dealt with have been solved,
or at least partially so, as there is a sameness to their problems, thus making
it difficult to present interesting reviews.
MASONIC RELIEF

Due to limited available space in the California Freemason, we have, for
the most part, restricted the reviews to jurisdictions of the United States, yet
the exceedingly heavy rains in the Philippine Islands in August, 1972 caused
disastrous flooding in this area. The entire island of Luzon and the Greater
Manila area were under water for weeks, resulting in widespread loss of crops,
starvation, homelessness and damage to homes and buildings. As much as 85
inches of rain fell in a period of four weeks. Contributions were received from
many Grand Lodges and were combined for fonvarding to the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines.
The staggering tragedy which occurred in Rapid City, South Dakota
required considerable assistance to relieve the suffering of Masons and their
families in that area, relief which was afforded generously by Grand Lodges,
constituent Lodges and other Masonic Bodies which responded to an appeal
sent out from South Dakota.
Later in the month, heavy rains caused serious flooding in the East, the
two hardest hit being New York and Pennsylvania. The Grand Lodges in
these two states had effective machinery set up and sufficient resources to
take care of the needs of distressed Masons and their families who suffered
losses because of the flood.
How the Grand Lodges of Pennsylvania and New York organized the
relief activities in their jurisdictions and provided help and assistance for the
Masonic victims of the flood is a heartwarming and inspiring story of Masonry
in action.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

225

THE HOSPITAL VISITATIONS PROGRAM

The Hospital Visitation Program of those jurisdictions which adopted this
program is bringing to the bedside of hospital veterans the friendly hand of
Freemasonry and the sympathetic ministrations of Brethren whose principle
satisfaction is to help those who have borne the battle and now need the
thoughtful assistance of their fellow citizens. The credit should go primarily
to those dedicated Masons who assist in various ways to bring comforting
service and encouragement to the patients in approximately 100 Veterans
Administration and Service Hospitals all over our country.
Grand Lodges, constituent Lodges, The Supreme Council, 33 of the
Southern jurisdictions of the Scottish Rite and many local Masonic bodies and
individual Masons, have kept the Hospital Visitation program in action in
V.A. and Service Hospitals.
GRAND LODGE ACTIVITIES

One of the Lodges of the State of Nevada, held an outdoor Third Degree
on a ranch east of Sparks, Nevada. Lodge furniture was constructed of
weathered lumber and antique nails. Jewels were made from old square railroad spikes and seating was on bales of hay. Several other open air degrees
were featured. Each Lodge has a Deputy Master of Instruction selected from
a list of three members submitted by the Master elect. It was recommended
that all religious ceremonies and prayers contained in ritual be assigned to the
chaplain except Master's benediction. A resolution carried over requires
Master Masons to learn the lecture within two months unless extended by the
Master for good cause.
Ohio just compJeted a three year inquiry into statewide jurisdiction
showing that the main reasons men became Masons were relatives friends
a.Dd co-workers. Ohio voted for statewide jurisdiction.
'
Of extreme interest to California Masons is that the Grand Lodge of
Alabama must vote dispensations to confer degrees on maimed candidates
and did so on 26 candidates during 1972. One successful program instituted
during the year was group Masonic education seminars involving various
lodges, and attendance was quite good.
The Grand Lodge of Vermont voted to continue assisting needy Masons
in their homes, but not to undertake a Masonic Home.
The Grand Lodge of Georgia maintains its own Print Shop at the Masonic
Home (which can do commercial jobs). The Home is in a rural setting and
the farm maintains its own dairy and beef herd for its own use and for sale
and also raises its own crops.
For many years most of the Masonic Temples in Illinois that housed
nothing but the Lodge Halls have been exempt from payment of Real Estate
Taxes on the basis of a non-profit organization, or because of the good relationship Illinois Masons have enjoyed with the tax assessors. This is no
longer the case in Illinois. Hundreds of Masonic Temples received tax statements for the first time in 19 72. The Grand Lodge of Illinois has been

Following is the combined report of the sub-committees and the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility.
Inter-Grand Lodge Research: under direction of Vice Chairman, Max H.
Rush, Jr. we have continued the authorized correspondence with official correspondents in other recognized United States jurisdictions. Through this
exchange we have furnished other Grand Lodges with samples of materials
and programs being used in California and Hawaii. They have been particularly interested in the California Masonic Widows Program, and some
have borrowed from it in pursuing their own plans. Some material received
has been transmitted to the Grand Lodge Library for reference.

The sub-committee has made monthly mailings to participa ting Lodges to
apprise them of jurisdiction-wide progress and procedures. The last survey to
ascertain participa tion by California and Hawaiian Lodges got a response
from 158 Lodges, up about 50 from 1972. However, these figures are misleading because, for instance, with a response from only three San Francisco
Lodges, a Master to Master survey following, showed that there were 20 participating San Francisco Lodges. We can therefore report with confidence that
the jurisdiction has embraced the program in substanti ally greater numbers
than the 158 which responded.
In 1972, just a year ago, 120 Lodges were represented at the Wednesd ay
morning meeting of the sub-committee to learn about the program and to
secure prospectu ses for organization. This year, there will be a repeat of this
meeting on Wednesd ay morning with new material developed and now prepared for interested Lodges.
Public Relations : led by C. Clifford Geddes, this group has led discussions and responded to requests for speakers to many Masonic and non1\fasonic groups througho ut the year. As previousl y reported, the theme of
most talks is patriotic with a light flavor of Masonry. The reception has been
most favorable to the Fraternit y as evidenced by the repeat invitations.
Research Lodge Studies: though the chairman of this group, David C.
Lee 492 was not a member of this Committee this year, he continued his
assi~nme~t to head the sub-committee group charged with the duty of passing
on all Research Lodge publications before they should be permitted to be put
into print.
Lodge Informat ion Programs: under the leadership of the two vice-chairmen, Louis I. Goldkind , and Max H. Rush, Jr., several experimental meetings
have been held at the request of Lodges and Districts to open subjects of
Masonic interest as selected. The meetings have demonstrated the value of
the Workshop approach as an educational medium in that the audience is
thus drawn into the discussion. The attendanc e is largely that of officers of
the Lodges invol ved, though open to all members at invitation of the Masters.
Experimentation has been aimed at broadening the appeal in interest to
members other than officers.
Grand Lodge Tuesday Evening Meeting: headed by the Masters of the
four Research Lodges, Stephen J. Dean, Jr., NCRL; Robert L. Karnes,
SCRL; A. Lincoln Zavertnik, ECRL; and George C. Holstein, CCRL, the
Committee on Masonic Information and Responsi bility bas sponsored a
demonstration of programs of interest to members of the Fraternit y and other
friends, available from the Research Lodges on request. The purpose of the
demonstrated programs is to increase interest in non-degree Masonry, and
to widen knowledge about it. It is hoped that use of such programs will increase attendanc e at the Lodges of members and friends other than the regular
attendees . It was planned that these samples of what the Research Lodges

can do will inspire the members of Grand Lodge to make use of these
facilities.

an Emergent Resolution, found at page 2 72 of the 1972 Proceedings, which
resolution was as follows:
" WHEREAS, the revised Masonic Code is not ready for submission
to Grand Lodge at the October 19 71, Communication;
NOW BE IT RESOLVED, that the draft of the proposed revised
California Masonic Code Annotated, prepared by the Committee on Code
Revision, be reviewed by the elective Grand Lodge officers and by the
members of the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General
Purposes; and that those sections of the said revised code which. shall be

be printed and shall become effective as the California Masonic Code
Annotated when so declared by the Grand Master, unless and until

available, on request, for inspection by any member of Grand L-Odge; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this resolution be considered
and adopted as an emergent matter pursuant to Section 104 of the California Masonic Code."
WHEREAS, · the revised Masonic Code has not been printed and is not

WHEREAS, your Special Committee on Code Revision and those working
