ORGANIZATION:
This committee is composed of seventeen members of the Grand Lodge of
California. Each member is appointed by the Grand Master after his installation at the annual communication of Grand Lodge. Each appointment is for
the term of one year to run concurrent with the term of the Grand Master.
Each member will serve in the capacity of Grand Lodge Committeeman until
he is replaced by the Grand Master.
The seventeen members are appointed as follows :
1. Chairman: A member appointed from any area in the Jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California. He is to chair all meetings of the
Committee and to have the function which his title implies. He is directly responsible to the Grand Master and is to work with the appointed liaison officer of the Grand Line.
2. Division.al Members: lVIembers will be appointed to this committee at
the rate of two, ( 2), for each Grand Lodge Division, for a total of 12
members. These members are to be responsible for their immediate
divisions. They are responsible to the Grand Master through the Chairman of the Committee.
3. Members at Large: These are four members of the Committee who
are appointed by the Grand Master at the recommendation of the
respective adult leaders. One representative from the Northern California DeMolay Jurisdiction recommended by the Jurisdictional Executive Officer. One representative from the Southern California DeMolay Jurisdiction recommended by the Jurisdictional Executive
Officer. One representative of the International Order of Job's Daughters recommended by the Grand Guardian.
One representative of the International Order of Rainbow for Girls recommended by the Supreme Deputy in California. Ia all cases the member
must meet the requirements of appointment. That is, he must be a Past
Master of a constituent Lodge of the Grand Lodge of California.

REPORT OF BOARD OF LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:

Your Board of Library Commissioners and our Volunteer Staff has had
the good fortune and great pleasure of serving our brethren and responding
to their specific requests for assistance in an increasing number of occasions
this past year. During the fiscal year concluded June 30, we have had an
increase in the number of books loaned through our lending library to a record
282. Our members and interested friends donated 239 volumes, another
significantly high number for a given year. Our Museum was the fortunate
recipient of 10 articles of historical Masonic value, all having been carefully
marked, catalogued and either placed on display in our very limited space or
placed in our archives for anticipated use when expanded and enlarged facilities are available. Within our limited financial resources we were able to
purchase 39 books of significant Masonic content. These are placed among a
book collection that, while limited in numbers of volumes, is of high quality
and true Masonic worth. In order to keep abreast of current publications and
also to be informed of rare items that might become available on the commercial market we subscribe to several book-finder services as well as to

237

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

periodicals published by significant research organizations throughout the
world.
During the past year one of our distinguished brothers, and a true l\fasonic
Scholar in the finest sense had his book KING SOLOMON AND His TEMPLE IN
MASONIC AND PoPULAH LEGEND published, and it is now available in our
library and elsewhere. Brother Alex Horne, Past Master of Doric Lodge
No. 216 has brought great honor to this Grand Lodge by his efforts in the
field of )Jasonic Research. Over the years our library has benefited greatly
from his wise counsel and great resource of Masonic knowledge. We salute

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
The special committee on insurance held several meetings during the 1973
Masonic year to study and reevaluate the insurance program for Grand Lodge
and its related entities.
Individual policies were reviewed to determine the adequacy of insurance
provided, in relationship to the probability of loss and the cost for such
insurance.
::\1embers of the committee were requested to present their comments,
suggestions, and rec9mmendations with regard to the present insurance program for Grand Lodge and related entities. It was agreed by committee
members that the special policy contracts for fraternal organizations provided
by the Travelers Insurance Companies, in many instances, afforded broader
additional coverages and/or conditions not usually found in the standard
policies.
A " Loss Record Register" has been maintained which includes a record of
all losses, and the final disposition of said losses. Through the cooperation of
Thompkins and Company, it was possible to obtain loss data dating back
several prior years. A summary of the losses sustained during the period of
July I, 1967 through June 30, 1973 was made. This summary provided an
excellent opportunity to review not only the dollar amount of los.ses, but also
the cause and frequency of such losses. This loss information is extremely
helpful also to determine what action may be taken to reduce similar losses
in the future.
The review of los.ses shows that the loss ratio for all policies, except for
lodge paraphernalia insurance, has been good. The adverse loss experience
for lodge paraphernalia is due primarily to a substantial loss at the P alo Alto
Masonic Temple in 1971.
After a st udy of the present insurance program for Grand Lodge, Masonic

238

239

PROCEEDfNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Homes of California, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and related
entities, the committee made several recommendations to the Grand Lodge
Secretary for further consideration.
Recommendations which subsequently have been adopted are as following:
1. The total amount of blanket insurance on buildings and contents for
Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes of California, and California Masonic
Memorial Temple properties should be increased to $18,600,000 which
represents approximately 90% of the replacement costs. This new
amount of insurance is based on a revaluation of 1973 labor and
material costs.
2. Based on a study of previous losses, it was the committee's decision
that a premium savings may be realized if the loss deductible were
increased from $100 to $1,000 on the blanket buildings and contents
coverage.
3. In view of the possibility of a catastrophic loss occurring at our Masonic properties, it was recommended that the limit of liability, provided in the comprehensive public liability policy applicable to Grand
Lodge, Masonic Homes of California, California Masonic Memorial
Temple, and California Masonic Foundation properties, be increased
from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 per occurrence.
4. A study of automobile physical damage losses that occurred during
the past six years, indicated that a possible saving could be realized by
a change of the collision deductible from $100 to $250 and by the
addition of a $50 deductible for comprehensive losses.

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITIEE

In addition to those policies to which recommendations were made, the
committee also analyzed other policies that are part of the insurance program
for Grand Lodge, including constituent Lodges, Masonic Homes of California,
California Masonic Memorial Temple, and California Masonic Foundation.
The committee felt that no changes in these other policies were necessary at
the present time.
I would like to take this opportunity to express the committee's commendation to the members of the individual Lodges, and to the managers and
employees of our Masonic properties for their conscientious efforts in maintaining our properties in a safe manner, thereby reducing the number of
losses.
A sincere " thank you" to the Grand Lodge office staff and to all others
who have been so cooperative and helpful to this committee during the past
year.
Respectfully submitted,

FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1973

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Although both the stock and bond markets suffered devastating losses
during the past year, the widely publicized decline in security prices had a
relatively small effect on the investment portfolio under the control of the
Investment Committee. Total market value, as delineated below, was
$40,518,869 at June 30, 1973, as compared with a total of $40,690,615 at
the close of the prior year.
Activities of the Committee are regulated generally by the Masonic Code,
which sets forth the three major categories (as groups) of securities allowable for investment. These categories may be summarized as follows:
( 1) Group I-Consists of cash, savings accounts, obligations of the
United States, obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions, and such other securities as are legal for savings banks in California
and Hawaii. In general, Group I may be said to consist of the highest grade
and most conservative securities. At least 20% of the funds available for
investment must be maintained in such securities .
(2) Group II-Consists generally of bonds, debentures, and other evidences of indebtedness which do not meet the qual ifications of Group I. It
also consists of preferred stocks which are listed on a National Securities
Exchange and the preferred stocks of corporations whose common stocks
are eligible for investment in Group III.
( 3) Group HJ-Consists of common stocks, which must be fully listed
and registered on a national exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, bank and insurance company stocks, shares of investment trusts, and savings accounts with savings and loan associations. Total
investments in Group III securities are generally limited to 60% of the total
portfolio.

During the past fiscal year the percentage of the portfolio in Group I
(bonds) has increased from approximately 25 % to 30%. The increase in
this area was made to take advantage of the attractive yields available in the
corporate bond sector of the market. Quality issues were purchased with
yields from 7.50% to 8.50% with non-refunding provisions in most cases
from 5 to 8 years.
Group II (convertibles) decreased from 20% to 17% mainly due to the
decrease in market value of the convertible issues held. This was caused by
both the decrease in prices of stocks into which the issues are convertible
and the lower bond prices occasioned by the dramatic increase in yields over
the past year. These issues do, however, appear to provide a good current
return and longer term appreciation potential for our fund.
Group III (common stocks) decreased from 55% to 52% due to lower
stock prices. Realized and unrealized net losses in the equity portfolio
amounted to about 3 % for the year. This compares favorably with the decline of 4% in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and a far greater decline
in most of the mutual funds surveyed by the Committee. Our investments in
common stocks are based upon recommendations of our investment advisor,
Alliance Capital Management Corporation. They continue to emphasize
companies with long-term growth characteristics, confined to a manageable
number of holdings concentrated in those areas of the economy believed to
be most attractive.
The primary goals of this Committee as stated many times before is to
provide the maximum income commensurate with the safety and preservation of capital. The portfolio as it is presently constituted should provide

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTTEE ON

INVESTMENT GOALS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Pursuant to that request of 16 April 1973 the Chairman of the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes, M.W. Theodore Meriam; Chairman of the
Committee on Retirement Pension Plan, M.W. Guy B. Mize; the President
of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes, M.W. Myron E. Smith; the
President of the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple, DeWald· M. Baum; the President of the Board of Directors of the
California Masonic Foundation , John S. Hunt; the Grand Treasurer, M.W.
Chester R. MacPhee; and the Grand Secretary, M.W. Edward H. Siems, met
at the Airport Marina Hotel in Los Angeles on May 5, 1973 to discuss the
investment program of the Grand Lodge insofar as it applies to the goals of
the several Grand Lodge entities.
M.W. Myron E. Smith of the Masonic Homes Board indicated the need
to retain some available funds for the redevelopment of the Masonic Home
at Union City. Brother Smith stated approximately eight million dollars will
be needed over a period of three years for this purpose. He also emphasized
the importance of maintaining Homes Board funds invested only in blue
chip common stocks to the limit allowed with hopes for favorable interest
rates on bonds and convertibles.
M.W. Guy B. Mize presented a letter outlining the views of his committee.
The letter indicated dissatisfaction with the efforts of Wells Fargo Bank. He
called attention to the need for high yield income necessary to hold down
employee and Grand Lodge contributions to the fund. Brother Mize wanted
the fund free of any speculative stocks and inves tments only in blue chip
stocks, where applicable, with high yield bonds in most of the portfolio.

242

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

M.W. Theodore Meriam, Chairman of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes, gave his views that the investment of funds should be in
accordance with the schedule adopted by the Grand Lodge and that no funds
for common stocks should be invested in other than blue chip stocks.
DeWald Baum, Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, observed that the Temple Board had no investment funds available at the present time but recited the fine goals accomplished by his Lodge, Los Angeles No. 42, wherein all stock investments are in
blue chip stocks. Brother Baum requested that future investments as to stocks
for the Temple Trustees should be limited to this type of stock.
John Hunt, President of the Board of Directors of the California Masonic
Foundation, stated their policy should be to have a combination of the two
different types of investment, perhaps leaning a little more heavily on the
high yield long term class double or triple A Bonds and the rest in high
quality common stock - approximately 607o in high yield bonds and 40%
in common stocks.
Brother John Sickenberger, Chairman of the Committee on Finance, the
other member of the committee, was unable to be present and his views were
solicited by telephone. Brother Sickenberger said, "As Chariman of the Committee on Finance, it has been my privilege to be a member of the Investment
Committee for the past few years and it is my feeling that we should continue our investment policy, which is in accord with the present Masonic Law,
and continue our attention in better grade equities (common stocks) and
convertibles as we have done in the past with the knowledge that in the
long run the total return will be quite adequate."
The Grand Lodge Committee on Investments was helpful to the committee in its deliberations and has been advised of the foregoing.

The Investment C otnmittee expressed its concurrence in the foregoing
statements.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON FISCAL AFFAIRS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In their last year's "Letter of Recommendations" addressed to our Grand
Master, our outside auditors, Touche Ross & Co., said in part "We recommended in last year's letter that an advisory committee be
formed to consult with and advise the Grand Secretary in accounting and tax
matters.
We believe there are several areas where a committee of Masons knowledgeable in accounting practices and tax matters could provide valuable assistance to the Grand Secretary and Chief Accountant.
The accounting department during the past few years has been assigned
several additional responsibilities such as tax return preparation, preparation
of special reports for the various Grand Lodge Committees and acting as
internal auditors. We recommend that an evaluation of the workload in the
accounting department be made to determine if all the tasks performed are
necessary and if there are sufficient qualified personnel."
Grand Master Price, under date of November 9, 1972 appointed this
"Special Advisory Committee on Fiscal Affairs" and directed that "This special committee should function in an advisory capacity to the
Grand Master and to the Grand Lodge in regard to the fiscal affairs of the
Grand Lodge."
During the course of the year various assignments were given the committee which were studied in depth and reports and recommendations were
returned to the Grand Master. In order to assure the brethren of the close
attention given the fiscal affairs of the Grand Lodge, this report will summarize those assignments.
In may be a mystery to many in Grand Lodge why such an apparent
large number of employees are found in the Grand Secretary's office. It is
probably all too seldom considered that the Grand Secretary of necessity is
the equivalent of the executive officer of four substantial corporations and
a large pension fund. The total assets involved exceed sixty million dollars;
the total cash receipts exceed nine and a half million dollars a year ; and the
investments in stocks and bonds amount to more than forty-two million
dollars. This kind of an organization requires people to do the work and we
are fortunate to have a capable and devoted staff.
Your committee made a rather comprehensive review of the personnel in
the office of the Grand Secretary. We obtained and analyzed job descriptions
of all the employees and examined the organization of the office. We then
made a comprehensive review of salaries and fringe benefits, comparing them
to the best available information on practices in the San Francisco Bay area.
A few salary adjustments were called for but, in general, it was found that
our employment practices in regards to salaries and benefits conformed to
general practice. It should be assuring to you that the personnel were found

245

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

to be necessary to perform the work the Grand Lodge has assigned to the
office. Your committee urges that continuing attention be given to proper
employee remuneration as this is not a proper area of economy.
Your committee participate d in discussions regarding the selection of the
outside auditors of Grand Lodge and its entities. A new auditing firm was
selected for the annual audits. It is a substantial local firm of certified public
accountant s in contrast to the use of large national firms in the past number
of years. Substantia l savings in audit costs will result from this change. It is
also believed the quality of the work will improve.
Well over ten years ago Grand Lodge purchased a relatively simple
bookkeeping machine for use in accounting. The machine reached the end
of its useful life during the current year. Your committee independen tly
reviewed the available equipment on the market, the studies prepared in the
Grand Secretary's office, and approved the action taken during the year in
purchasing a modern mini-computer accounting machine. It is generally
known that computers have made important contributio ns to data processing
and it is frequently understood that computers are extremely expensive equipment. Although the cash outlay appears to be high, we believe that savings
can be made with its proper utilization that will largely offset the cost and
will provide more and better informatio n than now available. We wish to
emphasize strongly that this is not the ultimate of computers for this organization. It is reasonable to believe that within five to ten years a far more
sophisticated computer will be available within realistic costs to provide much
greater services. We should be looking toward the future and preparing for
the time when we may make another advance.
Your committee has the full realization that the fiscal affairs of Grand
Lodge are becoming more critical. The per capita revenues of Grand Lodge are
not keeping pace with expanding costs. In the future, critical examinatio n
of the expenses of Grand Lodge will be increasingly necessary. In this respect
careful consideration was given to travel allowances and hotel expenses. The
Grand l\faster, in July 1973, set forth guidelines including transportat ion at
10¢ a mile or minimum air and public transportat ion fares, whichever is the
lesser. The Grand Master also presented arrangeme nts made at several first
class San Francisco hotels for rooms at special daily rates representing considerable savings over other hotels frequently used.
Kot minimizing in the slightest the awesome responsibilities of the Grand
Master and the demands made on the corporate officers and trustees of the
Masonic Homes of California, the California l\Jasonic l\Iemorial Temple an<l
the California Masonic Foundation , the Grand Secretary's office is the
instrument of Grand Lodge that holds it all together. It requires a Grand
Secretary to be competent in many fields as the only full-time executive.
Your committee believes that anyone looking at the position would agree
our complex organizatio n could not function without strong day to day
direction and leadership.
It may not be generally known that we pay our Grand Secretary $25,000

a year, of which $2,440 is returned to Grand Lodge as the amount of the
pension paid to him from the pension fund. The salaries and benefits of Grand
Lodge employees are reviewed each year and changes are made to keep pace
with the local labor market. The Grand Secretary's salary was last changed
eight years ago, in October 1965, at which time this Grand Lodge approved
the increase from $20,000 to $25,000 yearly. It is our definite opinion that
a change is past due.
It is the recommendation of this committee that the salary of the Grand
Secretary be increased to $30,000 a year, effective November 1, 1973, subject
to reduction by the amount of pension paid. Your committee feels this is
simple recognition of the importance of the office and is still only a token
as compared to the real worth of the position.

Respectful ly submitted,
W. STANLEY DAVIS, Chairman

The Committee on Finance:
Your Finance Committee has reviewed the Report of the Special Advisory
Committee on Fiscal Affairs. We feel that this Committee has produced information of essential value, and therefore add our support to t he Grand
Master's recommendation to continue the activity of this Committee next

year.
In our consideration of the specific recommendation to increase the Grand
Secretary's salaty to $30,000, we have endeavored to compare this rather
unique but important executive position to similar ones in the world of
business. From all that we have determined , we conclude that the proposed
salary is a modest figure in today's market.
It should be noted that over the years your Finance Committee, by necessity, has maintained a close relationshi p with the office of the Grand Secretary .
This relationship, in turn, has provided us with a first hand knowledge of
the complex duties connected with that office.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMIT TEE ON MUTUA L FUNDS
0972 GRAND MASTER'S RECOM MENDA TION NO. 4)
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Pursuant to the recommend ation of Grand Master Lester S. McElwain
at the Annual Communic ation of Grand Lodge in October 1972, a committee

246

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

was appointed to investigate the possibility of establishing a mutual fund
within Grand Lodge for use by those constituent Lodges who were desirous of
such service.
As the result of an exchange of ideas between committee members a
questionnaire was promulgated to be directed to each of the constituent
Lodges seeking the individual Lodges views on the subject matter.
The committee also sought the advice of the Grand Lodge Committee on
Investments as well as independent brokers and agents.
Three hundred eighty seven Lodges responded to the questionnaire and
that tabulation indicates 105 Lodges, or 29 % , of those who gave their views
were interested; some very interested and other passively interested in the
formation of a Grand Lodge Mutual Fund.
In view of the percentages of interest, as well as the substantial requirements and costs involved in undertaking such a program, your special
committee recommends against the establishment of a mutual fund within
the Grand Lodge at this time.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON AUDITING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Auditing, during the Grand Lodge year ending October
197 3 has reviewed Claims for Expense Reimbursement, in accordance with
the booklet of Instructions and Regulations issued by Grand Lodge. These
regulations have been supplemented from time to time by instructions from
Grand Masters.
While Expense Claims for reimbursement were generally moderate, we
would like to point out some items for better operation:
I. In view of declining Grand Lodge income and increasing expense, it is
necessary for every Grand Lodge member to be as economical as
possible when spending Grand Lodge money. This has a definite effect
on the per capita assessment to the Constituent Lodges.
2. Expense statements, to be processed promptly, should be submitted
monthly, with proper receipts, properly approved and stating the
Grand Lodge activity or meeting involved. This enables us to determine
relative costs of such meetings and activities.
This Committee suggests that a meeting, in the near future, with the
Grand Master and the Finance Committee Chairman, would be most helpful
in laying down further guidelines regarding actual dollar allowances for the
ensuing year, to supplement the Instructions and Regulations now in effect.

REPORT OF RETIREMENT PENSION PLAN COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your committee appointed to administer the California Masonic Retirement Plan respectfully presents its report for the Grand Lodge year ending
June 30, 1973. The figures used in the compilation of the actuarial reports are
for the calendar year 1972. However, the employer contribution rates for
1973 established for the Grand Lodge and its component organizations and
for the Masonic Homes of California are based on operations during 1972.
The District Director of the Internal Revenue Service on May 21, 1973
ruled the amendments to the Plan which were submitted to Grand Lodge at
the 1971 Annual Communication to be administrative in nature. The amendments stood approved without the necessity, or requirement, of special determination.
Analysis of the actuarial reports prepared by our actuaries, Coates and
Crawford, together with reports and financial statements prepared by the
Grand Lodge office, and by the Trustee, Wells Fargo Bank, again indicates
a general strengthening of the Plan in assets, in improved yields from investments and in its value to the employees who serve our several entities and who
are enrolled as participants in the Plan.
As of December 31, 1972, Trust Assets totaled $1,392,476 on a cost basis.
Recommendations by Alliance Capital Management Corporation to the Investment Committee of Grand Lodge, which were approved, resulted in a
considerable number of changes in the Plan's portfolio of securities.
From sales of securities, a net realized gain of $26,784 was derived in
1972. The number of securities held at the beginning of the year, January 1,
1972, was reduced materially. Securities added to the portfolio were fewer in
number but larger in dollar amounts.
On December 31, 1972, the market value of securities owned was approximately $58,000 less than their cost value. However, subsequent declines
in the securities market, due to economic conditions during the first six
months of 1973 have resulted in further diminishing the market value of the
'
.
.
Fund. With no pressure to sell on an adverse market, and with close attention
being given to the investment program as it relates to and affects the Retire-

249

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ment Pension Fund, it is anticipated that investments in securities owned by
the Fund will not be affected adversely.
For the calendar year 1972 the total investment income was $83,322, including realized gain of $26,784 from sale of securities, as opposed to $72,933
for the preceding year. The net investment income was $75,670, equivalent
to a yield of 5. 71 % on the cost value of invested funds. The comparable yield
for the preceding calendar year was 5.45 %Excluding realized gain from sale of securities, the net yield would be
4.28% as opposed to 2 .83% for the preceding year. If the yield were computed on the basis of excluding gain from sales, anrl before expenses charged
to the Fund, the yield on a cost basis would be 4.85 % as opposed to 3.6 l %
for the preceding year.
Since the early part of 1972, the average interest/dividend yielrl on
investments has been increased from 3.8% to approximately 5% using a
cost basis for determining the yield on investments. On a market basis, as of
June 30, 1973, the current investment yield was approximately 6'/o. These
yields are taken from reports compiled by the investment counselor.
The valuations established by the actuaries, for the purpose of determining
the employer contribution rate, have been made on the assumption that the
Trust would earn 4% per annum.
A review of schedules contained in the actuaries' reports shows that: for
the Masonic Homes of California, the number of active participating members in the Plan increased during 1972 from 108 to 117. The annual covered
payroll increased by $73,174 - from $720,923 to $794,097; and the average
annual salary of employees participating in the Plan was $6,673 - compared
with $6,675 last year. The number of retired members decreased by one (1)
- from 34 to 33. The annual pensions being paid increased by $654 - from
$24,461 to $25,115.
For the Grand Lodge of California anrl its components, the number of
active participating members in the Plan decreased by one ( 1) - from 18
to 17. The annual covered payroll decreased by $1,817 - from $133,868 to
$132,051. The average annual salary increased by $331 - from $7,437 to
$7, 768. The number of retired members increased by one ( 1) - from 16 to 17
and annual pensions being paid increased by $145 - from $21,333 to
$21,478.
To maintain this Plan in sound financial condition, continuing the employee contribution rate of 3%, assuming a 4% return on investments and
considering the portfolio of investments at cost value as of December 31, 19 72,
our actuaries have calculated an employer's contribution rate this year of
8.79% of payroll for Masonic Homes of California and 9.69% of payroll
for the Grand Lodge and its components. Last year the contribution rates were
9.17% and 10.83 % respectively.
In closing this report, your committee expresses its appreciation to the
Grand Secretary and the members of his staff for the full cooperation extended us during the year, and to the firm of Coates and Crawford for the

complete reports furnished and which are the basis for much of the information contained herein.
We request that an appropriation of $600 be included in the Grand Lodge
budget to cover operating expenses of the committee for the ensuing Grand
Lodge year.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON PUBLIC INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is the intent of this committee to inform the News Media of California
and Hawaii of the pure thoughts, good intentions and activities of Masonry.
Since the founding of this committee, each year has shown progress in
communication with the News Media. This has been most noticeable in the
past few years, to the extent that the Media is becoming curious about us.
We first experienced this at the two School Cornerstone Layings in Huntington Beach early in the year. Governor Ronald Reagan was present with hi&
staff to participate with our fraternity for the first time in his career. I later
received a letter from his Publicity Director expressing the Governor's pleasure in witnessing our ceremonies and stating that the Governor is looking
forward to being with us again in the future.
During the 197 2 session of Grand Lodge your Chairman and his wife met
with two of the Publishers of the three major Bay Area newspapers. We had
gone previously to the City Editors of these papers often and were well
received. We called the Publishers merely to express our appreciation for their
fine coverage of our Masonic events and were met with their request to meet
with them personally. We were cordially received in their respective offices.
The summation of this is that the News Media wants information about
our activities. Unfortunately your committee cannot cover every event up
and down the two States. We have therefore changed our section of the Lodge
Manual to offer more assistance to the various Lodges in obtaining publicity
of their activities. If you read and follow the instructions in this section of the
Manual it will be amazing how well your project will be received by the News
Media.
With the new changes in the Public Information section of the Lodge
Manual, the committee has assumed a much larger responsibility. All members will soon be prepared to fulfill this new function. This committee stands
ready at all times to assist in any Public Information matter. Please call on us.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report covering
the 124th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to mileage compensation are the Master, or in his absence,
the ranking \Varden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly
Elected Representative and Past Grand Masters, if they attend Grand Lodge
in such capacity only. However, when a Master and Warden from the same
Lodge are present at an Annual Communication, and one of said Officers
serves on a Grand Lodge Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, he shall be reimbursed accordingly; the other Officer shall receive reimbursement under Section 174, California Masonic Code, as the Officer representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California State
Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San
Francisco has been taken from the published reports of air lines, in accordance with Sections 174 and 176, California Masonic Code. No compensation
is allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of California has been computed on the
basis of ten ( 10) cents per mile, the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance.
Compensation of the members from the State of Hawaii has been figured on
the basis of published first class round-trip air rates of regularly scheduled
major air lines, from Honolulu to San Francisco, plus inter-island air fare to
Honolulu when necessary.

to us by the Committee on Credentials, and the amounts required to meet the
transportation costs for the 1973 Annual Communication are as follows:

II
England - Italy
We are pleased to report that harmonious relations exist between the
Grand Lodges with whom we are in amity. The United Grand Lodge of England has recognized the Grand Orient of Italy, finding that it is indisputably
the predominant Masonic organization in Italy ; that it has been meticulous
in avoiding any imputation of political interference ; that it does not recognize any Grand Lodge which England considers to be irregular or does not
recognize ; and its principles correspond closely with those of other recognized
Grand Lodges. This is the position which, on the recommendation of the late
William Rhodes Hervey, P.G.M., our Grand Lodge took al the 1952 Communication.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGN ITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Gra11d Lodge, F. & A. M. of California :

I
Gran Logia La Oriental Peninsular
This Grand Lodge has its seat in the City of lVIerida, State of Yucatan
and claims jurisdiction of that state, as well as the Territory of <!~inta~a
Roo and Belize. The first lodge in this area was chartered by Louisiana m
1820 and the charter was arrested in 1849. The Grand Lodge came into
exist~nce in 1883. There are about fifteen subordinate lodges, and a total
membership of six to seven hundred. Although it i~ a small and ~emote G~a~d
Lodge, it is a member of the Association Masomca Interamen ca and is m
fraternal relationship with the other l\Iexican State Grand Lodges.
The Commission on Information for Recognition of the Conference of
the Grand Masters of Masons in North America finds this Grand Lodge to
be worthy of recognition.
An interesting side light is a recent decree citing a subordinate lodge,
Nachi Cocom No. 6 with the distinction of being an Augusta, Benemerita y
Respectable Logia (August, Worthy and Venerable) in recognition of "SO
years of uninterrup ted, loyal, obedient and active labor in Masonry."
La Oriental Peninsular has been recognized by fourteen of our Grand
Lodges in the past year, in addition to the nine which had previously
granted recognition .
Jorge D. Martinez Herrera is Grand Master and Armando Alvarado Vera
is Grand Secretary. The temple is at Calle 63 No. 568 Apartado Postal 61,
Merida, Yucatan, Mexico.
Based on the foregoing, I move that the Gran Logia La Oriental Peninsular
be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.

Brazil
In the 1971 report, we mentioned certain correspondence with the Grand
Orient of Brazil, and recommended against recognition . This seems to be the
position of the American Grand Lodges which have considered the question.
Even Florida, which recognized the Grand Orient in 1971, has had second
thoughts and is reviewing the matter.

IV
Cuba
Your Committee shares the concern with :Masons throughout the world
for the continuance of Masonry in Cuba. Historically, dictators everywhere,
be they Fascist, Communist, or Falangist , have done their utmost to destroy
Masonry and all that it stands for. From the best information available to us,
the Grand Lodge of Cuba and its subordinate lodges continue to operate amid
some harassment but, as far as can be determined, still operating in a reasonably normal manner. Our Brethren in this troubled land need all the help
and support possible during these perilous times and we concur with the vast
majority of the other Grand Lodges of the United States, and most of the
Grand Lodges throughout the world, that we should continue to recognize
the Grand Lodge of Cuba until more definitive information is available that
would change our opinion and will so recommend to this Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, JR. , Chairman

In many Grand Jurisdictions, a Grand Master appomts a man to t e

261

bottom of the progressive line, whatever the office may be. In others, election
day witnesses nominations from the floor, with multiple candidates, followed
by balloting, sometimes run-off elections. In others, a Kominating Committee
presents a nominee for consideration. In others, a system similar to ours is
used. Most of the Grand Jurisdictions use a Nominating Committee or have
the Grand Master appoint a brother in the line.
In the California system the Past Grand Masters in effect perform the
function of a Nominating Committee. The principal difference is that by
custom in our jurisdiction the name of the recommendee for Junior Grand
Warden is circulated orally and at different times, whereas the Nominating
Committee's report of other jurisdictions is usually revealed by mailing
printed announcements or by a report at the Annual Communication.
In our Grand Lodge, the progressive line starts with the Junior Grand
Warden, and only a limited number of the membership at large have the
opportunity of observing the brother during his previous Masonic years. They
must therefore depend upon some one or some group to make that observation
and produce a recommendation.
Past Grand Masters have experienced the tasks involved, have travelled
throughout the jurisdiction, and have had an opportunity not only to meet
personally with potential candidates but to obtain the views of Masons
throughout the jurisdiction.
For these reasons we believe that the Past Grand Masters and the Grano
Master should constitute the Nominating Committee. This, in effect, has
been our previous practice.
We are aware that confusion has sometimes existed during the Annual
Communications of the Grand Lodge relating to the identity of the individual
recommended for consideration, and we are aware that the oral lines of
communication respecting the name of the brother recommended have sometimes faltered, and that the biographical data concerning the brother is often
lost enroute. Our proposed Resolution would correct this.
It is our belief that the procedure has worked reasonably well. Capable
and dedicated men have been elected to the office of Junior Grand \Varden
and the leadership thus provided to this Grand Lodge has been excellent. The
worldwide recognition of the high quality of California Freemasonry is testimony to the effectiveness of this leadership.
There are numerous questions to be resolved in the selection of a Junior
Grand Warden. The two most important are qualifications and availability.
T hese two break down into several subdivisions. Under qualifications, for
example, are knowledge of and devotion to Freemasonry, a firm acquaintance
with the operations of Grand Lodge, ritualistic proficiency, administrative
experience and ability, Masonic leadership characteristics, and condition of
health. Under availability may be classified willingness to serve, necessary
freedom from demands of business or profession or other organizational obligations, attitude of immediate family, and even to some extent, economic
independence. Moreover, in most cases, the brother elected, usually must plan

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

his business commitments and personal affairs well in advance; and qu_ite
probably many well qualified and otherwise available brethren would decline
to enter a contest for the office.
For these reasons, it would not be good for Freemason ry or Grand Lodge
for the Past Grand Masters or any Nominatin g Committee to place more
than one name before Grand Lodge as a candidate for Junior Grand Warden.
We believe that whatever problems have occurred in the past have been
the result of faulty communication and lack of follow-through on the extent
of communication. It is our belief that the Grand Master should be the one
man who should start an official process of communicating the name of the
brother recommended for the office of Junior Grand Warden, that an approved biographical sketch should be included, and that ~he inforn:ati?n? in
writing should be concurrent ly disseminated to all Lodges m the J unsd1Ct1on,
the Committeemen, Inspectors, and Grand Lodge Officers.
We therefore present the following Resolution:
RESOLVE D, that Section 32 of the California Masonic Code be amended
by adding thereto a new paragraph reading as follows:
"The Past Grand Masters and the Grand Master shall constitute a
Committee to recommend a brother to Grand Lodge for election as Junior
Grand Warden.
The recommendee shall alternately belong to a Lodge in Northern
California one year and to a Lodge in Southern California the next year.
The name of the recommendee and his biographical sketch shall be sent
to each Lodge, Inspector, Committeeman, Member of a Gran~. Lod~e
Board, Grand Lodge Officer, and others on the Grand Lodge ma1lmg hst
who are approved by the Grand Master not less tha~ 6~ or more than 90
days before the opening day of the Annual Commumcation. A representative of the Recommending Committee selected by them may orally
nominate the recommendee for election on election day. Any member of
Grand Lodge may also be nominated from ~he ~oor of Gra~d Lodge on
election day and if there is such other nomm~t10~ the el:ction shall be
by written ballot but if there is only one nommauon election may be by
viva voce vote."
RESOLVE D FURTHER , that to the extent that the procedure specified
in the foregoing paragraph may be or appear to be in c~nftict with any of the
provisions of Annotation 33Sb this amendmen t to. Section_ 32. shall supersede
said Annotation, but the Annotation shall otherwise remam m full force and
effect, and that Annotation 683n is hereby deleted.
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has thoroughly studied
and discussed in conference the very important elements incident to the election of a Junior Grand Warden, including the carefully prepared prefatory
statement of the Special Committee appointed by the Grand Master following
the 1972 Communication. The signers of Resolution No. l constituted the
Special Committee appointed by the Grand Master for the purpose of this
study. It is the sincere hope of the Policy and General Purposes Committee
that all of the members of the Grand Lodge here present have also given
careful thought and study to this critically important subject. Resolution No.
1 now provides an opportunit y for your well-considered action.
This Committee finds no justifiable unfavored criticism of the completely
frank description of the traditional method followed in this jurisdiction in the
annual election of a Junior Grand Warden. As stated in the resolution now
under consideration, the Past Grand Masters do in fact consult and in effect
perform the functions of a Recommending Committee alternating North and
South yearly, in agreeing on an eligible member of this Grand Lodge to be
recommended for election to the office of Junior Grand Warden. In a Jurisdiction as extensive as that of the Grand Lodge of California, the Committee
believes that there is no one in the membership of the Grand Lodge who has
had a better opportunit y to observe the Masonic Service and capacity of that
membership than those who have spent four years in the progressive line of
Grand Office. Cov~ring the entire area perhaps many times over in their
respective tours of duty as Grand Master, the Past Grand Masters have had
the opportunit y to discuss the subject with Masters, Wardens and Past
Masters and to consider and weigh their suggestions. Knowing from service
what the responsibilities and duties in the elected Grand Line consist of ;
knowing what it takes in mental, physical and financial capacity; knowing
what the necessary absences from employment or professional occupation may
mean; it is the opinion of this Committee that the basic method which has
been used has worked well.
That there has been the lack of communication referred to in the resolution is also the opinion of this Committee and your Committee also believes
this has resulted in many situations where some of the members of this Grand
Lodge have been called upon to vote without having any idea as to the
identity of the candidate recommended for election to the office of Junior
Grand Warden. To the extent that this condition exists the efforts of our
brethren to best serve the interests of Masonry in California are wasted. It
appears to this committee, therefore, that the need to be filled without losing
the advantage and strength of actual experience in Grand Office is to improve
and strengthen the channels of communication to the end that the brethren

264

PROCEED INGS OF THE

constituting the membership of this Grand Lodge may know who is recommended for their consideration - and why.
Your Committee is also of the opinion that the membership of a committee
to recommend a member of this Grand Lodge for election to the office of
Junior Grand Warden woul<l be strengthened by the appointm ent by the
Grand Master of three Grand Lodge members who are not past or present
elected Grand Officers, an<l who would serve on such Committee for a single
term only concurrent with the term of the appointing Grand Master.
The Committee believes that much of the communication failure coul<l
well have been caused by the fact that a general dissemination of the identity
an<l qualifications of a "recommendee" througho ut the entire area of this
Grand Jurisdiction could possibly result in discomfiture or embarrassment to
the brother so identified. Your Committee also believes that the Masonic
capstone "Mouth-t o-Ear" to maintain confidentiality should be preserved.
The proponents of Resolution No. 1 have indicated their agreement that the
purposes to be served can be met with the following changes in the first
paragrap h of the " Resolved " portion of the resolution so as to read as
follows:
RESOLVED , that Section 32 of the California Masonic Code be amended
by adding thereto a new paragrap h reading as follows:
"The Past Grand Masters and three members of this Grand Lodge,
to be appointed annually by the Grand Master to serve for a single term
only and concurren tly with the term of the Appointing Grand Master and
who are not past or present elected Grand Officers, shall constitute a committee to recommend to the Grand Lodge a member thereof for election
as Junior Grand Warden.
The recommendee, alternatel y, shall be a member of a Lodge in the
North and of a Lodge in the South. The name of the recommendee and his
biographical sketch shall be sent to each Inspector, and may be sent to
such other members of the Grand Lodge as the Grand Master may determine, within 30 days following the selection by the Recommending
Committee but in no case later than 60 days prior to the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. All dissemination of this information thereafter shall be oral and not by any other means of reproduction. It is
expected that the information shall be communicated promptly and as
often as necessary by the Inspectors to the Masters and Wardens on each
Inspectoral District and through them to other members of the Grand
Lodge in their respective Lodges."
It is the unanimous opinion of the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes that no further wording in Section 32 is needed to accomplish the
desired purpose. The Committee recommends the adoption of the substitut e
resolution.

OPERATI ON OF MASONIC PROPERTIES

(3)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, Masonic Temples are hard pressed to keep pace with the
present demands of the high cost of living, the pressures of inflation, higher
maintenance costs, higher taxes, etc., with no visible means of increasing
income to subsidize the same, and
WHEREAS, it might be well at this time to consider new methods of
Jetting l\lasonically-owned properties be self supporting through conunercial
income where practical, notwithstand ing there could be the loss of a non
profit tax status on the portion that was showing a profit which would be far
less disadvantageous than having to pay income tax on substantial rental income that can be adjusted, commensurat e with the time and place, and
WHEREAS, this is a pressing problem and should require attention from
persons who have time and ability to devote their efforts to it, and
WHEREAS, the present Committee on Lodge Financing is already overburdened, and
WHEREAS, there are many good and qualified persons located throughout this Grand Jurisdiction who are engaged in, or are thoroughly familiar
with the operations of real property management and who could make good
and timely suggestions and could outline procedures pertinent to Masonic
Lodge and Temple Association operations which could be compiled and put
into printed form, to be distributed to Masonic Lodges and Temple Associations, already in existence, and to those contemplatin g building temples or
buying real property for that purpose, and
WHEREAS, it is well known throughout our Grand Jurisdiction that this
is not a new problem but one that has existed for many years, and
WHEREAS, it is also well known that some very fine Masonic Temples
have been lost from Masonry due to unfortunate circumstances or perhaps
the lack of proper management, and
WHEREAS, it is the present thinking of some of the Committee on
Lodge Financing that Masonic Lodges or Temple Associations should not
engage in any kind of commercial development that could be made a good
source of additional income needed to help defray the expense of upkeep,
including higher taxes, higher maintenance costs, inflationary pressures and
numerous other expenses, and
WHEREAS, it is well known that the foregoing expenditures can not be
met with a normal dues structure applicable to those on fixed incomes or from
rents derived from the average tenant of a Masonic Temple, and
WHEREAS, we are all of the same family and we all share the same
problems, especially the youth groups, whom it should be within our province
to assist when possible through lower rents, and

CONSTITUENT LODGE TEMPLE BUILDING FUND
(5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, many Masonic Temples in California and Hawaii are becoming inadequate due to age and size, even necessitating Lodges using other
non-masonic facilities, and
WHEREAS, the availability of construction funds are limited, and due
to the high cost of money, many Lodges are unable to remodel existing
temples or construct new needed ones, and,
WHEREAS, it is the intention of this Resolution through the participation of every Mason in the State of California and Hawaii to institute a fund
to be known as~ Building Assistance Fund, whereby Lodges in the jurisdiction
can acquire financial assistance to remodel the existing Temple or for the
construction of a new Temple, and,
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California would be in control of this
fund and would receive the interest therefrom for its services,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that each Mason in the State
of California and Hawaii on January 1, 1974 be assessed $5.00 to create a
fund , and on January !st of the next ten ( 10) years, each Mason be assessed
an additional $2.00.
That the committee of Grand Lodge establish guidelines for the administration of the funds and guidelines for the qualifications for the use of the
funds.
That upon application and due qualification, any Lodge may acquire
loans at a very nominal interest rate to be repaid on terms set by the committee.
Respectfully submitted,
TERRENCE M. PARKER, P.M.,
JAMES E. VANCE, M., No. 167
No. 167
ORVILLE SEXTON, S.W., No. 167
WILLIAM: BECK, P.M., No. 167

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General Purposes, on Finance, and on Lodge Financing:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to assess every Master Mason in this Grand
Jurisdiction $5.00 and an additional $2.00 each year to create a fund for the
remodeling of Masonic Temples or the construction of new ones.
Your Committee is aware that many Lodges have been able to afford to
build or remodel their Temples only because the brethren have participated in
the actual work. This sharing of labor has generated great enthusiasm and a
strong sense of pride of ownership among the Lodge's membership much to
the benefit of the Lodge.
In addition, the funds being provided by Grand Lodge will inevitably mean
more regulation by Grand Lodge and less control for the local Lodge. One of
the great strengths of Masonry is the concept of Lodges joining together
to form a Grand Lodge. Local control has many virtues including a sense of
personal accomplishment.
I move the adoption of the resolution and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Lodge Financing:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing has considered Resolution No. 5
and makes the following observations:
It is questionable whether any real value will come from establishment of
the proposed building fund since, if the proposed purchase or construction is
not a good risk for a commercial lender, it is probably also not a good investment for Grand Lodge.
Distinct problems can be expected in regard to repayment of loans would Grand Lodge not be reluctant to foreclose on a Temple Association?
If foreclosure does occur, what does one do with a single purpose Masonic
Temple? Would Grand Lodge not be looked to to advance additional monies
where Lodge or Temple Association funds could be made available? Is not
incentive removed or reduced for Lodges or Temple Associations?
We see also an immediate dues raise for all Lodges to create a fund of
some $6,000,000.00 - an increase which is unfair to those dedicated brethren
who have scraped, saved and slaved to build and pay for their own temples
- an increase which, if taken by Lodges desiring to build or having financial
problems, could, in most cases, serve to eliminate those problems without
penalizing all other Lodges.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing therefore recommends most strongly
a "No" vote.

The Committ ee on Finance:
Your Committee on Finance recognizes the well intended motive expressed
in this resolution by its proponents. It is our firm opinion, however, that it
does not reach, in depth, the issues facing our Lodges with respect to the
future of their Temples.
It is further evident to us that, while the resolution may answer t~e
financial needs of some Lodges, it would at the same time place a substantial
burden on others.
While the resolution proposes an assessment, your Committee is una?le to
consider it as anything other than a substantial addition to the per capita.
Any attempt to raise funds must be weighed in relati_onship to other
priority rlemands and financial needs of Grand Lodge. This proposal does
not warrant such a priority at this time.
Your Committee on Finance recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been
referred, reports as follows:
A form of Resolution which would accomplish the purpose of the offered
text is as follows:
BE IT RESOLVED that Section 283 of the Masonic Code be amended
by inserting as the first paragraph of subparagraph 5th the following language:
" For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of Jan. 1, 1974 the
sum of $5.00, and for each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of
Jan. 1 in the years 1975 to 1984, both inclusive, the sum of $2.00 in each
of said years. Said sums shall be placed in the Building Assista~ce Fund
of Grand Lodge. Said sums shall be assessed by the Lodge agamst each
member of a Lodge other than plural members thereof and those whose
dues have been remitted."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that there be added to the Masonic
Code a new Article V-B providing as follows :
"Section 256. Building Assistance Fund.
There is hereby created a Building Assistance Fund to consist of the
funds received by Grand Lodge from contributions to such fund pursuant
to Section 283, subparagraph Sth of this Code, which funds shall be
placed in the custody of the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge to be
held by him as such, and to be by him accounted for as other ~r~nd
Lodge funds are accounted for and disbursed pursuant to the provisions
of this Article V-B."
"Section 257. Objective and Loans.
The purpose of said Fund is to assist Lodges and Lodge T emple
Associations in remodeling existing Masonic Temples, or constructing new

274

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Masonic Temples by loaning the Fund to them at nominal interest rates
and repayable on terms established as hereinafter set forth, which loans
shall be evidenced by Promissory Notes secured or unsecured as determined by the Committee. The income from loans shall be added to the
Fund."
"Section 258. Committee.
The Grand Master shall appoint a Committee on Building Assistance
to consist of three ( 3) members who shall, with the approval of the
Grand Master, establish rules and regulations for the lending of the
funds, including terms and rates of interest, and who shall pass upon all
applications of Lodges and Lodge Temple Associations for loans. The
Grand Master shall name the Chairman of the Committee. The members
of the Committee shall be reimbursed from the Fund for their necessary
expenses incurred in the performance of their duties pursuant to Section
176 of this Code."
"Section 259. Disbursement of Funds.
The Grand Treasurer shall disburse the Fund to such Lodges or Lodge
Temple Associations as directed by the Committee and shall hold all
notes, security documents and evidences of the indebtedness in connection with any loans."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 192 be amended by adding
at the end of the second sentence the following language:
"and the Committee on Building Assistance."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 576 be amended by adding
at the end thereof the phrase:
"except as provided in Section 283."
The Committee makes no recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

SERVING BEER AND WINE WITH MEALS IN LODGES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General
Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolutions No. 6 and 7 both have to do with the amending of Sec. 324.2
of the California Masonic Code which prohibits the serving of alcoholic beverages in a Masonic Temple or in the temples of Masonically affiliated organizations, and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has chosen
to make its recommendation on these two resolutions in one report.
Resolution No. 6 proposes that wine and beer be served in the Temple at
banquets. Resolution No. 7 proposes that alcoholic beverages be served by
a liquor caterer to non-affiliated tenants for dinners, trade shows, wedding
receptions, charitable bazaars, etc. in the Temple as a money raising function.
Our present regulations concerning the serving of liquor were made after
much careful study and consideration by you, the members of Grand Lodge,
and it is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that
the existing rules reflect not only current social practices and custom but also
the dignity, the serious purpose, and the recognized quality of the institution of Freemasonry. We believe that in accordance with decorum and propriety, there is never any reason why beverages with alcoholic content should
be served in Masonic Temples.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 6 and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 6 was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Your Committee presents the following resolution:
RESOLVED that Section 324.2 of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows: Insert after the words, "Master Mason", in line eleven
the following: "except that wine and beer may be served by the Lodge with
food in such Temples, buildings and structures" and
RESOLVED further that Section 408 of the California Masonic Code
be amended by adding at the end thereof, "except as provided in Section
324.2 of this Code."
A majority voted against the resolution.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General
Purposes:

The Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 8 proposes to add words to subdivision 2 of Section 349
of the California Masonic Code which would specifically allow the Treasurer of a Masonic Lodge to receive such compensatio n for his services as
the Lodge may direct.
Subdivision (c) of Section 411 of the California Masonic Code, a decision of the Grand Master in 1932, provides that paying a Lodge Treasurer
a nominal salary equal to his dues is improper for there is no more reason
for paying him than for paying the Master.
As a matter of policy, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
does not believe that a Treasurer of a Lodge should receive any compensation
for his services to the Lodge.
I move the adoption of the resolution and the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence :
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution was referred,
reports as follows:
This Resolution would permit a Lodge to provide compensation for the
services of its Treasurer in such an amount as the Lodge may determine.
The Resolution would require the Amendment of Section 349 of the California Masonic Code.
In addition to the amendment, the deletion of Annotation 41 lc would
be necessary.
The proper form for the proposed legislation would be as follows:
BE IT RESOLVED that Annotation 41 lc be deleted and that Section
349 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Section 2. He may receive such compensatio n for his services as the
Lodge may direct; and he shall, within fifteen days after the installation,
execute a good and sufficient bond to the Master, for the faithful performance

SPECIAL TRUST FUND FOR SOCIAL PURPOSES

(9)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS , Section 409 of the California Masonic Code specifies that
the fu nds of a Lodge are trust funds set apart for payment of the necessary
expenses of the Lodge and for the special calls for charity for which it was
instituted, and
WHEREAS, our Grand Lodge has historically taken the position that
social activi ties should be paid for separately by those who desire to participate and that the funds of a Lodge should be conserved for necessary
expenses and special calls for charity, and
WHEREAS, it is not clear how voluntary contributions for activities of
a social nature and which were not intended for necessary expenses or special
calls for charity are to be handled, and
WHEREAS, each Lodge should have the right to determine a procedure
for the receipt and handling of voluntary contributions, disbursements therefrom, accounting therefor, and disposal of surplus from activities of a social
nature;
NOW, THEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED , that the following paragraph
be added to the present two paragraphs of Section 409:
" F unds collected by an officer, committee, or member of a Lodge from
members of the Lodge for social purposes of the Lodge or its members
are received in trust as special funds an d are not funds of a Lodge, and
receipts and disbursemen ts thereof need not be entered in the Lodge books,
or disposited in or withdrawn from the Lodge bank account. The Lodge
shall approve a p roced ure for receiving contributions , making disbursements, presenting accountings for such funds, and disposing of surplus.
Surplus may be designated for an object or purpose which will be to the
benefit or welfare of the Lodge, but may not be accumulated for more
than one year at which time it shall, if undesignated , become part of the
funds of the Lodge. All funds shall be subject to audit annually or more
frequen tly as the Lodge may direct."
Respectfully submitted,
HowARD M. McGUFFEY, M., No. 450MORRIS D . TUCKER, M., No. 768

Referred to Committe es on Jurisprud ence and on Policy and General
Purposes:

The Committe e on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 11 proposes that no brother may be installed as Master
of his Lodge unless he shall have attended the Annual Commun ication of the
Grand Lodge at least once within the three past calendar years prior to his
installatio n. The resolution does p rovide for exceptions in emergency situations by issuance of a dispensat ion by the Grand Master or a statemen t from
the Grand Secretary as to the existence of an emergency.
While your Committe e on Policy a nd General Purposes is thorough ly in
accord with the desirabili ty of all incoming Masters having had the experience of attending Grand L-Odge, we do not believe that non-atten dance
should bar a broth.er from serving as Master of his Lodge. The requirem ents
of one's occupatio n may make it impossible to attend Grand Lodge, and it
is hardly conceivable that such requirem ents could be classified as emergency in nature. A brother, unable to attend Grand Lodge because of his
occupatio n, might be thorough ly qualified and very available to discharge
the duties of Master of his L-Odge; in such cases t he Lodge should not be
deprived of its opportun ity to benefit from his leadershi p.
In many of our small Lodges, especially those in the more remote and
sparsely populated regions in our Jurisdiction, difficulty is often experienced
in securing officers for the Lodge. Frequentl y, Past Masters are called upon
to serve again. It would be wrong to impose additional requireme nts for eligibility to serve as Master of such L-Odges; the best possible leadership for the
Lodge is meager at best and the Lodge cannot afford to pay the expense necessary to send an officer to Grand L-Odge; and if the brother designate d to
be M aster cannot afford to attend, surely he should not be disqualified to be
Master.
We believe attendanc e at Grand Lodge should be encouraged in every
way possible. This strengthe ns both the Grand Lodge and the constitue nt

284

PROCEED INGS OF THE

Lodges, as well as providing both inspiratio n and additiona l expertise for
those who attend. But we do not believe that attendanc e should be forced,
and such would be the effect of adopting Resolution No. 11.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 11 and your Committe e on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committe e on Jurisprudence:
By this resolution the proponen ts would require the person, who is to be
installed as Master t~ have attended at least one Commun ication of Grand
Lodge within the p'receding three years or receive a special dispensation excusing him from such attendanc e. This would be in addition to the present
requirem ents.
Your Committe e on Jurisprud ence offers the following legislation to implement this resolution:
BE IT RESOLV ED that Section 476 of the California Masonic Code
setting forth the qualifications of Master be amended by adding at the end
thereof, after the words "governm ent of the Lodge" the words " and that he
has a certificate from the Grand Secretary that he has attended at least one

( 3) years or been excused therefrom by a Dispensa tion from the Grand

excusing such attendanc e."

REDUCE MINIM UM AGE LIMIT
(12)
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
WHERE AS, the term "non-age " as used in Section 511 (a) of the California Masonic Code is defined as being a person under the age of 21 years;
and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

285

WHERE AS, the laws of the State of Californi a were amended in 1971 to
define " minors" as being "all persons under the age of 18 years"; and
WHERE AS, in 1971 the Congress of the United States adopted the 26th
Amendment to the Constitut ion of the United States of America reducing the
minimum voting age from 21 years to 18 years in State and Federal elections,
which Amendm ent was ratified and thereupon made law by the required ;Y4 of
the 50 States within a period of less than one year; and
\\'HEREA S, by both our State and Federal law minors are now regarded
as being all persons under the age of 18 years; and
\VHERE AS, the term " non-age" in its Masonic intent and use is in conflict
with the general legal definition of that term; and
WHERE AS, the Supreme Court of the State of Californi a has concurred
that there is " no magic in the age of 21" in its recognition that the age of 21
as the mark of adulthood was of 11th Century origin as being regarded as the
age when men were physically capable of carrying into battle the heavy armor
of the period; and
WHERE AS, the Masonic use and definition of the term "dotage" is not
regulated or determined by a fixed number of years in determining eligibility
and should not be so regulated in the applicatio n of the term "non-age "; and
WHEREA S, eligibility for Masonry is not in fact a matter of months and
years but one of mental, moral and spiritual capacity for development which,
all other things being equal, State and Federal law now sets as being at age
18; and
WHERE AS, the ever-declining roster of members and the ever-increasing
average age of the membership makes it vitally necessary to inspire a desire
for Masonic membersh ip in young men by the admission of young men into
the Fraternit y before the burdens of marriage and family create burdens
which potentiall y good ~asons cannot or will not carry;
BE IT THEREF ORE RESOLV ED that Article V, Section 511, Annotation (a) be deleted and a new Annotatio n Sll{r) be added as follows: "A
Lodge cannot receive or act upon the petition of an applicant for degrees
until he has arrived at the age of eighteen years."
Respectfu lly submitted ,

Resolutions No. 12 and No. 13 propose the same objective, to lower the
age from 21 to 18 when a ma n can apply for the degrees of Masonry.
The proponents collectively advance as reasons that civil laws have reduced the age of majority to 18, that young men of 18 serve in our military,
that eligibility for Masonry is not a matter of months or years but one of
mental, moral a nd spiritual capacity, that since the term dotage in Masonic
usage is not regulated or determined by a fixed number of years, neither
should the term non-age be, a nd finally that the admission of young men is
"vitally necessary" to meet the "ever declining roster of members a nd the
ever-increasing average age of the membership."
In considering this Resolution, your Committee recognizes a primary
duty to Freemasonry, and a secondary d uty to D eMolay.
One cannot select, by any means known to Masonry, many who most need
exposure to M asonry. On the other hand , DeMolay is allowed, yes, urged, to
select and invite boys and young men to join. This is but one of the numerous
reasons why Freemasonry should not only support, but protect, the Order
of D eMolay.
Because of o ur interest in and support of DeMolay we should at least
survey some of the probable effec ts on DeMolay, and will discuss these first.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

287

U nder DeMolay law, a Master Mason can be a chaperon of a co-educational group on a trip. It can be seriously questioned whether a young man of
eighteen even though a Master Mason is suitable for such responsibility.
A DeMolay remains such until his twenty-first birthday. If he becomes
a Mason at 18 he is a mem ber of both institutions and has concurrent obligations to both. Also, we a re advised that D eMolays generally do not want a
Mast er Mason presiding over their chapter as Master Counselor - what
they want and need are Master Mason advisors.
It is reliably reported to your Committee that the Grand Master of
D eMolay is opposed to the concept of reducing the age limit.
The older age group of DeMolay ( 18 - 21) have special training programs
and activities in their p riories. Eleven priories have been established in
Southern California, one in Northern California - and more may be established. Their purposes are especially constructive, a nd should not be obstructed
by obligations to the affairs of a Masonic Lodge.
A Master Mason by custom is addressed as " Dad" by DeMolays. It
would appear anachronistic for a 19 year old DeMolay to call an 18 year old
" Dad", and would tend to degrade the respect intended, or to impair the
custom.
We t urn now, to the direct subject of the effect of the p roposed a ge reduction on Freemasonry.
Historical references do not reveal any Ancient ch arges, Landmarks or old
Constitutions, which specify the age in years requi red for initiation. Various
terms appear, such as "mature and discreet," " lawful age," " adult." Coil, in
his Masonic Encyclopedia states that lawful age means the age of maturit y
fixed by civil law unless there is a special Masonic rule.
The Regulations of 1663 contain the following: "6. That no person shall
be accepted, unless he be twenty-one years old or more. " Cal. Masonic Code,
Appendix, p. 34 7.
General Regulation IV of 1723 required t he petitioner to be 25 years of
a ge and that remained in effect until 1756. Even then a son of a Mason was
admitted at age 18. That is provided in the Constitution of the Grand Lodge
of Scotland, and the Grand Lodge of England permits it by special dispensation. It may be noted that George Washington was received at the age of
20 years and 8 months.
T he origi nal Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Californa adopted
April 19, 1850, made no mention of qualifications for Masonic membership.
The fi rst specific reference to a ge by the legislation of the Grand Lodge
of California with which your Committee is familiar, is Grand Master Wells'
decision in 1902, adopted by Grand Lodge, and codified as annotation 511 a,
C.M.C.
T urning now to the reasons advanced by the proponents of the Resolution, you r committee fi rmly rejects as a valid reason a need for new members. Firmly, and perpe t ually, rooted in Freemasonry is quality of membership, not quantity .
