PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The fact that by civil law today a young man reaches his "majority" for
some , but not all purposes, at 18, or that he has served in the armed forces,
is relevant, but not persuasive.
The civil law has fluctuated.
California Statutes in 1854 provided that mal es shall be deemed of full
and legal age when they shall be twenty-one years old , and females shall be
deemed of full and legal age when they shall be eighteen years old.
The Civil Code of Caliiornia in 1955 made the age 21 applicable to both
males and females.
At some point along the way, 18 year olds, male or female, if lawfully
married, were considered as reaching their majority.
By amendment in 1971 ":Minors are all persons under 18 years of age."
Civil Code of Cal. § 25. However, a ddi tional sections make it clear tha t a
person of 18 does not possess all the benefits or obligations which a person of
21 has.
The fact that a young man of 18 can handle a rifle or a grenade, understand and follow orders, and whether a volunteer or a draftee willingly ri sk,
or forfeit, his life for his country, does not in itself qualify him mentall y fo r the
philosophy of Masonry. Boys much younger can ha ndle firearms, manage
a vessel, and perform technical tasks.
In the age bracket of 18 to 21, young men ar e still in DeMolay, many
are in college and b elong to fraternities. As pointed out above, to accept
those eligible for D eM olay would encroach upon, and destructively cause
confusion in that Order; aside from D el\Iolay, young men in col1ege, especially away from home, might find themselves members of Lodges distant
from their ultimate residences, if, indeed, they had the fund s for a<lmission
in the college location. Moreover, does Masonry desire to compete with, or
usurp, college fraternities?
Granting that physical maturity is present at the age of 18, that does
not fulfill the qualifications for Masonic affiliation .
The crux of the test is mental, moral and spiritual maturity. That is t o
say, an ability to absorb, comprehend, and respond to, the teaching of Masonry. The civil law says nothing about moral or spiritual capacity. By implication only, does it recognize mental maturity. W e are talking about the
average man, neither the genius nor the imbecile. Although a male 18 years
old today may be possessed of more facts than his predecessor of 100 or 200
years ago, it does not follow that he is more mentally, morally, or spiritually
mature. Actually, a century or two ago, the youth were forced into the realities
of life the need to study, to work, the need to accept responsibilities, much
more ~han they are at the same age today. Their conveniences and facilities
were meager, their life expectancy shorter - they had to be men by the time
they reached 18. Yet they were not regarded as rt-aching a majority before the
a ge of 21.

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

289

We acknowledge that despite the general p revalence of moral laxity , and
depression in ch urch membership, there are many young men of 18 who are
morally a nd spiritually good - witness DeMolay.
The rituals of Del\lolay and of college fraternities and the ritual of Freemasonry are the essential foundations for the organizations. Without them,
either would be just anot her associat ion. And when you compare the rit uals,
you find the Masonic ritual so different and so far advanced, that the mental
capacity to learn and gai n from either of the others does no t establish that at
the same time the person is ready for the l\Iasonic ritual and the teachings
therei n contained.
For the pu rposes of possessing the requisite in telligence and informa t ion
necessa ry to vote at the age of 18, your committee takes no issue. T he civil
law has not yet recognized that they are qualified to consume alcoholic beverages. Presumably that "privilege" must await some kind of additional
maturity.
It is ou r position that the th ree years elapsing between the ages of 18
and 21 a re essential for the maturity necessary to benefit from , and cont ribute t o, Freemasonry.

adop tion of Resolution No. 12, but for the reasons stated, the majority of
the Committee on Policy a nd General Purposes recommends a "No" volt-.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General Purposes:

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 14 proposes a change in the present regulations concerning jurisdiction of Lodges in accepting applications for the degrees of Masonry. Specifically, the existing residential qualification of six months within
the jurisdiction of a Lodge would no longer be required. The requirement
of residing within the jursdiction of the Grand Lodge for a twelve-month
period would be r.etained.
This resolution would therefore permit an applicant to petition any Lodge
of his choice within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge, after the residential
time requirement has been met.
Section 517 of the California Masonic Code requires that an applicant
for the degrees must have been a resident within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge during twelve months, and within the jurisdiction of the Lodge during
six months next preceding the date of his application, together with certain
exceptions as noted in the California Mar;onic Code.
Section 518 deals with concurrent jurisdiction whereby if two or more
Lodges are located within the corporate limits of any city, town, or place, any
of these Lodges can receive and act on an application for degrees of a resident.
This proposal would simplify the jurisdiction provisions of the California
Masonic Code by eliminating the confusion which now exists in the interpretation of such items as normal jurisdiction, concurrent jurisdiction, and extended "ten-mile rule" jurisdiction. Variances in jurisdiction would be eliminated by providing uniform jurisdiction applicable to all applicants for the
degrees.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Section 529g requires that members of an Investigating Committee must
be members of the Lodge to which an application is made.
To expedite the timely investigation of such a candidate, Resolution No.
14 would provide for a cou rtesy investigation to be made by another Lodge
close to the applicant's residence, the investigation report to be made with
the same scrutiny and dili~ence as if the applicant was applying to the Lodge
of which the Investigating Committee a re members.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is in agreement with the
intent of this resolution.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 14, and the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

date of his initiation as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall direct the
Secretary to forward to such candidate, either by registered letter or
certified mail, with return receipt requested, deposited in the U.S. Post
Office, addressed to him at his last known address, a notice advising him

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

299

that unless he shall present himself for advancement, on or before a specified date (at least sixty days in advance) his fees for the unconferred
degrees and all of his previous contributions will be declared forfeited."
However, when the amendment to this Section 546 was reprinted in the
1972 Supplement to the California Masonic Code, the second and third paragraphs of that section were inadvertently omitted. They rightfully are a part
of that section and read as follows:
"On the date specified, the Master shall declare the fees forfeited
unless further time shall have been granted by a vote of the Lodge.
A candidate thus denied advancement shall be considered only as an
Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft with the right of applying for the
remaining Degree or Degrees, and paying the fees and contributions
therefor, subject to investigation and election, the same as any other
candidate."
Resolution No. 17 now proposes to change the time limitation in the first
paragraph of this Section 546 from five years to three years.
After careful consideration it is the opinion of the Policy and General
Purposes Committee that the proposed change should be made, for the shorter
period seems to be sufficient time for the candidate to qualify for advancement.
However, the Policy and General Purposes Committee believes that the
Master and Secretary should not take the action authorized by the first
paragraph of Section 546 until after a careful investigation has been made
as to why the candidate has failed to qualify for the Degree or Degrees involved.
We are informed that the Committee on Jurisprudence concurs in this
viewpoint and, ,w ith the approval of the signers of Resolution No. 17, will
draft the required legislation to effect the foregoing.
Therefore, I move the adoption of the resolution and the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This Resolution proposes to red uce the time limit within which a candidate must present himself qualified for the Second and Third Degrees from
the date of bis initiation as an Entered Apprentice as presently provided by
Section 546 of the California Masonic Code.
Your Committee notes that the proponents of this Resolution have approved a recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that an additional sentence be added at the end of the first paragraph of
Section 546 relating to the appointment of a Committee by the Master to
investigate and report to the Master why the Candidate had not so presented
himself qualified for the Degree or Degrees involved. In addition, it is noted
that when the amendment to Section 546 was printed in the 1972 Supplement
to the California Masonic Code the second and third paragraphs of the Section were inadvertently omitted. These paragraphs should be added to the
19 73 Supplement.

"Section 546. Forfeiture of Fees. If a candidate does not present himself
qualified for the Second and Third Degrees within a period of three years from
the date of his initiation as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall direct
the Secretary to forward to such candidate either by registered letter or certified mail, with return receipt requested, deposited in the U.S. Post Office,
addressed to him at his last known address, a notice advising him that unless
he shall present himself for advancement, on or before a specified date (at
least sixty days in advance) his fees for the unconferred degrees and all of
his previous contributions will be declared forfeited.
The foregoing action shall not be taken by the Master or Secretary, however, until after the Master has appointed a committee of two or more members of the Lodge to investigate and report back to the Master why the candidate has not presented himself qualified for the Degree or Degrees involved.
On the date specified, the Master shall declare the fees forfeited unless
further time shall have been granted by a vote of the Lodge.
A candidate thus denied advancement shall be considered only as an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft with the right of applying for the remaining Degree or Degrees, and paying the fees and contributions therefore,
subject to investigation and election, the same as any other candidate."

(19)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and Genera l Purposes, and on F inance:

WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code presently provides for life
memberships in constituent Lodges on a fixed fee basis only; and
WHEREAS, junior members are generally not in a financial position to
take advantage of a life membership because of the high dollar level which
most such memberships currently require; and
WHEREAS, senior members are often reluctant to buy a life membership
because the annual dues equivalen t is unrealistically high with respect to life
expectancy; and
WHEREAS, many Lodges are called upon to suspend for non-payment or
to remit dues of senior members who, in retirement, must live on sharply
reduced income ; and
WHEREAS, it would be in the interests of both Lodges and members to
plan for life memberships made attracti ve by sound financing of such; and
WHEREAS, other organizations are exp eriencing success and satisfaction
with life membership progra ms of the type proposed herein ; therefore
BE IT RESOLVED that the Grand Lodge adopt in principle the concept
of life memberships in constituent Lodges based on actuarial data as incorporated in life annuities; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the program devised reflect the following considerations:
a. Optional with individual Lodges, but if adopted, it shall be the only
life membership program ;
b. Use of uniform actuarial table by participating Lodges;
c. Protection of the individual's life membership status in the event of
Lodge merger or dissolution; and

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
Resolution No. 19 contains first a proposal for affirmative action on the
part of Grand Lodge by way of adopting a policy, and second that the recommendation be referred for study and action to certain Grand Lodge Committees including the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The policy proposed is in substance that Grand Lodge adopt in principle
the concept that life membership fees may, at the option of a Lodge, be ba~d
upon a uniform actuarial table, and that the program also assure protection
for the individual's life membership status "in the event of Lodge merger or
dissolution."
This Resolution having been referred by the Grand Master to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, the latter has made a careful study,
and here offers its report on the merits of the policy proposed.
Adoption by a Lodge of the plan proposed would be in contrast to the
present C.M.C. Section 573 which provides that whe~ dues are $ 1.2.00 the
minimum life membership fee shall be $250, and that 1f dues are higher the
life membership shall be proportionately higher .
The objective of the present formula by which the life membership is
approximately 20 times the annual dues theoretically is to provide that a
conservative investment income will assure the Lodge of a return approximately equivalent to the dues. As the fund grows, this sometimes is achieved,
but due to restrictions on investments, it has not a lways worked out, and some
L odges do not encourage life memberships.
We presume that the proponents refer to an actuarial table as a computation of life expectancy. For a given amount of life insu rance a younger man

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

304

305

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

pays smaller premiums than an older man because the younger one is expected to make more payments during his lifetime.
When you relate that to a life membership in a Lodge, which is paid in
cash at one time, the younger man would pay a greater sum than the older
man. But, as pointed out in the Resolution, junior members are generally not
in a position to take advantage of a life membership. The Resolution makes
mention also that senior members are often reluctant to buy a life membership because the annual dues equivalent is unrealistically high with respect
to life membership.
It would appear that the rationale of the proponents is that somewhere
in between, when a man's economic condition is favorable, and the price is
right, he would be inclined to buy the life membership.
Your committee does not favor this Resolution for a number of reasons:
First, the uniform practice has been, and continues to be, that annual
dues of a Lodge are the same for all members regardless of age.
Second, the proposal for life membership on an actuarial basis is made
optional, and we believe that the dues structure should be the same for all
Lodges.
Third, the actuarial basis would present complications which many
Lodges would find it difficult to solve.
Fourth and finally, the fluctuation and especially the historical average
devaluation of the dollar, could place the Lodge at a distinct disadvantage in
the future, if the prevailing price of life memberships were made sufficiently
attractive that a large proportion of the membership purchased them.
In order to place the Resolution before Grand Lodge, I move the adoption
of Resolution No. 19, but for reasons stated, the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence in the recommendation
of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated that no legislative language would
be required to accomplish the intent of the proponents.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The C om.mittee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has studied in detail the
considerati ons which brought the matter of dues remissions to the attention
of this Grand Lodge. The subject is a difficult matter to deal with because
it seems to involve the tenets of Masonry where the duty to "aid and assist"
becomes apparent; however, in the opinion of this Committee this Resolution
does not in any way affect the duty of a Lodge - being, a~ it is, a certain
nu~b~r of brethren duly assembled to assist a deserving brother by the
rem1ss1on of accrued and current dues where inability to pay is established .
The Resolution does provide, however, that except in those marginal cases
where .payment of dues is possible only by creating hardship in meeting other
financial burdens, "need" shall be the sole basis for remission and that
continu~ng remission shall depend entirely upon continuing need.
~e~t1on S7 ~ of the .~alifornia Masonic Code deals with the subject of dues
rem1ss1on b.ut its pr?v1s1ons, as they now stand, make the act of remission by
the Lodge m some mstances a matter of reward for Masonic services to the
Lodge, or as the result. of a certain number of years of membershi p or by
reason of an accumulati on of years in age; all three of which are reasons far
removed from the basic reason for the practice of remission - which is the
inability to pay dues; in one word, "Need."
With the cooperatio n of Lodge Secretaries , a study on the subject of the
average a ge of ~ur membe~ship in t his Grand Jurisdictio n was completed as
recently as Apnl 30 of this year. Among other vital statistics it indicated
that 74.73% of our members are SO or more years of age and that less than
3 ,000 members, or 1.38%, are less than 30 years of age. When three of every
four members of Lodges in this Jurisdictio n are SO or more years of age it is
reasonable to assume that completely justified remissions will also increase
proportion ately to age increase. It becomes critically important therefore
1
that remissions not justified by present and continuing need are eliminated'.
The annual reports of the Grand Secretary will show that with a loss of
practically 18,000 members in the 9-year period from 1964 to 1972 the
1
numbe r of remissions per year increased from 3S04 in 1964 to 3871 in 1972
and in the 1973 report has reached a total of 3921. Fewer members but more
remissions indicates that our Lodges are granting remission of dues more or
less automatica lly and without proper annual review, or on some basis far
removed from the condition which remission of dues was designed to ameliorate; namely "Need."
Annotation (h) of Section 577 of the C.l\I.C. is recommend ed for deletion
in this Resolution only because its purpose at origin anrl in current use is in
relation to remissions for reasons other than that of need. It presents very
eloquent!~, however, the privilege and duty of every Mason to help meet the
costs of his Lodge and of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdictio n when given by
th.e Supreme Grand Master of the Universe the ability to do so. Whether in
~.Jtual or Law an~ with the elimination of the specific references to considerations of age, serVIce or length of membershi p, this Committee believes that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

307

this definition of right and duty should be retained.

vote on Resolution No. 20.

REMIT DUES FIFTY YEAR MEMBERS
(22)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, these brethren who have had fifty year membership in this
jurisdiction only and have paid their dues regularly for this time, and
WHEREAS, there are many fifty year members of this jurisdiction who
are unable to pay dues freely because of fixed income, age increase cost of
living, ill health, unable to attend lodge and other hardships, and
WHEREAS, this is a practice of many other Grand Lodge jurisdictions
to remit dues to fifty year members with no cost to their Lodge or Grand
Lodge thus giving notice that when a member receives this commendation it
creates a deep satisfaction to others to reach this goal, and
WHEREAS, they deserve this recognition and be free of dues, if they wish
to donate to the Masonic Homes Endowment, other youth organizations,
charities if they so desire instead, and
WHEREAS, these monies were donated in many cases when monies were
more plentiful and easy to come by, instead of taking a life membership, and
WHEREAS, the remission of dues to fifty year members would add an
incentive and avoid disappointment to our brethren attaining fifty years
of Masonry and improve their image in the community, of which he lives and
equal to fifty year membership in the Order of the Eastern Star of which he
could be a member also, and
WHEREAS, the feeling of the brother who has reached this achievement.
is in his heart more gratified that he has obtained this recognition and just
reward , and
WHEREAS, his past membership, efforts, feelings and gratitude have been
finally rewarded.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the necessary deletions
additions and amendments be made to appropriate sections of the Californi~
Masonic Code to provide for automatic remission of said dues in advance to
all Master Masons under this jurisdiction only, who have received or enti~led
to receive a fifty year button, from the Grand Lodge of California.
Respectfully submitted,
HoNALD C. FRANDSEN, P.11!., No. 4Sl

STUDY ESTABLISHMENT OF MASONIC
HISTORICAL SITES
(23)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, with the passage of time the opportunity for acquisition,
restoration and preservation of significant and important Masonic historical
sites becomes less possible as such sites deteriorate, are destroyed or become
unavailable due to other usage, and
WHEREAS, ~ith the same passage of time the importance and value of
preservation of much that remains to remind us of our Masonic heritage is
increasingly important, and
WHEREAS the Grand Lodge of California, despite some significant ac.
'
complishments of historical site preservation, such as the Masomc Tem~le
at Columbia and the old Masonic Hall at Los Angeles, has no clear pohcy
with respect to the acquisition, restoration and preservation of Masonic historical sites, and
WHEREAS, without the establishment of policy valuable time and opportunity may be forever lost,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the policy of the Grand
Lodge of California for the acquisition, restoration and preservation of Masonic Historical Sites be as follows:
I. The Grand Lodge of California desires to restore and preserve, whenever possible, buildings and related sites which have important historical significance and which will portray to present and future generations examples and reminders of our heritage, both as to important
events and fraternal environment.

~OW T!"fEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Grand Lodge of Califorma permit the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau to reinstitute the employment activities.

authorized to establish Employment Bureaus as a needed service to the Craft.
The expense incurred for the operations of such Employment Bureaus were
generally subsidized by Grand Lodge.
After a detailed review of the experience of the Masonic Employment
Bureaus, the Board of Con trol, who supervise the operations and activities
of the Masonic Service Bureaus, recommended to the Grand Master that all
Employment Bureaus be discontinued. The study indicated that placements
by the Bureaus reached a peak of 18,368 in 1941 a t a cost per placement of
$ 1.76. Some 25,000 jobs were offered by employers. The study further revealed
that since 1948 there had been a steady decline in the number of placements
and of positions offered by employers while the cost per placement had increased sharply. During the fiscal year 1966 the placements as well as th e
number of positions offered through the Employment Bureaus were down to
their lowest level since the establishment of the Bureaus. This decline paralleled the rapid growth and extensions of the free state employment services.
The cost per placement in 1966 ranged from $53. 70 to a high of $261.37.
The Grand Master concluded that the need for the services of Employment Bureaus had so diminished as to make their further maintenance no
longer necessary or feasible and discontinued their operations as of June 30,
1967. This ac tion was subsequently approved by Grand Lodge. The directive
did not, nor was intended to precl ude Masonic Service Bureaus from making
job referrals, where available.
It is well recognized that the Employment Bureaus in concept and performance had exemplified the finest tradition of our Craft and contributed to
the image of Freemasonry and possibly its service cannot be measured in
dollars and cents.
The employment situation, however, at the present time is rather stable
and si milar to that which existed in 1967 and which prompted the dissolution
of the Employment Bureaus. To now increase the operational costs of our
Service Bureaus to take on t he added responsibilities of an employment
bureau cannot be justified merely because the Los Angeles l\lasonic Service
Bureau has sufficient assets to maintain such facilities without subsidy from
the Grand Lodge. To permit t he re-establishmen t of a ~Iasonic Employment
Office in the Los Angeles l\lasonic Service Bureau only on the basis of adequate funds would destroy the uniformity of all Service Bureaus which we
have so earnestly sought to preserve.
I move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes ~ecommends a " No" vote.

Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and to the Board
of Control:

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to permit the Los Angeles Masonic Service
Bureau to reinstate the employment activities.
Historically, the Employment Service Bureau was established in the Los
Angeles l\fasonic Service Bureau, formerly the Masonic Board of Relief in
1906. Subsequently, four other Boards in the larger metropolitan areas ~ere

The Board of Control:
Your Board of Control to whom Resolution No. 24 has been referred has
considered it point by point. We would from the very first, point out that this
resolution, if adopted, pertains only to the Los Angeles Masonic Service
Bureau, and thus would by its own language be discriminatory toward the
other eighteen Masonic Service Bureaus in this Grand Lodge jurisdiction. This

316

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

legislation in itself would not be conducive to your Board of Control exercising a standardization of the work within the Masonic Service Bureaus, as
now required by Section 263, C.M.C.
This resolution would also establish the Los Angeles Masonic Service
Bureau as the sole Bureau responsible for rendering "employment assistance
to all Brother Masons and dependents, regardless of their geographic area."
We are of the opinion that this would create an untenable situation for the
operation of the other eighteen Bureaus.
Each of us should be ever mindful of the continuing need to assist any
worthy brother Master Mason, his widow and orphans in any time of need
and at this point in time your Board of Control has not been presented with
any report whereby the action of Most Worshipful Laurence E. Dayton,
P.G.M. and this Grand Lodge in 1967 in discontinuing the Masonic Employment Bureaus has created a disservice to the members of the fraternity.
\Ve commend the brethren who have submitted this resolution for their
concern in this area, but suggest that existing governmental employment
services be utilized insofar as possible until documentation can be presented
that such services are not fulfilling the need of the fraternity.
We move the adoption of this resolution, but recommend a "No" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

IN GRAND LODGE
Friday, October 12, 1973
At 9:30 A.M. Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding.
This session was raised by Worshipful William A. Swift, Master of Summit
Lodge No. 112 and Worshipful Robert P. Torp, Master of San Pedro Lodge
No. 332. The invocation was delivered by the Grand Chaplain. The minutes
of the morning and afternoon sessions of Thursday, October 11, 19 73 were
read and approved.

ANNUAL ELECTION
The Grand Master announced that the hour had arrived for the Annual
Election and directed the Grand Secretary to read the sections of the Constitution applying thereto.
The R :.w:.Raymond A. Ebbage, Capital City Lodge No. 499, was
elected Grand Master.
The R: .w: .Burton Meyer, Jr., Golden State Lodge No. 358, was elected
Deputy Grand Master.
The R: .W." .John F. Roberts, Jr., Palo Alto Lodge No. 346, was elected
Senior Grand Warden.
The
.Kermit A. Jacobson, Carmelita Lodge No. 599, was elected
Junior Grand Warden.
The M." .w: .Chester R . MacPhee, Past Grand Master, Golden West
Lodge No. 455, was reelected Grand Treasurer.
The l\·L :.w:.Edward H . Siems, Past Grand Master, Plymouth Lodge
No. 560, was reelected Grand Secretary.
The v:.w:.H. Douglas Lemons, Bixby Knolls Lodge No. 699, was
reelected Grand Lecturer.

Pursuant to emergent legislation adopted by Grand Lodge Thursday,
October 11, 1973, Grand Lodge was called off for the purpose of admitting
Masons and friends to witness the first "open" installation of Grand Lodge
officers in the history of the Grand Lodge.

INSTALLATION OF OFFICERS
Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith, Past Grand Master, acted as Master
of Ceremonies and the officers, elected and appointed, were installed by the
retiring Grand Master in accordance with the Ritual.
The retiring Grand Master then presented the Grand Master's lapel pin
to the incumbent Grand Master and the other chair officers exchanged the
Arthur S. Crites lapel pins.
The Worshipful Harlan Huebner presented to the newly installed Grand
Orator, Walker S. Kisselburgh, the Grand Orator's pin.
The newly retiring Grand Master presented to Most Worshipful Raymond
A. Ebbage the Grand Master's jewel. Eugene S. Hopp, Past Grand Master,
in turn presented to the Junior Past Grand Master, William H. Price, a certificate evidencing his having served as Grand Master. Past Grand Master
Theodore Meriam then presented him with a Past Grand :Master's apron.

326

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Past Grand Master Lester S. McElwain presented the retiring Grand Master
with a Past Grand Master's lapel pin. The pin was presented as a token of
appreciation for the services which the Grand Master rendered to them from
the Trustees of our Masonic Homes.
Most Worshipful Chester R. MacPhee, on behalf of the members of
Grand Lodge, presented a gift to the new Past Grand Master for his wife,
J ane. Most Worshipful William H . Price, on her behalf, expressed their appreciation for this thoughtful gift.
Following proclamation of the installation, newly installed Grand Master
Raymond A. Ebbage expressed his humility for having been elected to this
high Masonic office and his appreciation to the Brethren for this indication
of their confidence in him and his pledge for devoted service to the fraternity.
He introduced and welcomed a large number of friends and Brethren who
had traveled from Sacramento and elsewhere to witness the installation.
At 1: 10 P.M., all business being completed, Grand Lodge closed in
due form.

Summary of Accounting Policies
The more important accounting pol icies are s ummarized as

follows:
Basis of Accounting
The fina n cial sta tements are stat ed o n a mo difi ed cash b a si s
of a c c o unting.

Generall y , re v e n u es are recorded at the time o f rece ipt

and exp e nses are accrued at y e ar end.
Inves t ments
I nvestments in securi t ies purchased are reco rded at cost
and securities received by gift or bequest a re reco r d ed at appr oximate
market v a l ue o n the date received.
0t~~

Th e s e assets

a re r ecorded at the n ominal val ue o f $ l each for a ccountabi l ity.
Payments by t he Homes of ob l i g ations of the assignors secu red by thes e
asset s are added t o t he nominal v a l ue , with t he exception o f life
insurance premiums which ar e ch arged t o expense when paid.
Pro per ty
Larid, b u ildin gs and equ i pment are r ecord ed a t o riginal c o st
and no d eprec i ation is take n.

Pensions
A pension plan has been establis hed covering all
fulltime employees. The total pension expense for the years
ended June 30 , 1973 and 1972 , was approximately $71,000 and
$64,000, respectively . All prior ser vice and current service
costs have been funded.
Federal ~ fil.ill ~ on Income
The Homes is exempt from fede r al a nd state taxes
on income.

assigned to the Homes by residents of Decoto and from r eal
es tat e received as gifts or bequests by Homes.

and mineral rights assign ed or bequeathed t o t he Homes.

385

Al tenburq Fund
This fund is used to provide loans to stude nts.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
The Foundation was established on January 11, 1969 ,
primarily for charitable, educational and scientific purposes.
Currently the income from the general fund is u sed for student
scholarships.
Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are presented on a modified
cash basis of accounting. Generally, reven ues are recorded at
the time of receipt and expenses are accrued at year end.
Investments
Investments in securities purchased are recorded at
cost and securities received by gift or bequest are recorded
at approximate market value on the date received.
Federal Excise Taxes
The Foundation is exempt from federal and state income
taxe s but is subject to a 4% excise tax on its net investment
income.
S ale of Real Property
The Masonic Clubhouse at the University of California
at Los Angeles, together with a related oil and gas lease, were
sold on February 9, 1973, for $ 550,000. The Foundation received
a promissory note f o r $ 480,000 and cash for the balance, whi c h,
after payment of costs o f the sale, amounted to$ 38, 7 20.
The
n o te is secured by a deed of trust and is payable in installments
to February 9, 1988.

l"Jnaranth Fund
During 1972 the Fou ndation received $ 115, 000 in ca s h
and was assigned a promissory note, secured by a deed of trust,
for $ 102,791 f rom the l"Jnaranth Homes of California.
The us e of
these funds is restricted by a trust agreemen t with the l"Jnaranth
Homes o f California which specifies that the principal is to be
invested and that the income is to b e used to provide educa tional
grants to women under age 21.
